metadata.title: Dynamically syndetic sets and the combinatorics of syndetic, idempotent filters

extraction_notes.note: The 'if' direction of Theorem 3.18 is proved in running text spread over Sections 3.3.1-3.3.7 (shift-punch machinery). It is represented as two prose proof parts (setup at the start of 3.3.7, conclusion after Theorem 3.32), linked by a continuation uses edge, plus the 3.3.1 outline as an alternative proof sketch; the 'only if' direction is the proof environment.

The proof-sketch rule asks for rigor: semi_formal on the sketch, but the rigor rule (and the finishing step) forbid rigor on proof nodes; rigor was dropped and the sketch's proves edge carries alternative: true.
Remark 5.10 is an alternative combinatorial proof of PS ⊆ dPS in Theorem 5.9; retyped as proof with an alternative proves edge (remark is the other option).

The text says Theorems C and D follow from Theorems 4.7 and 4.8 'respectively', but C (pointwise recurrence) matches 4.8 and D (dynamical thickness) matches 4.7; the combining sentence is one proof node proving both.

Many introduction statements are restated in the body; one node was kept and the other copy put in also_stated_at. The definition of dynamically thick sets is word-for-word identical in Sections 1.2 and 4.1, so the first occurrence is the node.
The node starts after a sentence ending in closing TeX quotes (finite sums.''), which the finishing step reads as mid-sentence; the boundary is a real sentence start.

Lists of 'quick to check' facts about dual families, ⊓ and filters, attributed to Choquet/Schmidt; each list is one external claim node, not one node per item, since the items are referenced only collectively or by \eqref to an item label.

Section 1.1.4 (a peek into the proofs), motivational and organizational prose, the containment figure, and discussion paragraphs around open questions (except explicitly posed questions) were not made nodes.
Remaining defined-term warnings are other-sense matches (uniformly recurrent, pairwise disjoint sets, minimal ultrafilters, strongly central) and were left without edges.

metadata.extraction_comment: Edge pass 2 (defined terms) was generated from the definiendum lists chosen for each definition, mirroring the finishing step's term matching (plus plural 'sets of'), and accounts for most uses edges.

nodes.section: 1.1.2 The main result: a characterization of dynamically syndetic sets

nodes.name: Theorem A: characterization of dynamically syndetic sets
nodes.statement: Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. The following are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item The set $A$ is dynamically syndetic. \item There exists a nonempty subset $B \subseteq A$ that satisfies: for all finite $F \subseteq B$, the set $\bigcap_{f \in F} (B-f)$ is syndetic. \item There exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ for which the set $A - n$ belongs to a syndetic, idempotent filter on $\mathbb{N}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 1.1.2 The main result: a characterization of dynamically syndetic sets
nodes.statement_short: A set is dynamically syndetic iff it has a nonempty subset B with all finite intersections of translates B-f syndetic iff some translate lies in a syndetic idempotent filter.
conclusions: The following are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item The set $A$ is dynamically syndetic. \item There exists a nonempty subset $B \subseteq A$ that satisfies: for all finite $F \subseteq B$, the set $\bigcap_{f \in F} (B-f)$ is syndetic. \item There exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ for which the set $A - n$ belongs to a syndetic, idempotent filter on $\mathbb{N}$. \end{enumerate}
equivalent_conditions: The set $A$ is dynamically syndetic.
There exists a nonempty subset $B \subseteq A$ that satisfies: for all finite $F \subseteq B$, the set $\bigcap_{f \in F} (B-f)$ is syndetic.
There exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ for which the set $A - n$ belongs to a syndetic, idempotent filter on $\mathbb{N}$.
nodes.label: mainthm_ds_equivalents

nodes.name: Proof that (1.1) is not dynamically syndetic
nodes.statement: Let us use it to see that the set in \eqref{eqn_intro_even_odd}, call it $A$, is not dynamically syndetic. If $B \subseteq A$ satisfies the condition in \eqref{item_intro_ds_combo_condition}, then it must be syndetic. Every syndetic subset of $A$, in particular, $B$, must contain both an even integer, $b_0$, and an odd integer, $b_1$. It is quick to see, however, that the set $(A - b_0) \cap (A-b_1)$ is not syndetic, contradicting what we had supposed about $B$.
nodes.section: 1.1.2 The main result: a characterization of dynamically syndetic sets
nodes.statement_short: Any B as in Theorem A(ii) is syndetic, so contains an even and an odd element; the intersection of the corresponding translates of A is not syndetic.

nodes.name: Kennedy-Raum-Salomon characterization of dynamically syndetic sets
nodes.statement: In the context of the positive integers, it is a consequence of their result that a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is dynamically syndetic if and only if there exists $B \subseteq A$ such that for all finite $F_1 \subseteq B$ and $F_2 \subseteq \mathbb{N} \backslash B$, the set \begin{align}\ \bigcap_{f_1 \in F_1} \big(B - f_1\big) \cap \bigcap_{f_2 \in F_2} \big((\mathbb{N} \backslash B) - f_2\big) \end{align} is syndetic.
nodes.section: 1.1.2 The main result: a characterization of dynamically syndetic sets
nodes.statement_short: A is dynamically syndetic iff it contains B whose finite intersections of translates of B and of its complement are all syndetic.
conclusions: $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is dynamically syndetic if and only if there exists $B \subseteq A$ such that

nodes.statement: \ \bigcap_{f_1 \in F_1} \big(B - f_1\big) \cap \bigcap_{f_2 \in F_2} \big((\mathbb{N} \backslash B) - f_2\big)
nodes.section: 1.1.2 The main result: a characterization of dynamically syndetic sets
nodes.label: eq:new_B'

nodes.name: KRS condition iff 1_B uniformly recurrent
nodes.statement: It is not hard to see that a set $B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ satisfies the condition in \eqref{eq:new_B'} if and only if its indicator function $1_B$ is a uniformly recurrent point in the full shift $(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}, \sigma)$; see \cref{sec_top_dynamics} for the notation and terminology.

nodes.name: Theorem B: characterization of dynamically central syndetic sets
nodes.statement: Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. The following are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item The set $A$ is dynamically central syndetic. \item There exists a subset $B \subseteq A$ that satisfies: for all finite $F \subseteq B$, the set $B \cap \bigcap_{f \in F} (B-f)$ is syndetic. \item The set $A$ belongs to a syndetic, idempotent filter on $\mathbb{N}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 1.1.2 The main result: a characterization of dynamically syndetic sets
nodes.statement_short: A set is dynamically central syndetic iff it has a subset B with B and all finite intersections of its translates syndetic iff it lies in a syndetic idempotent filter.
conclusions: The following are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item The set $A$ is dynamically central syndetic. \item There exists a subset $B \subseteq A$ that satisfies: for all finite $F \subseteq B$, the set $B \cap \bigcap_{f \in F} (B-f)$ is syndetic. \item The set $A$ belongs to a syndetic, idempotent filter on $\mathbb{N}$. \end{enumerate}

There exists a subset $B \subseteq A$ that satisfies: for all finite $F \subseteq B$, the set $B \cap \bigcap_{f \in F} (B-f)$ is syndetic.
The set $A$ belongs to a syndetic, idempotent filter on $\mathbb{N}$.

nodes.name: Sum of ultrafilters
nodes.statement: For the purposes of this introduction, it suffices to know that $\beta \mathbb{N}$ is a compact Hausdorff space, and that there is a natural way to lift addition from $\mathbb{N}$ to $\beta \mathbb{N}$, turning $\beta \mathbb{N}$ into a semigroup: if $\mathscr{F}$ and $\mathscr{G}$ are ultrafilters, then \begin{align} \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G} \vcentcolon= \Big\{ A \subseteq \mathbb{N} \ \Big| \ \big\{ n \in \mathbb{N} \ \big| \ A - n \in \mathscr{G} \big\} \in \mathscr{F} \Big\} \end{align} is an ultrafilter.
nodes.section: 1.1.3 A new tool: the algebra of idempotent families
nodes.statement_short: The sum of ultrafilters F+G consists of the sets A for which {n : A-n in G} belongs to F.

nodes.name: Sum of families (intro)
nodes.statement: \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G} \vcentcolon= \Big\{ A \subseteq \mathbb{N} \ \Big| \ \big\{ n \in \mathbb{N} \ \big| \ A - n \in \mathscr{G} \big\} \in \mathscr{F} \Big\}
nodes.section: 1.1.3 A new tool: the algebra of idempotent families
nodes.label: eqn_sum_of_families_intro

nodes.name: Canonical idempotent filter of a point
nodes.statement: In the setting of topological dynamics, the canonical example of an idempotent filter is one of the form \begin{align} \mathscr{F} \vcentcolon= \uparrow \big\{ R_T(x,U) \ \big| \ U \subseteq X \text{ is open and contains $x$} \big\}, \end{align} where $x$ is a point in a dynamical system $(X,T)$ and the upward arrow indicates the upward closure of the collection of sets.
nodes.section: 1.1.3 A new tool: the algebra of idempotent families
nodes.statement_short: For a point x of a system, the upward closure of the return-time sets R_T(x,U), U an open neighbourhood of x, is an idempotent filter.

nodes.name: Canonical return-time filter
nodes.statement: \mathscr{F} \vcentcolon= \uparrow \big\{ R_T(x,U) \ \big| \ U \subseteq X \text{ is open and contains $x$} \big\},
nodes.section: 1.1.3 A new tool: the algebra of idempotent families
nodes.label: eqn_canonical_sif

nodes.name: Proof that the canonical filter is idempotent
nodes.statement: That $\mathscr{F}$ is a filter is clear. To see that this is an idempotent filter, one needs only to show and interpret the following: for all open $U \subseteq X$ containing $x$, \[R_T(x,U) \subseteq \big\{n \in \mathbb{N} \ \big| \ R_T(x,U) - n \in \mathscr{F}\big\}.\] If $n \in R_T(x,U)$, then $x \in T^{-n}U$, whereby $R_T(x,U) - n = R_T(x,T^{-n}U)$ is a member of $\mathscr{F}$. Since $R_T(x,U) \in \mathscr{F}$, we see from the inclusion that $\{n \in \mathbb{N} \ | \ R_T(x,U) - n \in \mathscr{F}\} \in \mathscr{F}$, demonstrating that $R_T(x,U) \in \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$. Since every member of $\mathscr{F}$ contains a set of the form $R_T(x,U)$, this shows that $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$.
nodes.section: 1.1.3 A new tool: the algebra of idempotent families
nodes.statement_short: Direct verification: for n in R_T(x,U), R_T(x,U)-n = R_T(x,T^{-n}U) lies in the filter, so R_T(x,U) is in F+F.

nodes.name: Syndetic filter
nodes.statement: A \emph{syndetic filter} is a filter whose members are all syndetic.
nodes.section: 1.1.3 A new tool: the algebra of idempotent families

nodes.name: Canonical filter of a minimal system is syndetic idempotent
nodes.statement: If $(X,T)$ is a minimal system, the filter in \eqref{eqn_canonical_sif} is an example of a syndetic, idempotent filter.
nodes.section: 1.1.3 A new tool: the algebra of idempotent families
conclusions: the filter in \eqref{eqn_canonical_sif} is an example of a syndetic, idempotent filter

nodes.name: Furstenberg: return-time filter of a distal point is C*
nodes.statement: By a theorem of Furstenberg \cite[Thm. 9.11]{furstenberg_book_1981}, if $x$ is a distal point, the filter defined in \eqref{eqn_canonical_sif} is a $\mathcal{C}^*$, idempotent filter.
nodes.section: 1.1.3 A new tool: the algebra of idempotent families
conclusions: the filter defined in \eqref{eqn_canonical_sif} is a $\mathcal{C}^*$, idempotent filter

nodes.name: Dynamically thick set
nodes.statement: A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is \emph{dynamically thick} if for all minimal systems $(X,T)$ and all points $x \in X$, the set $\{T^n x \ | \ n \in A\}$ is dense in $X$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Part II: Dynamically thick sets
nodes.statement_short: A is dynamically thick if every orbit in every minimal system, sampled along A, is dense.

nodes.name: Set of measurable recurrence
nodes.statement: A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is called a \emph{set of measurable recurrence} if in every probability measure preserving system, every set of positive measure recurs at some time in $A$.
nodes.section: 1.2.1 Motivation: set and point recurrence

nodes.name: Szemerédi's theorem
nodes.statement: Szemer\'edi's theorem \cite{Szemeredi-on_the_sets}, a cornerstone of additive combinatorics, states that every set of positive integers of positive upper density contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions.
nodes.section: 1.2.1 Motivation: set and point recurrence

nodes.name: Set of topological recurrence
nodes.statement: A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is a \emph{set of topological recurrence} if for all minimal systems $(X,T)$ and all nonempty, open sets $U \subseteq X$, there exists $n \in A$ such that the set $U \cap T^{-n}U$ is nonempty.
nodes.section: 1.2.1 Motivation: set and point recurrence

nodes.name: Pavlov: zero Banach density sets are not sets of pointwise recurrence
nodes.statement: Indeed, he showed that if a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has zero upper Banach density ($\limsup_{N \to \infty} \max_{n \in \mathbb{N}} |A \cap \{n, \ldots, n + N\}| / N = 0$) then the set $A$ is not a set of pointwise recurrence: there is a totally minimal, totally uniquely ergodic, and topologically mixing system $(X, T)$ and uncountably many points $x \in X$ for which $x \not\in \overline{\{T^n x \ \big| \ n \in A\}}$.
nodes.section: 1.2.1 Motivation: set and point recurrence
assumptions: a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has zero upper Banach density
conclusions: the set $A$ is not a set of pointwise recurrence

nodes.name: Interpolation set for minimal systems
nodes.statement: A set $I \subseteq \mathbb{N}_0$ is \emph{interpolation set for minimal systems} if for every bounded function $f: I \to \mathbb{C}$, there exists a minimal system $(X, T)$, a point $x \in X$, and a continuous function $F: X \to \mathbb{C}$ such that $f(n) = F(T^n x)$ for all $n \in I$.
nodes.section: 1.2.1 Motivation: set and point recurrence
nodes.origin_citation: Glasner & Weiss; Koutsogiannis, Le, Moreira, Pavlov, Richter

nodes.name: Interpolation sets are exactly the non-piecewise-syndetic sets
nodes.statement: It was proved in \cite{Glasner-Weiss-Interpolation, Koutsogiannis_Le_Moreira_Pavlov_Richter_interpolation_sets} that $I \subseteq \mathbb{N}_0$ is an interpolation set for minimal systems if and only if $I$ is not piecewise syndetic.
nodes.section: 1.2.1 Motivation: set and point recurrence
nodes.origin_citation: Glasner & Weiss; Koutsogiannis, Le, Moreira, Pavlov, Richter
conclusions: $I \subseteq \mathbb{N}_0$ is an interpolation set for minimal systems if and only if $I$ is not piecewise syndetic
equivalent_conditions: $I \subseteq \mathbb{N}_0$ is an interpolation set for minimal systems
$I$ is not piecewise syndetic

nodes.name: Interpolation proof that sets of pointwise recurrence are piecewise syndetic
nodes.statement: If $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is not piecewise syndetic, then $I \vcentcolon= A \cup \{0\}$ is not piecewise syndetic, so there is minimal system $(X, T)$, a point $x \in X$, and a continuous function $F: X \to \mathbb{C}$ such that \[ F(T^n x) = \begin{cases} 1 \text{ if } n = 0 \\ 0 \text{ if } n \in A \end{cases}. \] It follows that $A$ is not a set of pointwise recurrence. Contrapositively, a set of pointwise recurrence must be piecewise syndetic, recovering the results in \cite[Prop. 4.4]{dong_shao_ye_2012} and, hence, in \cite[Thm. 2.4]{huang_ye_2005} as well.
nodes.section: 1.2.1 Motivation: set and point recurrence
nodes.statement_short: Contrapositive via interpolation: if A is not piecewise syndetic, interpolate 1 at time 0 and 0 on A to get a point that does not return along A.

nodes.name: Host-Kra-Maass: pointwise recurrence properly contained in topological recurrence
nodes.statement: They observed that the family of sets of pointwise recurrence is properly contained in the family of sets of topological recurrence.
nodes.section: 1.2.1 Motivation: set and point recurrence

nodes.name: Combinatorial characterization of sets of topological recurrence
nodes.statement: There is a useful and well-known combinatorial characterization for sets of topological recurrence (cf. \cite[Thm. 2.4]{bergelson_mccutcheon_1998}): a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is a set of topological recurrence if and only if for all syndetic sets $S' \subseteq S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, the set $A \cap (S - S')$ is nonempty.
nodes.section: 1.2.2 Combinatorial characterizations of dynamically thick sets
conclusions: a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is a set of topological recurrence if and only if for all syndetic sets $S' \subseteq S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, the set $A \cap (S - S')$ is nonempty
equivalent_conditions: a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is a set of topological recurrence
for all syndetic sets $S' \subseteq S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, the set $A \cap (S - S')$ is nonempty

nodes.name: Theorem C: combinatorial characterization of sets of pointwise recurrence
nodes.statement: Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. The following are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item $A$ is a set of pointwise recurrence. \item For all $B \supseteq A$, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq \mathbb{N} \backslash B$ such that the set $B \cup \big( B-F \big)$ is thick. \item For all syndetic $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq A$ such that for all syndetic $S' \subseteq S$, \[F \cap (S - S') \neq \emptyset.\] \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 1.2.2 Combinatorial characterizations of dynamically thick sets
nodes.statement_short: Sets of pointwise recurrence are characterized by thickness of B ∪ (B-F) for supersets B, and by a quantitative intersection condition with S - S'.
conclusions: The following are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item $A$ is a set of pointwise recurrence. \item For all $B \supseteq A$, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq \mathbb{N} \backslash B$ such that the set $B \cup \big( B-F \big)$ is thick. \item For all syndetic $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq A$ such that for all syndetic $S' \subseteq S$, \[F \cap (S - S') \neq \emptyset.\] \end{enumerate}
equivalent_conditions: $A$ is a set of pointwise recurrence.
For all $B \supseteq A$, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq \mathbb{N} \backslash B$ such that the set $B \cup \big( B-F \big)$ is thick.
For all syndetic $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq A$ such that for all syndetic $S' \subseteq S$, \[F \cap (S - S') \neq \emptyset.\]
nodes.label: mainthm_dct_combo_characterizations

nodes.name: Theorem D: combinatorial characterization of dynamically thick sets
nodes.statement: Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. The following are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item $A$ is dynamically thick. \item For all $\mathbb{N} \supsetneq B \supseteq A$, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq \mathbb{N} \backslash B$ such that the set $B-F$ is thick. \item For all piecewise syndetic $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq A$ such that the set $S-F$ is thick. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 1.2.2 Combinatorial characterizations of dynamically thick sets
nodes.statement_short: A is dynamically thick iff every proper superset B has a finite F outside B with B-F thick iff every piecewise syndetic S has finite F in A with S-F thick.
conclusions: The following are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item $A$ is dynamically thick. \item For all $\mathbb{N} \supsetneq B \supseteq A$, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq \mathbb{N} \backslash B$ such that the set $B-F$ is thick. \item For all piecewise syndetic $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq A$ such that the set $S-F$ is thick. \end{enumerate}
equivalent_conditions: $A$ is dynamically thick.
For all $\mathbb{N} \supsetneq B \supseteq A$, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq \mathbb{N} \backslash B$ such that the set $B-F$ is thick.
For all piecewise syndetic $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq A$ such that the set $S-F$ is thick.
nodes.label: mainthm_dt_characterizations

nodes.name: Dynamically thick set from primes and thick sets
nodes.statement: The statement in \cref{mainthm_dt_characterizations} \eqref{item:intro_dyn_thick_idempotent} can be used to produce novel examples of dynamically thick sets, such as \begin{equation} A \vcentcolon= \bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} \big((p_i \mathbb{N} + 1) \cap H_i \big), \end{equation} where $(p_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a sequence of distinct primes and $(H_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ is a sequence of thick sets.
nodes.section: 1.2.2 Combinatorial characterizations of dynamically thick sets
nodes.statement_short: Union over distinct primes p_i of (p_i N + 1) ∩ H_i with H_i thick is dynamically thick.

nodes.name: Prime-progression example set
nodes.statement: A \vcentcolon= \bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} \big((p_i \mathbb{N} + 1) \cap H_i \big),
nodes.section: 1.2.2 Combinatorial characterizations of dynamically thick sets

nodes.name: Recurrent point
nodes.statement: A point $x$ in a dynamical system $(X,T)$ is \emph{recurrent} if for all open $U \subseteq X$ containing $x$, the set $R_T(x,U)$ is nonempty.
nodes.section: 1.2.3 Dynamical thickness in the context of disjointness

nodes.name: Pointwise recurrence of R_T(x,U) and product recurrence
nodes.statement: The following, then, is immediate from the definitions: for all open $U \subseteq X$ containing $x$, the set $R_T(x,U)$ is a set of pointwise recurrence if and only if for all minimal system $(Y,S)$ and all $y \in Y$, the point $(x,y)$ is recurrent in the product system $(X \times Y, T \times S)$.
nodes.section: 1.2.3 Dynamical thickness in the context of disjointness

nodes.name: F_s-PR point
nodes.statement: Dong, Shao, and Ye \cite{dong_shao_ye_2012} call points $x$ with this property \emph{$\mathcal{F}_s$-PR points}.
nodes.section: 1.2.3 Dynamical thickness in the context of disjointness

nodes.name: Theorem E: partition of dynamically central syndetic sets
nodes.statement: Every dynamically central syndetic set can be partitioned into infinitely many, pairwise disjoint dynamically central syndetic sets.
nodes.section: 1.2.3 Dynamical thickness in the context of disjointness
conclusions: can be partitioned into infinitely many, pairwise disjoint dynamically central syndetic sets
nodes.label: mainthm_partition_of_dcs_sets

nodes.name: Joining
nodes.statement: A \emph{joining} of two topological dynamical systems $(X,T)$ and $(Y,S)$ is a nonempty, closed set $Z \subseteq X \times Y$ that satisfies: $(T \times S) Z \subseteq Z$, $\pi_X Z = X$, and $\pi_Y Z = Y$, where $\pi_X, \pi_Y$ are the projections from $X \times Y$ to $X$ and $Y$, respectively.
nodes.section: 1.2.3 Dynamical thickness in the context of disjointness

nodes.name: Disjoint systems
nodes.statement: Furstenberg \cite[Thm. II.2]{Furstenberg-disjointness} defined two topological systems $(X,T)$ and $(Y,S)$ to be \emph{disjoint} if their only joining is $X \times Y$.
nodes.section: 1.2.3 Dynamical thickness in the context of disjointness

nodes.name: Disjointness from minimal systems via dynamically thick return sets
nodes.statement: To relate the notions of disjointness and dynamical thickness, let $(X,T)$ be a system and $x \in X$ be a point with a dense orbit. The following is simple to verify from the definitions: the system $(X,T)$ is disjoint from every minimal system if and only if for all nonempty, open $U \subseteq X$, the set $R_T(x,U)$ is dynamically thick.
nodes.section: 1.2.3 Dynamical thickness in the context of disjointness

nodes.name: Furstenberg: the full shift is disjoint from every minimal system
nodes.statement: Furstenberg proved \cite[Thm. II.2]{Furstenberg-disjointness} that the full shift $(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}, \sigma)$ is disjoint from every minimal system.
nodes.section: 1.2.3 Dynamical thickness in the context of disjointness

nodes.name: Theorem F: structure of dynamically thick sets
nodes.statement: Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. The set $A$ is dynamically thick if and only if there exist a robustly syndetic collection $\mathscr{C}$ of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ and, for each $B \in \mathscr{C}$, a thick set $H_B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that \begin{align} A = \bigcup_{B \in \mathscr{C}} \big( B \cap H_B\big). \end{align}

nodes.name: Theorem G: containments among central and piecewise syndetic families
nodes.statement: Denote by $\mathcal{C}$, $\mathcal{PS}$, $d\mathcal{PS}$, and $dc\mathcal{PS}$ the families of central, piecewise syndetic, dynamically piecewise syndetic, and dynamically central piecewise syndetic sets, respectively. The following inclusions hold: \[ \mathcal{C} \subsetneq dc\mathcal{PS} \subsetneq d\mathcal{PS} = \mathcal{PS}. \] In particular, a set is dynamically piecewise syndetic if and only if it is piecewise syndetic.
nodes.section: 1.3.2 Dynamically piecewise syndetic sets are piecewise syndetic
nodes.statement_short: C ⊊ dcPS ⊊ dPS = PS; dynamically piecewise syndetic equals piecewise syndetic.

nodes.name: Furstenberg-Sárközy theorem
nodes.statement: By a result of Furstenberg \cite{furstenberg_book_1981} and S\'{a}rk\"{o}zy \cite{sarkozy_1978}, the set of perfect squares, for example, is such a set of measurable recurrence.

nodes.name: Set of multiple topological recurrence
nodes.statement: A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is called a \emph{set of multiple topological recurrence} if for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$, all minimal systems $(X, T)$, and all nonempty, open sets $U \subseteq X$, there exists $n \in A$ such that \[ U \cap T^{-n} U \cap \cdots \cap T^{-kn} U \neq \emptyset. \]
nodes.section: 1.3.3 Sets of polynomial recurrence and combinatorial configurations in dynamically central piecewise syndetic sets

nodes.name: Frantzikinakis-Lesigne-Wierdl: recurrence does not imply multiple recurrence
nodes.statement: While it is known that a set of topological recurrence is not necessarily a set of multiple topological recurrence \cite{frantzikinakis_lesigne_wierdl_2006}, Host, Kra, and Maass \cite[Question 2.14]{HostKraMaass2016} asked whether or not a set of pointwise recurrence is a set of multiple topological recurrence.
nodes.section: 1.3.3 Sets of polynomial recurrence and combinatorial configurations in dynamically central piecewise syndetic sets

nodes.name: Set of polynomial multiple measurable recurrence for commuting transformations
nodes.statement: A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is a \emph{set of polynomial multiple measurable recurrence for commuting transformations} if for all $k, \ell \in \mathbb{N}$, all commuting measure preserving systems $(X, \mu, T_1, \ldots, T_k)$ (see \cref{sec_dcps_and_set_recurrence}), all $E \subseteq X$ with $\mu(E) > 0$, and, all polynomials $p_{i,j} \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$ with $p_i(0) = 0$ and $p_i(\mathbb{N}_0) \subseteq \mathbb{N}_0$, $1 \leqslant i \leqslant k$, $1 \leqslant j \leqslant \ell$, there exists $n \in A$ such that \[ \mu\Big( \big(T_1^{p_{1,1}(n)} T_2^{p_{2,1}(n)} \cdots T_k^{p_{k,1}(n)} \big)^{-1} E \cap \cdots \cap \big(T_1^{p_{1,\ell}(n)} T_2^{p_{2,\ell}(n)} \cdots T_k^{p_{k,\ell}(n)} \big)^{-1} E \Big) > 0. \]
nodes.section: 1.3.3 Sets of polynomial recurrence and combinatorial configurations in dynamically central piecewise syndetic sets
nodes.definiendum: set of polynomial multiple measurable recurrence for commuting transformations

nodes.name: Polynomial measurable recurrence implies multiple topological recurrence
nodes.statement: Because any minimal topological dynamical system admits an invariant measure of full support, sets of polynomial multiple measurable recurrence for commuting transformations are sets of multiple topological recurrence.
nodes.section: 1.3.3 Sets of polynomial recurrence and combinatorial configurations in dynamically central piecewise syndetic sets

nodes.name: Theorem H: dcPS sets are sets of polynomial multiple recurrence
nodes.statement: Dynamically central piecewise syndetic sets are sets of polynomial multiple measurable recurrence for commuting transformations.
nodes.section: 1.3.3 Sets of polynomial recurrence and combinatorial configurations in dynamically central piecewise syndetic sets
conclusions: are sets of polynomial multiple measurable recurrence for commuting transformations
nodes.label: thm:dcps_multiple_recurrence

nodes.name: Integers, non-negative and positive integers
nodes.statement: The set of integers, non-negative integers, and positive integers are denoted by $\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathbb{N}_0$, and $\mathbb{N}$, respectively.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Power set of N
nodes.statement: The power set of $\mathbb{N}$ is denoted $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Initial interval [N]
nodes.statement: For $N \in \mathbb{N}_0$, we define $[N]$ to be $\{0, 1, \ldots, N - 1\}$.
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Translates and dilates of a set
nodes.statement: For $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, we define \begin{align*} A+n &\vcentcolon= \{a + n \ | \ a \in A \}, & nA & \vcentcolon= \{ na \ | \ a \in A\}, \\ A-n &\vcentcolon= \{m \in \mathbb{N} \ | \ m + n \in A \}, & A/n & \vcentcolon= \{ m \in \mathbb{N} \ | \ mn \in A\}. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries
nodes.statement_short: Defines A+n, nA, A-n = {m : m+n in A} and A/n = {m : mn in A}, all as subsets of N.

nodes.name: Sumset and difference set
nodes.statement: For $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, we define \begin{align*} A+B &\vcentcolon= \bigcup_{b \in B} (A + b), & A-B &\vcentcolon= \bigcup_{b \in B} (A-b). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 2 Preliminaries

nodes.name: Upward closure
nodes.statement: Let $\mathscr{F}$ be a collection of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$. The \emph{upward closure} of $\mathscr{F}$ is \[\uparrow \mathscr{F} \vcentcolon= \big\{ B \subseteq \mathbb{N} \ \big| \ \exists A \in \mathscr{F}, \ B \supseteq A \big\}.\]
nodes.section: 2.1 Families of positive integers

nodes.name: Upward-closed collection
nodes.statement: The set $\mathscr{F}$ is \emph{upward-closed} if $\mathscr{F} = \uparrow \mathscr{F}$.
nodes.section: 2.1 Families of positive integers

nodes.name: Family
nodes.statement: We will call an upward-closed collection of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ a \emph{family}.
nodes.section: 2.1 Families of positive integers

nodes.name: Proper family
nodes.statement: A family is \emph{proper} if it is neither $\emptyset$ nor $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$, that is, it is both nonempty and does not contain the empty set.
nodes.section: 2.1 Families of positive integers

nodes.name: Dual family
nodes.statement: The \emph{dual} of a family $\mathscr{F}$ of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ is \[\mathscr{F}^* \vcentcolon= \big\{ B \subseteq \mathbb{N} \ \big | \ \forall A \in \mathscr{F}, \ B \cap A \neq \emptyset \big\},\] the collection of all those sets which have nonempty intersection with all elements of $\mathscr{F}$.
nodes.section: 2.1.1 Dual families and intersections

nodes.name: Basic facts on dual families
nodes.statement: The following facts are quick to check and will be used without mention: \begin{enumerate} \item $(\mathscr{F}^*)^* = \mathscr{F}$, whereby it makes sense to say that $\mathscr{F}$ and $\mathscr{F}^*$ are \emph{dual}; \item the empty family $\emptyset$ and $\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$ are dual, while the dual of a proper family is a proper family; \item $A \in \mathscr{F}$ if and only if $\mathbb{N} \backslash A \not\in \mathscr{F}^*$; \item $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{G}$ if and only if $\mathscr{G}^* \subseteq \mathscr{F}^*$.\\ \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 2.1.1 Dual families and intersections
nodes.statement_short: (F*)* = F; the empty family and P(N) are dual; A in F iff complement not in F*; containment reverses under duality.

nodes.name: Family intersection operation
nodes.statement: For nonempty families $\mathscr{F}$ and $\mathscr{G}$, we define \[\mathscr{F} \sqcap \mathscr{G} \vcentcolon= \big\{ A \cap B \ \big| \ A \in \mathscr{F} \text{ and } B \in \mathscr{G} \big\}.\]
nodes.section: 2.1.1 Dual families and intersections

nodes.name: Basic facts on the operation ⊓
nodes.statement: The following facts are quick to check for all families $\mathscr{F}$ and $\mathscr{G}$: \begin{enumerate} \setcounter{enumi}{4} \item the collection $\mathscr{F} \sqcap \mathscr{G}$ is a family that contains both $\mathscr{F}$ and $\mathscr{G}$ (despite what is suggested by the notation); \item if $\mathscr{F}$ is a proper family, then $\mathscr{F} \sqcap \mathscr{F}^*$ is a proper family; \item if $\mathscr{F}_1 \subseteq \mathscr{G}_1$ and $\mathscr{F}_2 \subseteq \mathscr{G}_2$, then $\mathscr{F}_1 \sqcap \mathscr{F}_2 \subseteq \mathscr{G}_1 \sqcap \mathscr{G}_2$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 2.1.1 Dual families and intersections

nodes.name: Partition regular family
nodes.statement: A family $\mathscr{F}$ is \emph{partition regular} if for all $A \in \mathscr{F}$ and all finite partitions $A = A_1 \cup \cdots \cup A_k$, some piece $A_i$ belongs to $\mathscr{F}$.
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Filters, partition regularity, and ultrafilters

nodes.name: Filter
nodes.statement: The family $\mathscr{F}$ is a \emph{filter} if for all $A_1, A_2 \in \mathscr{F}$, the set $A_1 \cap A_2 \in \mathscr{F}$.
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Filters, partition regularity, and ultrafilters

nodes.name: P filter
nodes.statement: If $P$ is a property of families, we call a family that has property $P$ and that is also a filter a \emph{$P$ filter}.
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Filters, partition regularity, and ultrafilters

nodes.name: Basic facts on filters and partition regularity
nodes.statement: The following facts are quick to check: \begin{enumerate} \item a family $\mathscr{F}$ is partition regular if and only if the dual family $\mathscr{F}^*$ is a filter; \item if $\mathscr{F}$ is a proper filter, then $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{F}^*$; \item if $\mathscr{F}$ and $\mathscr{G}$ are filters, then $\mathscr{F} \sqcap \mathscr{G}$ is the smallest filter containing both $\mathscr{F}$ and $\mathscr{G}$; in particular, if $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{G}$, then $\mathscr{F} \sqcap \mathscr{G} = \mathscr{G}$.\\ \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Filters, partition regularity, and ultrafilters
nodes.statement_short: F is partition regular iff F* is a filter; a proper filter lies in its dual; F ⊓ G is the smallest filter containing filters F and G.

nodes.name: Lemma 2.1: F ⊓ F* is partition regular
nodes.statement: Let $\mathscr{F}$ be a family and define $\mathscr{G} \vcentcolon= \mathscr{F} \sqcap \mathscr{F}^*$. The family $\mathscr{G}$ is partition regular and its dual, $\mathscr{G}^*$, is a filter. Moreover, for $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, the following are all equivalent to the set $A$ belonging to $\mathscr{G}^*$: \begin{enumerate} \item for all $B \in \mathscr{F}$, the set $A \cap B \in \mathscr{F}$; \item for all $B \in \mathscr{F}^*$, the set $A \cap B \in \mathscr{F}^*$; \item for all $B \in \mathscr{G}$, the set $A \cap B \in \mathscr{G}$; \item for all $B \in \mathscr{G}^*$, the set $A \cap B \in \mathscr{G}^*$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Filters, partition regularity, and ultrafilters
nodes.statement_short: For a family F, G = F ⊓ F* is partition regular, G* is a filter, and membership in G* is equivalent to A ∩ B staying in F (or F*, G, G*) for B there.
assumptions: Let $\mathscr{F}$ be a family and define $\mathscr{G} \vcentcolon= \mathscr{F} \sqcap \mathscr{F}^*$.
conclusions: The family $\mathscr{G}$ is partition regular and its dual, $\mathscr{G}^*$, is a filter.

nodes.statement:
If $\mathscr{F}$ is not proper, then $\mathscr{G} = \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$, which is partition regular. Otherwise, the partition regularity of $\mathscr{G}$ is shown in \cite[Prop. 2.5 (h)]{christopherson_johnson_2022}. That its dual, $\mathscr{G}^*$, is a filter is mentioned as item \eqref{item_pr_filter_duality} before the statement of this lemma. We will show that \eqref{item_a_cap_b_is_in_family} is equivalent to $A$ belonging $\mathscr{G}^*$; the other statements follow analogously and are left to the reader. Suppose $A \in \mathscr{G}^*$ and $B \in \mathscr{F}$. To see that $A \cap B \in \mathscr{F}$, we will show that for all $C \in \mathscr{F}^*$, the set $A \cap B \cap C$ is nonempty. Let $C \in \mathscr{F}^*$. The set $B \cap C \in \mathscr{G}$, and since $A \in \mathscr{G}^*$, we have that $A \cap B \cap C 
eq \emptyset$, as desired. Conversely, suppose that \eqref{item_a_cap_b_is_in_family} holds. To see that $A \in \mathscr{G}^*$, we will show that for all $D \in \mathscr{G}$, the set $A \cap D 
eq \emptyset$. Let $D \in \mathscr{G}$. There exists $B \in \mathscr{F}$ and $C \in \mathscr{F}^*$ such that $D = B \cap C$. Then $A \cap D = A \cap B \cap C$. By assumption, $A \cap B \in \mathscr{F}$, whereby $ A \cap B \cap C 
eq \emptyset$, as desired.

nodes.statement: If $\mathscr{F}$ is not proper, then $\mathscr{G} = \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{N})$, which is partition regular. Otherwise, the partition regularity of $\mathscr{G}$ is shown in \cite[Prop. 2.5 (h)]{christopherson_johnson_2022}. That its dual, $\mathscr{G}^*$, is a filter is mentioned as item \eqref{item_pr_filter_duality} before the statement of this lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Partition regularity of G (cited) and filter property of G*.
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Filters, partition regularity, and ultrafilters

nodes.name: Show A in G* implies (i) by testing against C in F*
nodes.statement: We will show that \eqref{item_a_cap_b_is_in_family} is equivalent to $A$ belonging $\mathscr{G}^*$; the other statements follow analogously and are left to the reader. Suppose $A \in \mathscr{G}^*$ and $B \in \mathscr{F}$. To see that $A \cap B \in \mathscr{F}$, we will show that for all $C \in \mathscr{F}^*$, the set $A \cap B \cap C$ is nonempty. Let $C \in \mathscr{F}^*$. The set $B \cap C \in \mathscr{G}$, and since $A \in \mathscr{G}^*$, we have that $A \cap B \cap C \neq \emptyset$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Show A in G* implies (i) by testing against C in F*.
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Filters, partition regularity, and ultrafilters

nodes.name: Show (i) implies A in G* using D = B ∩ C
nodes.statement: Conversely, suppose that \eqref{item_a_cap_b_is_in_family} holds. To see that $A \in \mathscr{G}^*$, we will show that for all $D \in \mathscr{G}$, the set $A \cap D \neq \emptyset$. Let $D \in \mathscr{G}$. There exists $B \in \mathscr{F}$ and $C \in \mathscr{F}^*$ such that $D = B \cap C$. Then $A \cap D = A \cap B \cap C$. By assumption, $A \cap B \in \mathscr{F}$, whereby $ A \cap B \cap C \neq \emptyset$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Show (i) implies A in G* using D = B ∩ C.
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Filters, partition regularity, and ultrafilters

nodes.name: Ultrafilter
nodes.statement: A proper family is called an \emph{ultrafilter} if it satisfies one (equivalently, all) of the properties in the following lemma.
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Filters, partition regularity, and ultrafilters

nodes.name: Characterizations of ultrafilters
nodes.statement: Let $\mathscr{F}$ be a proper family of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$. The following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item the family $\mathscr{F}$ is a proper filter and is maximal (by containment) amongst proper filters; \item the family $\mathscr{F}$ is contained in a proper filter and is self-dual, ie., $\mathscr{F} = \mathscr{F}^*$; \item the family $\mathscr{F}$ is partition regular and a filter. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Filters, partition regularity, and ultrafilters
assumptions: Let $\mathscr{F}$ be a proper family of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$.
conclusions: The following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item the family $\mathscr{F}$ is a proper filter and is maximal (by containment) amongst proper filters; \item the family $\mathscr{F}$ is contained in a proper filter and is self-dual, ie., $\mathscr{F} = \mathscr{F}^*$; \item the family $\mathscr{F}$ is partition regular and a filter. \end{enumerate}
equivalent_conditions: the family $\mathscr{F}$ is a proper filter and is maximal (by containment) amongst proper filters;
the family $\mathscr{F}$ is contained in a proper filter and is self-dual, ie., $\mathscr{F} = \mathscr{F}^*$;
the family $\mathscr{F}$ is partition regular and a filter.
nodes.label: lemma_equiv_ultrafilter

nodes.statement: \eqref{item_family_is_maximal} $\implies$ \eqref{item_family_is_self_dual} \ Suppose $\mathscr{F}$ is a proper filter and is maximal amongst proper filters. Since $\mathscr{F}$ is a proper filter, we have that $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{F}^*$. Let $B \in \mathscr{F}^*$. It is quick to check that $\mathscr{G} \vcentcolon= \uparrow \{A \cap B \ | \ A \in \mathscr{F} \}$ is a proper filter that contains $\mathscr{F}$. Since $\mathscr{F}$ is maximal, we have that $\mathscr{F} = \mathscr{G}$, whereby $B \in \mathscr{F}$. Since $B \in \mathscr{F}^*$ was arbitrary, we have that $\mathscr{F} = \mathscr{F}^*$. \eqref{item_family_is_self_dual} $\implies$ \eqref{item_family_is_maximal} \ Suppose that $\mathscr{F}$ is contained in a proper filter and is self-dual. To conclude \eqref{item_family_is_maximal}, it suffices to show that for all proper filters $\mathscr{G}$ containing $\mathscr{F}$, we have $\mathscr{G} = \mathscr{F}$. Let $\mathscr{G}$ be a proper filter containing $\mathscr{F}$. Since $\mathscr{G}$ is a proper filter, we have that $\mathscr{G} \subseteq \mathscr{G}^*$. Since $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{G}$, we have that $\mathscr{G}^* \subseteq \mathscr{F}^* = \mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{G} \subseteq \mathscr{G}^*$. Therefore, $\mathscr{F} = \mathscr{G}$, as desired. \eqref{item_family_is_self_dual} $\implies$ \eqref{item_family_is_pr_and_filter} \ Suppose that $\mathscr{F}$ is contained in a proper filter and is self-dual. It is shown in the proof of \eqref{item_family_is_self_dual} implies \eqref{item_family_is_maximal} that $\mathscr{F}$ is a proper filter. It follows from fact \eqref{item_pr_filter_duality} from the beginning of this section, then, that $\mathscr{F}^*$ is partition regular. By assumption, $\mathscr{F}^* = \mathscr{F}$, hence $\mathscr{F}$ is partition regular, as desired. \eqref{item_family_is_pr_and_filter} $\implies$ \eqref{item_family_is_self_dual} \ Suppose $\mathscr{F}$ is a proper filter that is partition regular. Since $\mathscr{F}$ is proper, we have that $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{F}^*$. Since $\mathscr{F}$ is proper and partition regular, the family $\mathscr{F}^*$ is a proper filter, whereby $\mathscr{F}^* \subseteq (\mathscr{F}^*)^* = \mathscr{F}$. Thus, $\mathscr{F} = \mathscr{F}^*$, as desired.
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Filters, partition regularity, and ultrafilters
nodes.statement_short: Cycle of implications (i)⇒(ii)⇒(i), (ii)⇒(iii)⇒(ii) using duality of proper filters and partition regularity.

nodes.name: (i)⇒(ii): maximality forces every member of F* into F
nodes.statement: \eqref{item_family_is_maximal} $\implies$ \eqref{item_family_is_self_dual} \ Suppose $\mathscr{F}$ is a proper filter and is maximal amongst proper filters. Since $\mathscr{F}$ is a proper filter, we have that $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{F}^*$. Let $B \in \mathscr{F}^*$. It is quick to check that $\mathscr{G} \vcentcolon= \uparrow \{A \cap B \ | \ A \in \mathscr{F} \}$ is a proper filter that contains $\mathscr{F}$. Since $\mathscr{F}$ is maximal, we have that $\mathscr{F} = \mathscr{G}$, whereby $B \in \mathscr{F}$. Since $B \in \mathscr{F}^*$ was arbitrary, we have that $\mathscr{F} = \mathscr{F}^*$.
nodes.statement_short: (i)⇒(ii): maximality forces every member of F* into F.
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Filters, partition regularity, and ultrafilters

nodes.name: (ii)⇒(i): a proper filter containing F is squeezed between F and its d
nodes.statement: \eqref{item_family_is_self_dual} $\implies$ \eqref{item_family_is_maximal} \ Suppose that $\mathscr{F}$ is contained in a proper filter and is self-dual. To conclude \eqref{item_family_is_maximal}, it suffices to show that for all proper filters $\mathscr{G}$ containing $\mathscr{F}$, we have $\mathscr{G} = \mathscr{F}$. Let $\mathscr{G}$ be a proper filter containing $\mathscr{F}$. Since $\mathscr{G}$ is a proper filter, we have that $\mathscr{G} \subseteq \mathscr{G}^*$. Since $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{G}$, we have that $\mathscr{G}^* \subseteq \mathscr{F}^* = \mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{G} \subseteq \mathscr{G}^*$. Therefore, $\mathscr{F} = \mathscr{G}$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: (ii)⇒(i): a proper filter containing F is squeezed between F and its dual.
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Filters, partition regularity, and ultrafilters

nodes.name: (ii)⇒(iii): F* is partition regular and equals F
nodes.statement: \eqref{item_family_is_self_dual} $\implies$ \eqref{item_family_is_pr_and_filter} \ Suppose that $\mathscr{F}$ is contained in a proper filter and is self-dual. It is shown in the proof of \eqref{item_family_is_self_dual} implies \eqref{item_family_is_maximal} that $\mathscr{F}$ is a proper filter. It follows from fact \eqref{item_pr_filter_duality} from the beginning of this section, then, that $\mathscr{F}^*$ is partition regular. By assumption, $\mathscr{F}^* = \mathscr{F}$, hence $\mathscr{F}$ is partition regular, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: (ii)⇒(iii): F* is partition regular and equals F.
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Filters, partition regularity, and ultrafilters

nodes.name: (iii)⇒(ii): F* is a proper filter, giving F = F*
nodes.statement: \eqref{item_family_is_pr_and_filter} $\implies$ \eqref{item_family_is_self_dual} \ Suppose $\mathscr{F}$ is a proper filter that is partition regular. Since $\mathscr{F}$ is proper, we have that $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{F}^*$. Since $\mathscr{F}$ is proper and partition regular, the family $\mathscr{F}^*$ is a proper filter, whereby $\mathscr{F}^* \subseteq (\mathscr{F}^*)^* = \mathscr{F}$. Thus, $\mathscr{F} = \mathscr{F}^*$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: (iii)⇒(ii): F* is a proper filter, giving F = F*.
nodes.section: 2.1.2 Filters, partition regularity, and ultrafilters

nodes.name: Translation algebra: A - F and F + G
nodes.statement: For $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and families $\mathscr{F}$ and $\mathscr{G}$ of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$, we define \begin{align*} A - \mathscr{F} &\vcentcolon= \big\{ n \in \mathbb{N} \ \big| \ A-n \in \mathscr{F} \big\},\\ \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G} &\vcentcolon= \big\{ B \subseteq \mathbb{N} \ \big| \ B - \mathscr{G} \in \mathscr{F} \big\}. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 2.1.3 Translation algebra
nodes.statement_short: A - F is the set of n with A - n in F; F + G is the family of B with B - G in F.

nodes.name: Lemma 2.3: algebra of family sums
nodes.statement: Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, and $\mathscr{F}, \mathscr{G}, \mathscr{F}_1, \mathscr{F}_2, \mathscr{G}_1, \mathscr{G}_2$ be families. \begin{enumerate} \item If $\mathscr{F}$ and $\mathscr{G}$ are proper, then $\mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G}$ is proper. \item $(A - \mathscr{F}) \cap (B - \mathscr{G}) \subseteq (A \cap B) - (\mathscr{F} \sqcap \mathscr{G})$, with equality if $\mathscr{F} = \mathscr{G}$ is a filter. \item If $\mathscr{F}$ and $\mathscr{G}$ are filters, then $\mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G}$ is a filter. \item $(A -n) - \mathscr{F} = (A - \mathscr{F}) - n$. \item $A - (\mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G}) = (A - \mathscr{G}) - \mathscr{F}$. \item If $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{G}$, then $A - \mathscr{F} \subseteq A - \mathscr{G}$. \item If $\mathscr{F}_1 \subseteq \mathscr{G}_1$ and $\mathscr{F}_2 \subseteq \mathscr{G}_2$, then $\mathscr{F}_1 + \mathscr{F}_2 \subseteq \mathscr{G}_1 + \mathscr{G}_2$. \item $(\mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G})^* = \mathscr{F}^* + \mathscr{G}^*$. \item $(\mathscr{F}_1 + \mathscr{F}_2) \sqcap (\mathscr{G}_1 + \mathscr{G}_2) \subseteq (\mathscr{F}_1 \sqcap \mathscr{G}_1) + (\mathscr{F}_2 \sqcap \mathscr{G}_2)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 2.1.3 Translation algebra
nodes.statement_short: Nine algebraic rules for family sums: properness, filters, translates, associativity-type identities, monotonicity, duality and ⊓.

\eqref{item_family_prop_zero} \ Suppose $\mathscr{F}$ and $\mathscr{G}$ are proper. Since $\emptyset 
ot\in \mathscr{G}$, we have $\emptyset - \mathscr{G} = \emptyset$. Since $\emptyset 
ot\in \mathscr{F}$, we have $\emptyset 
ot\in \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G}$. Since $\mathscr{F}$ and $\mathscr{G}$ both contain $\mathbb{N}$, we see that $\mathbb{N} \in \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G}$. Since $\mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G}$ does not contain $\emptyset$ but contains $\mathbb{N}$, it is proper. \eqref{item_family_prop_one_new} \ Suppose $n \in (A - \mathscr{F}) \cap (B - \mathscr{G})$. Since $A - n \in \mathscr{F}$ and $B - n \in \mathscr{G}$, we have that $(A \cap B) - n = (A-n) \cap (B-n) \in \mathscr{F} \sqcap \mathscr{G}$. Thus, $n \in (A \cap B) - (\mathscr{F} \sqcap \mathscr{G})$, as desired. If $\mathscr{F} = \mathscr{G}$ is a filter, then $\mathscr{F} \sqcap \mathscr{G} = \mathscr{F}$. We wish to show in this case that $(A \cap B) - \mathscr{F} \subseteq (A- \mathscr{F}) \cap (B-\mathscr{F})$. Suppose $n \in (A \cap B) - \mathscr{F}$ so that $(A - n) \cap (B-n) \in \mathscr{F}$. Since $\mathscr{F}$ is upward closed, we have that $A -n \in \mathscr{F}$ and $B-n \in \mathscr{F}$. Therefore, $n \in (A - \mathscr{F}) \cap (B-\mathscr{F})$, as desired. \eqref{item_family_prop_two} \ Suppose $\mathscr{F}$ and $\mathscr{G}$ are filters. Since $\mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G}$ is a family, we need only to show that for all $A, B \in \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G}$, the set $A \cap B \in \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G}$. Let $A, B \in \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G}$. Thus, $A - \mathscr{G}, B - \mathscr{G} \in \mathscr{F}$, whereby $(A-\mathscr{G}) \cap (B-\mathscr{G}) \in \mathscr{F}$. By \eqref{item_family_prop_one_new}, it follows that $(A \cap B) - \mathscr{G} \in \mathscr{F}$, whereby $A \cap B \in \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G}$, as desired. \eqref{item_family_prop_three} \ Note that $m \in (A -n) - \mathscr{F}$ if and only if $A-n-m \in \mathscr{F}$, which happens if and only if $A-(m+n) \in \mathscr{F}$. We see that this happens if and only if $m+n \in A-\mathscr{F}$, that is, if and only if $m \in (A-\mathscr{F}) - n$, as desired. \eqref{item_family_prop_four} \ We see that $n \in A - (\mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G})$ if and only if $A-n \in \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G}$, which happens if and only if $(A-n) - \mathscr{G} \in \mathscr{F}$. By \eqref{item_family_prop_three}, this happens if and only if $(A-\mathscr{G}) - n \in \mathscr{F}$, which happens if and only if $n \in (A - \mathscr{G}) - \mathscr{F}$, as desired. \eqref{item_family_diff_containment} \ If $n \in A - \mathscr{F}$, then $A - n \in \mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{G}$, whereby $n \in A - \mathscr{G}$. \eqref{item_filter_sums_containment} \ Suppose $A \in \mathscr{F}_1 + \mathscr{F}_2$. Then $A-\mathscr{F}_2 \in \mathscr{F}_1 \subseteq \mathscr{G}_1$. Since $\mathscr{F}_2 \subseteq \mathscr{G}_2$, we have that $A - \mathscr{F}_2 \subseteq A - \mathscr{G}_2$. Since $\mathscr{G}_1$ is upward closed and $A- \mathscr{F}_2 \in \mathscr{G}_1$, we see that $A - \mathscr{G}_2 \in \mathscr{G}_1$. Therefore, $A \in \mathscr{G}_1 + \mathscr{G}_2$, as desired. \eqref{item_sum_dual} We will show first that $\mathscr{F}^* + \mathscr{G}^* \subseteq (\mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G})^*$. Suppose $A \in \mathscr{F}^* + \mathscr{G}^*$, and let $B \in \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G}$. Since $A - \mathscr{G}^* \in \mathscr{F}^*$ and $B - \mathscr{G} \in \mathscr{F}$, we have that there exists $n \in (A - \mathscr{G}^*) \cap (B - \mathscr{G})$. We see that $A - n \in \mathscr{G}^*$ and $B - n \in \mathscr{G}$. It follows that $(A-n) \cap (B-n) 
eq \emptyset$, whereby $A \cap B 
eq \emptyset$, as desired. Now we can write \[\mathscr{F}^* + \mathscr{G}^* \subseteq (\mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G})^* =  ig((\mathscr{F}^*)^* + (\mathscr{G}^*)^*  ig)^* \subseteq  ig((\mathscr{F}^* + \mathscr{G}^*)^*  ig)^* = \mathscr{F}^* + \mathscr{G}^*,\] where the first containment follows from the previous paragraph and the second containment follows from the previous paragraph applied to the dual classes. This shows the desired equality. \eqref{item_cap_sums} \ Suppose $\mathscr{F}_1 + \mathscr{F}_2 = \emptyset$ or $\mathscr{G}_1 + \mathscr{G}_2 = \emptyset$. If $\mathscr{F}_1 + \mathscr{F}_2 = \emptyset$, then either $\mathscr{F}_1 = \emptyset$ or $\mathscr{F}_2 = \emptyset$. In the first case, the desired inclusion simplifies to $\mathscr{G}_1 + \mathscr{G}_2 \subseteq \mathscr{G}_1 + (\mathscr{F}_2 \sqcap \mathscr{G}_2)$, which follows from \eqref{item_filter_sums_containment}. The second case is shown similarly. The case that $\mathscr{G}_1 + \mathscr{G}_2 = \emptyset$ is handled analogously. Otherwise, we have that $\mathscr{F}_1 + \mathscr{F}_2 
eq \emptyset$ and $\mathscr{G}_1 + \mathscr{G}_2 
eq \emptyset$. To see the desired inclusion, let $C \in (\mathscr{F}_1 + \mathscr{F}_2) \sqcap (\mathscr{G}_1 + \mathscr{G}_2)$. There exists $A \in \mathscr{F}_1 + \mathscr{F}_2$ and $B \in \mathscr{G}_1 + \mathscr{G}_2$ such that $C = A \cap B$. It follows from point \eqref{item_family_prop_one_new} that $(A-\mathscr{F}_2) \cap (B-\mathscr{G}_2) \subseteq (A \cap B) - (\mathscr{F}_2 \sqcap \mathscr{G}_2)$. Since $A-\mathscr{F}_2 \in \mathscr{F}_1$ and $B-\mathscr{G}_2 \in \mathscr{G}_1$, we see that that $(A \cap B) - (\mathscr{F}_2 \sqcap \mathscr{G}_2) \in \mathscr{F}_1 \sqcap \mathscr{G}_1$, whereby $A \cap B \in (\mathscr{F}_1 \sqcap \mathscr{G}_1) + (\mathscr{F}_2 \sqcap \mathscr{G}_2)$, as desired.
nodes.section: 2.1.3 Translation algebra
nodes.statement_short: Item-by-item verification from the definitions of A - F and F + G; duality (viii) by a two-sided containment argument.

nodes.name: (i) properness of F+G
nodes.statement:
\eqref{item_family_prop_zero} \ Suppose $\mathscr{F}$ and $\mathscr{G}$ are proper. Since $\emptyset 
ot\in \mathscr{G}$, we have $\emptyset - \mathscr{G} = \emptyset$. Since $\emptyset 
ot\in \mathscr{F}$, we have $\emptyset 
ot\in \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G}$. Since $\mathscr{F}$ and $\mathscr{G}$ both contain $\mathbb{N}$, we see that $\mathbb{N} \in \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G}$. Since $\mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G}$ does not contain $\emptyset$ but contains $\mathbb{N}$, it is proper.
nodes.statement_short: (i) properness of F+G.
nodes.section: 2.1.3 Translation algebra

nodes.name: (ii) containment, with equality for a filter
nodes.statement: \eqref{item_family_prop_one_new} \ Suppose $n \in (A - \mathscr{F}) \cap (B - \mathscr{G})$. Since $A - n \in \mathscr{F}$ and $B - n \in \mathscr{G}$, we have that $(A \cap B) - n = (A-n) \cap (B-n) \in \mathscr{F} \sqcap \mathscr{G}$. Thus, $n \in (A \cap B) - (\mathscr{F} \sqcap \mathscr{G})$, as desired. If $\mathscr{F} = \mathscr{G}$ is a filter, then $\mathscr{F} \sqcap \mathscr{G} = \mathscr{F}$. We wish to show in this case that $(A \cap B) - \mathscr{F} \subseteq (A- \mathscr{F}) \cap (B-\mathscr{F})$. Suppose $n \in (A \cap B) - \mathscr{F}$ so that $(A - n) \cap (B-n) \in \mathscr{F}$. Since $\mathscr{F}$ is upward closed, we have that $A -n \in \mathscr{F}$ and $B-n \in \mathscr{F}$. Therefore, $n \in (A - \mathscr{F}) \cap (B-\mathscr{F})$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: (ii) containment, with equality for a filter.
nodes.section: 2.1.3 Translation algebra

nodes.name: (iii) sum of filters is a filter, using (ii)
nodes.statement: \eqref{item_family_prop_two} \ Suppose $\mathscr{F}$ and $\mathscr{G}$ are filters. Since $\mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G}$ is a family, we need only to show that for all $A, B \in \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G}$, the set $A \cap B \in \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G}$. Let $A, B \in \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G}$. Thus, $A - \mathscr{G}, B - \mathscr{G} \in \mathscr{F}$, whereby $(A-\mathscr{G}) \cap (B-\mathscr{G}) \in \mathscr{F}$. By \eqref{item_family_prop_one_new}, it follows that $(A \cap B) - \mathscr{G} \in \mathscr{F}$, whereby $A \cap B \in \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G}$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: (iii) sum of filters is a filter, using (ii).
nodes.section: 2.1.3 Translation algebra

nodes.name: (iv) translation commutes with A - F
nodes.statement: \eqref{item_family_prop_three} \ Note that $m \in (A -n) - \mathscr{F}$ if and only if $A-n-m \in \mathscr{F}$, which happens if and only if $A-(m+n) \in \mathscr{F}$. We see that this happens if and only if $m+n \in A-\mathscr{F}$, that is, if and only if $m \in (A-\mathscr{F}) - n$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: (iv) translation commutes with A - F.
nodes.section: 2.1.3 Translation algebra

nodes.name: (v) A - (F+G) = (A-G) - F via (iv)
nodes.statement: \eqref{item_family_prop_four} \ We see that $n \in A - (\mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G})$ if and only if $A-n \in \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G}$, which happens if and only if $(A-n) - \mathscr{G} \in \mathscr{F}$. By \eqref{item_family_prop_three}, this happens if and only if $(A-\mathscr{G}) - n \in \mathscr{F}$, which happens if and only if $n \in (A - \mathscr{G}) - \mathscr{F}$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: (v) A - (F+G) = (A-G) - F via (iv).
nodes.section: 2.1.3 Translation algebra

nodes.name: (vi) monotonicity of A - F
nodes.statement: \eqref{item_family_diff_containment} \ If $n \in A - \mathscr{F}$, then $A - n \in \mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{G}$, whereby $n \in A - \mathscr{G}$.
nodes.statement_short: (vi) monotonicity of A - F.
nodes.section: 2.1.3 Translation algebra

nodes.name: (vii) monotonicity of sums
nodes.statement: \eqref{item_filter_sums_containment} \ Suppose $A \in \mathscr{F}_1 + \mathscr{F}_2$. Then $A-\mathscr{F}_2 \in \mathscr{F}_1 \subseteq \mathscr{G}_1$. Since $\mathscr{F}_2 \subseteq \mathscr{G}_2$, we have that $A - \mathscr{F}_2 \subseteq A - \mathscr{G}_2$. Since $\mathscr{G}_1$ is upward closed and $A- \mathscr{F}_2 \in \mathscr{G}_1$, we see that $A - \mathscr{G}_2 \in \mathscr{G}_1$. Therefore, $A \in \mathscr{G}_1 + \mathscr{G}_2$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: (vii) monotonicity of sums.
nodes.section: 2.1.3 Translation algebra

nodes.name: (viii) duality of sums by double containment
nodes.statement: \eqref{item_sum_dual} We will show first that $\mathscr{F}^* + \mathscr{G}^* \subseteq (\mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G})^*$. Suppose $A \in \mathscr{F}^* + \mathscr{G}^*$, and let $B \in \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G}$. Since $A - \mathscr{G}^* \in \mathscr{F}^*$ and $B - \mathscr{G} \in \mathscr{F}$, we have that there exists $n \in (A - \mathscr{G}^*) \cap (B - \mathscr{G})$. We see that $A - n \in \mathscr{G}^*$ and $B - n \in \mathscr{G}$. It follows that $(A-n) \cap (B-n) \neq \emptyset$, whereby $A \cap B \neq \emptyset$, as desired. Now we can write \[\mathscr{F}^* + \mathscr{G}^* \subseteq (\mathscr{F} + \mathscr{G})^* = \big((\mathscr{F}^*)^* + (\mathscr{G}^*)^* \big)^* \subseteq \big((\mathscr{F}^* + \mathscr{G}^*)^* \big)^* = \mathscr{F}^* + \mathscr{G}^*,\] where the first containment follows from the previous paragraph and the second containment follows from the previous paragraph applied to the dual classes. This shows the desired equality.
nodes.statement_short: (viii) duality of sums by double containment.
nodes.section: 2.1.3 Translation algebra

nodes.name: (ix) ⊓ of sums, with degenerate cases first
nodes.statement: \eqref{item_cap_sums} \ Suppose $\mathscr{F}_1 + \mathscr{F}_2 = \emptyset$ or $\mathscr{G}_1 + \mathscr{G}_2 = \emptyset$. If $\mathscr{F}_1 + \mathscr{F}_2 = \emptyset$, then either $\mathscr{F}_1 = \emptyset$ or $\mathscr{F}_2 = \emptyset$. In the first case, the desired inclusion simplifies to $\mathscr{G}_1 + \mathscr{G}_2 \subseteq \mathscr{G}_1 + (\mathscr{F}_2 \sqcap \mathscr{G}_2)$, which follows from \eqref{item_filter_sums_containment}. The second case is shown similarly. The case that $\mathscr{G}_1 + \mathscr{G}_2 = \emptyset$ is handled analogously. Otherwise, we have that $\mathscr{F}_1 + \mathscr{F}_2 \neq \emptyset$ and $\mathscr{G}_1 + \mathscr{G}_2 \neq \emptyset$. To see the desired inclusion, let $C \in (\mathscr{F}_1 + \mathscr{F}_2) \sqcap (\mathscr{G}_1 + \mathscr{G}_2)$. There exists $A \in \mathscr{F}_1 + \mathscr{F}_2$ and $B \in \mathscr{G}_1 + \mathscr{G}_2$ such that $C = A \cap B$. It follows from point \eqref{item_family_prop_one_new} that $(A-\mathscr{F}_2) \cap (B-\mathscr{G}_2) \subseteq (A \cap B) - (\mathscr{F}_2 \sqcap \mathscr{G}_2)$. Since $A-\mathscr{F}_2 \in \mathscr{F}_1$ and $B-\mathscr{G}_2 \in \mathscr{G}_1$, we see that that $(A \cap B) - (\mathscr{F}_2 \sqcap \mathscr{G}_2) \in \mathscr{F}_1 \sqcap \mathscr{G}_1$, whereby $A \cap B \in (\mathscr{F}_1 \sqcap \mathscr{G}_1) + (\mathscr{F}_2 \sqcap \mathscr{G}_2)$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: (ix) ⊓ of sums, with degenerate cases first.
nodes.section: 2.1.3 Translation algebra

nodes.name: Translate of a family
nodes.statement: For $m \in \mathbb{N}$ and a family $\mathscr{F}$ of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$, we define \[\mathscr{F} - m \vcentcolon= \big\{ B - m \ \big| \ B \in \mathscr{F} \big\}.\]
nodes.section: 2.1.4 Translation-invariant and idempotent families

nodes.name: Translation-invariant family
nodes.statement: The family $\mathscr{F}$ is \emph{translation invariant} if $\mathscr{F} - n \subseteq \mathscr{F}$ for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.section: 2.1.4 Translation-invariant and idempotent families

nodes.name: Idempotent family
nodes.statement: The family $\mathscr{F}$ is \emph{idempotent} if $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$, equivalently, if for all $A \in \mathscr{F}$, $A - \mathscr{F} \in \mathscr{F}$.
nodes.section: 2.1.4 Translation-invariant and idempotent families
also_stated_at: We define a family $\mathscr{F}$ to be \emph{idempotent} if $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$.

nodes.name: Lemma 2.4: ⊓ preserves idempotence and translation invariance
nodes.statement: Let $\mathscr{F}$ and $\mathscr{G}$ be families. \begin{enumerate} \item If $\mathscr{F}$ and $\mathscr{G}$ are idempotent, then $\mathscr{F} \sqcap \mathscr{G}$ is idempotent. \item If $\mathscr{F}$ and $\mathscr{G}$ are translation invariant, then $\mathscr{F} \sqcap \mathscr{G}$ is translation invariant. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 2.1.4 Translation-invariant and idempotent families
conclusions: $\mathscr{F} \sqcap \mathscr{G}$ is idempotent
$\mathscr{F} \sqcap \mathscr{G}$ is translation invariant
$\mathscr{F} \sqcap \mathscr{G}$ is idempotent
$\mathscr{F} \sqcap \mathscr{G}$ is translation invariant

nodes.label: lemma_idempotent_classcap_is_idempotent

nodes.statement: \eqref{item_class_cap_of_idempotent_is_idempotent} \ We appeal to \cref{lemma_fam_dual_sums} \eqref{item_cap_sums} with $\mathscr{F}_1 = \mathscr{F}_2 = \mathscr{F}$ and $\mathscr{G}_1 = \mathscr{G}_2 = \mathscr{G}$. Thus, \[\mathscr{F} \sqcap \mathscr{G} \subseteq (\mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}) \sqcap (\mathscr{G} + \mathscr{G}) \subseteq (\mathscr{F} \sqcap \mathscr{G}) + (\mathscr{F} \sqcap \mathscr{G}),\] as desired. Statement \eqref{item_class_cap_of_trans_inv} follows similarly and is left to the reader.
nodes.section: 2.1.4 Translation-invariant and idempotent families
nodes.statement_short: Apply Lemma 2.3(ix) with F1 = F2 = F and G1 = G2 = G.

nodes.name: Showing idempotency on generating sets
nodes.statement: The following situation arises several times in this paper. A family $\mathscr{F}$ is defined as the upward closure of a collection of special subsets of $\mathbb{N}$. To show that $\mathscr{F}$ is idempotent, it suffices to show that for all special sets $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, the set $A - \mathscr{F}$ belongs to $\mathscr{F}$. Indeed, if $B \in \mathscr{F}$, then $B$ contains some special set $A$. If we show that $A-\mathscr{F} \in \mathscr{F}$, then since $A- \mathscr{F} \subseteq B - \mathscr{F}$, we have that $B - \mathscr{F} \in \mathscr{F}$, as desired.
nodes.section: 2.1.4 Translation-invariant and idempotent families
nodes.statement_short: To show an upward closure F is idempotent it suffices to check A - F in F for the generating sets A.
nodes.label: rmk_showing_idempotency

nodes.name: Idempotent ultrafilter
nodes.statement: It appears that there are two different definitions of ``idempotent ultrafilter.'' In the literature, a family $\mathscr{F}$ is an idempotent ultrafilter if it is an ultrafilter and satisfies $\mathscr{F} = \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$.
nodes.section: 2.1.4 Translation-invariant and idempotent families

nodes.name: Maximal idempotent filters are idempotent ultrafilters
nodes.statement: Let $\mathscr{F}$ be a family. The following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item the family $\mathscr{F}$ is a proper, idempotent filter and is maximal (by containment) in the set of proper, idempotent filters; \item the family $\mathscr{F}$ is an ultrafilter that satisfies $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$; \item the family $\mathscr{F}$ is an ultrafilter that satisfies $\mathscr{F} = \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$. \end{enumerate} In particular, every proper, idempotent filter is contained in an idempotent ultrafilter.
nodes.section: 2.1.4 Translation-invariant and idempotent families
nodes.statement_short: Maximal proper idempotent filters, ultrafilters with F ⊆ F+F, and ultrafilters with F = F+F coincide; every proper idempotent filter lies in an idempotent ultrafilter.
conclusions: The following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item the family $\mathscr{F}$ is a proper, idempotent filter and is maximal (by containment) in the set of proper, idempotent filters; \item the family $\mathscr{F}$ is an ultrafilter that satisfies $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$; \item the family $\mathscr{F}$ is an ultrafilter that satisfies $\mathscr{F} = \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$. \end{enumerate} In particular, every proper, idempotent filter is contained in an idempotent ultrafilter.
every proper, idempotent filter is contained in an idempotent ultrafilter
equivalent_conditions: the family $\mathscr{F}$ is a proper, idempotent filter and is maximal (by containment) in the set of proper, idempotent filters;
the family $\mathscr{F}$ is an ultrafilter that satisfies $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$;
the family $\mathscr{F}$ is an ultrafilter that satisfies $\mathscr{F} = \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$.
nodes.label: thm_equiv_forms_of_max_idempot_filter

nodes.statement: \eqref{item_max_prop_idemp_filter} $\implies$ \eqref{item_ultra_idemp} \ We will prove first that every proper, idempotent filter is contained in an idempotent family that is an ultrafilter. Supposing this is so, if $\mathscr{F}$ is a maximal proper, idempotent filter, then it is contained in an idempotent family $\mathscr{G}$ that is an ultrafilter. By the maximality of $\mathscr{F}$ as a proper, idempotent filter, we have that $\mathscr{F} = \mathscr{G}$, giving \eqref{item_ultra_idemp}, as desired. Suppose $\mathscr{F}$ is a proper, idempotent filter and is maximal as such. We claim that the set $\overline{\mathscr{F}} \vcentcolon= \bigcap_{A \in \mathscr{F}} \overline{A}$ is a nonempty, compact subsemigroup of $(\beta \mathbb{N}, +)$. Because ultrafilters are maximal filters, there is an ultrafilter containing $\mathscr{F}$, and so $\overline{\mathscr{F}}$ is nonempty. The set $\overline{\mathscr{F}}$ is compact because it is closed and $\beta \mathbb{N}$ is compact. Suppose $q_1, q_2 \in \overline{\mathscr{F}}$. Since $\mathscr{F} \subseteq q_1$ and $\mathscr{F} \subseteq q_2$, it follows from \cref{lemma_filter_sums_containment} \eqref{item_filter_sums_containment} and the idempotency of $\mathscr{F}$ that \[\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F} \subseteq q_1 + q_2.\] Therefore, we have that $q_1 + q_2 \in \overline{\mathscr{F}}$. Finally, since $\overline{\mathscr{F}}$ is a nonempty, compact subsemigroup of $(\beta \mathbb{N}, +)$, by \cite[Thm. 2.5]{hindman_strauss_book_2012}, there exists an idempotent ultrafilter containing $\mathscr{F}$. \eqref{item_ultra_idemp} $\implies$ \eqref{item_ultra_strong_idemp} \ Suppose $\mathscr{F}$ is an ultrafilter that satisfies $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$. By \cref{lemma_filter_algebra} \eqref{item_family_prop_zero} and \eqref{item_family_prop_two}, the family $\mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$ is a proper filter. Since $\mathscr{F}$ is a maximal proper filter, we have that $\mathscr{F} = \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$, as desired. \eqref{item_ultra_strong_idemp} $\implies$ \eqref{item_max_prop_idemp_filter} \ If $\mathscr{F}$ is an ultrafilter that satisfies $\mathscr{F} = \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$, then it is a proper, idempotent filter. Since it is maximal amongst proper filters, it is maximal amongst proper, idempotent filters.

nodes.statement_short: The closed set of ultrafilters containing F is a compact subsemigroup of βN, so contains an idempotent (Ellis); remaining implications from maximality.

nodes.statement: \eqref{item_max_prop_idemp_filter} $\implies$ \eqref{item_ultra_idemp} \ We will prove first that every proper, idempotent filter is contained in an idempotent family that is an ultrafilter. Supposing this is so, if $\mathscr{F}$ is a maximal proper, idempotent filter, then it is contained in an idempotent family $\mathscr{G}$ that is an ultrafilter. nodes.statement: \eqref{item_ultra_idemp} $\implies$ \eqref{item_ultra_strong_idemp} \ Suppose $\mathscr{F}$ is an ultrafilter that satisfies $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$. By \cref{lemma_filter_algebra} \eqref{item_family_prop_zero} and \eqref{item_family_prop_two}, the family $\mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$ is a proper filter. Since it is maximal amongst proper filters, it is maximal amongst proper, idempotent filters.

nodes.name: Existence of idempotents without Zorn's lemma
nodes.statement: A routine application of Zorn's lemma gives the existence of maximal proper, idempotent filters. It follows from \cref{thm_equiv_forms_of_max_idempot_filter} that these are ultrafilters. The proof given here relies on the fact that a compact, Hausdorff, right-topological semigroup contains an idempotent element (see \cite[Thm. 2.5]{hindman_strauss_book_2012} and the end-of-chapter notes). A short, topology-free proof of this was given by Papazyan \cite{papazyan_1989}, and a proof without the full strength of Zorn's Lemma was given by Di Nasso and Tachtsis \cite{dinasso_tachtsis_2018}. Another routine application of Zorn's lemma gives the existence of maximal proper, translation-invariant filters. It is an easy exercise to show that there are no translation-invariant ultrafilters on $\mathbb{N}$. Therefore, in contrast to maximal proper, idempotent filters, maximal proper, translation-invariant filters are not ultrafilters.
nodes.section: 2.1.4 Translation-invariant and idempotent families
nodes.label: rmk_idempotents_without_zorn

nodes.name: Idempotent filter with strict inclusion F ⊊ F+F
nodes.statement:
The definition of idempotent family we give in this section matches the one for filters given implicitly in \cite{papazyan_1989} and explicitly in \cite{Krautzberger_2009}. It may seem more natural to require equality in the definition: $\mathscr{F} = \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$. While certainly some families do satisfy this -- in particular, idempotent ultrafilters (\cref{thm_equiv_forms_of_max_idempot_filter}) -- equality appears to be rather rare. Here is an example of a dynamically simple idempotent filter $\mathscr{F}$ which satisfies $\mathscr{F} \subsetneq \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$. See \cref{sec_top_dynamics} for the notation. Fix $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}  ackslash \mathbb{Q}$, and consider the irrational rotation $(\mathbb{R} / \mathbb{Z}, T_{\alpha}: x \mapsto x + \alpha)$. Put \[\mathscr{F} \vcentcolon= \uparrow  ig\{ R(0, B_\varepsilon(0)) \  ig| \ \varepsilon > 0 ig\}.\] The family $\mathscr{F}$ is an idempotent filter. This can be easily checked (see, eg., the proof of the ``only if'' statement of \cref{thm_dcs_iff_cs}). Let $(k_i)_{i=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be such that the only limit point of $i \mapsto k_i \alpha$ is $0$. For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the quantity \[\varepsilon_n \vcentcolon= \min  ig\{ \|k_i \alpha - n \alpha \|/2 \  ig| \ i \in \mathbb{N}, \ k_i > n  ig\},\] where $\| \cdot \|: \mathbb{R} / \mathbb{Z} 	o [0,1/2)$ denotes the Euclidean distance to $\mathbb{Z}$, is non-zero. We claim that the set \[A \vcentcolon=  igcup_{n = 1}^\infty  ig( R(0, B_{\varepsilon_n}(0) ) + n  ig)\] belongs to $\mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$ but not to $\mathscr{F}$. Indeed, for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the set $A - n$ contains $R(0, B_{\varepsilon_n}(0) ) \in \mathscr{F}$, and so $A \in \{\mathbb{N}\} + \mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$. To see that $A

ot\subseteq A$. Let $\delta > 0$, and let $i \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $k_i \in R(0,B_{\delta}(0))$. Now, for all $n < k_i$, we have that $\|k_i \alpha - n \alpha\| \geqslant 2\varepsilon_n$, whereby $k_i 
otin R(0,B_{\varepsilon_n}(0)) + n$. For all $n \geqslant k_i$, we have that $k_i

nodes.statement_short: For an irrational rotation, the filter of return times to balls around 0 is idempotent but strictly contained in F+F.
