nodes.name: Closure, interior and boundary
nodes.statement: For a set $U$ in a topological space $X$, we denote by $\overline U$, $U^\circ$, and $\partial U \vcentcolon= \overline{U} \backslash U^\circ$ the closure, interior, and boundary of $U$, respectively.
nodes.section: 2.2 Topology and dynamics

nodes.name: Open ball
nodes.statement: In a metric space $(X,d)$, we denote by $B_\varepsilon(x)$ the open ball centered at a point $x \in X$ with radius $\varepsilon > 0$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Topology and dynamics

nodes.name: Topological dynamical system
nodes.statement: A \emph{(topological dynamical) system} $(X,T)$ is a nonempty, compact metric space $(X,d_X)$ together with a continuous self-map $T: X \to X$.
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Topological dynamics

nodes.name: Subsystem
nodes.statement: A \emph{subsystem of $(X,T)$} is a system of the form $(Y,T)$, where $Y \subseteq X$ is nonempty, closed (equivalently, compact), and \emph{$T$-invariant}, meaning $TY \subseteq Y$.
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Topological dynamics

nodes.name: Minimal system
nodes.statement: A system $(X,T)$ whose only subsystem is itself is called \emph{minimal}.
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Topological dynamics

nodes.name: Factor map
nodes.statement: Given two systems $(X,T)$ and $(Y,S)$, a continuous surjection $\pi: X \to Y$ that satisfies $S \circ \pi = \pi \circ T$ is called a \emph{factor map} of systems.
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Topological dynamics

nodes.name: Invertible system
nodes.statement: Thus, even in the event that $T$ is a homeomorphism (in which case, the system $(X,T)$ is called \emph{invertible}), the emphasis will be on non-negative iterates of the map $T$.
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Topological dynamics

nodes.name: Not-necessarily-metrizable system
nodes.statement: A \emph{not-necessarily-metrizable system} is a nonempty, compact Hausdorff space $X$ together with a continuous self-map $T: X \to X$.
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Topological dynamics

nodes.name: Orbit along a set
nodes.statement: Given a system $(X,T)$, a point $x \in X$, and a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, we define \[T^A x \vcentcolon= \big\{ T^a x \ \big| \ a \in A \big\}.\]
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Topological dynamics

nodes.name: Orbit and orbit closure
nodes.statement: The \emph{orbit of $x$} is the set $T^{\mathbb{N}} x$ and the \emph{orbit closure of $x$} is the set $\overline{T^{\mathbb{N}}x}$.
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Topological dynamics

nodes.name: Return-time set R(x,U)
nodes.statement: Given a system $(X,T)$, a set $U \subseteq X$, and a point $x \in X$, we write \begin{align*} R(x, U) &\vcentcolon= \big\{n \in \mathbb{N} \ \big | \ T^n x \in U \big\} \end{align*} for the times at which the point $x$ visits the set $U$.
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Topological dynamics

nodes.name: Syndetic set
nodes.statement: A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is \emph{syndetic} if there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $A \cup (A-1) \cup \cdots \cup (A-N) = \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Topological dynamics
also_stated_at: A subset of $\mathbb{N}$ is \emph{syndetic} if it has bounded gaps, that is, if there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that it has nonempty intersection with every interval of length $N$.

nodes.name: Minimality and syndetic return times
nodes.statement: Indeed, let $(X,T)$ be a not-necessarily-metrizable system. Both of the facts below are not hard to show following the results in \cite[Ch. 1, Sec. 4]{furstenberg_book_1981}. \begin{enumerate} \item Let $x \in X$. The subsystem $(\overline{T^{\mathbb{N}_0}x}, T)$ is minimal if and only if for all open $U \subseteq X$ containing $x$, the set $R(x,U)$ is syndetic. In this case, the point $x$ is said to be \emph{uniformly recurrent.} \item The system $(X,T)$ is minimal if and only if for all $x \in X$ and all nonempty, open $U \subseteq X$, the set $R(x,U)$ is syndetic. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Topological dynamics
nodes.statement_short: A point has minimal orbit closure iff its return times to neighbourhoods are syndetic (uniform recurrence); a system is minimal iff all return-time sets to nonempty open sets are syndetic.

nodes.name: Isolated points in minimal systems
nodes.statement: Let $(X,T)$ be a minimal system. There exists an isolated point in $X$ if and only if $X$ is finite and the system $(X,T)$ is periodic.
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Topological dynamics
conclusions: There exists an isolated point in $X$ if and only if $X$ is finite and the system $(X,T)$ is periodic.
equivalent_conditions: There exists an isolated point in $X$
$X$ is finite and the system $(X,T)$ is periodic
nodes.label: lemma_isolated_points_and_minimal_systems

nodes.statement: If $x \in X$ is isolated, the set $U \vcentcolon= \{x\}$ is open. Since $(X,T)$ is minimal, the set $R(x,U)$ is syndetic. In particular, there exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $T^n x = x$, whereby $x$ is a periodic point. Since $(X,T)$ is minimal, the set $X$ is equal to the (finite) orbit of $x$ and $(X,T)$ is periodic. The converse is trivial.
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Topological dynamics
nodes.statement_short: An isolated point has syndetic return times to itself, so is periodic; minimality makes X its finite orbit.

nodes.name: Proximal points
nodes.statement: Let $(X,T)$ be a system and $x, y \in X$. The points $x$ and $y$ are \emph{proximal} if $\inf_{n \in \mathbb{N}} d_X(T^n x, T^n y) = 0$.
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Topological dynamics

nodes.name: Distal point
nodes.statement: The point $x$ is called \emph{distal} if it is proximal only to itself.
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Topological dynamics

nodes.name: Distal system
nodes.statement: The system $(X,T)$ is called \emph{distal} if every point is distal.
nodes.section: 2.2.1 Topological dynamics

nodes.name: Symbolic space
nodes.statement: We denote the space of 0--1 valued functions on $\mathbb{N}$ by $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$.
nodes.section: 2.2.2 Symbolic space and full shift

nodes.name: Evaluation of a symbolic point
nodes.statement: We write $\omega(i)$ for the value of the function $\omega$ at $i$.
nodes.section: 2.2.2 Symbolic space and full shift

nodes.name: Cylinder set
nodes.statement: Given $k \in \{0,1\}$, the \emph{cylinder set} of all those functions in $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ that evaluate to $k$ at $i$ is denoted by $[k]_i$.
nodes.section: 2.2.2 Symbolic space and full shift

nodes.name: Support
nodes.statement: The \emph{support} of $\omega$ is \[{\normalfont\text{supp}}\, (\omega) \vcentcolon= \big\{ n \in \mathbb{N} \ \big| \ \omega(n) = 1 \big\}.\]
nodes.section: 2.2.2 Symbolic space and full shift

nodes.name: Left shift
nodes.statement: We define the (left) shift $\sigma: \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}} \to \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ at the function $\omega$ by the rule $(\sigma \omega)(i) = \omega(i+1)$, $i \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.section: 2.2.2 Symbolic space and full shift

nodes.name: Full shift
nodes.statement: The \emph{full shift} is the system $(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}, \sigma)$.
nodes.section: 2.2.2 Symbolic space and full shift

nodes.name: Stone-Čech compactification as ultrafilters
nodes.statement: As a set, we realize $\beta \mathbb{N}$ as the set of all ultrafilters on $\mathbb{N}$ (cf. \cref{sec_filter_pr_and_ufs}).
nodes.section: 2.2.3 Dynamics on the space of ultrafilters

nodes.name: Basic clopen sets of βN
nodes.statement: Sets of the form \[\overline{A} \vcentcolon= \big\{p \in \beta \mathbb{N} \ \big| \ A \in p \big\}, \quad A \subseteq \mathbb{N},\] form a base for a non-metrizable, compact Hausdorff topology on $\beta \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.section: 2.2.3 Dynamics on the space of ultrafilters

nodes.name: Sum of two ultrafilters is an ultrafilter
nodes.statement: It follows by combining \cref{lemma_equiv_ultrafilter} \eqref{item_family_is_self_dual} and \cref{lemma_filter_algebra} \eqref{item_family_prop_zero}, \eqref{item_family_prop_two}, and \eqref{item_sum_dual} that the sum of two ultrafilters is an ultrafilter.
nodes.section: 2.2.3 Dynamics on the space of ultrafilters

nodes.name: Left ideal
nodes.statement: A nonempty subset $L \subseteq \beta \mathbb{N}$ with the property that $p + L \subseteq L$ for all $p \in \beta \mathbb{N}$ is called a \emph{left ideal}.
nodes.section: 2.2.3 Dynamics on the space of ultrafilters

nodes.name: Minimal left ideal
nodes.statement: A left ideal that is minimal amongst all left ideals is called a \emph{minimal left ideal}.
nodes.section: 2.2.3 Dynamics on the space of ultrafilters

nodes.name: Left addition by 1 on βN
nodes.statement: Denoting addition by 1 on the left by $\lambda_1: \beta \mathbb{N} \to \beta \mathbb{N}$, we see that $(\beta \mathbb{N}, \lambda_1)$ is a non-metrizable topological dynamical system.
nodes.section: 2.2.3 Dynamics on the space of ultrafilters

nodes.name: Minimal ultrafilter
nodes.statement: It is not hard to see that $\beta \mathbb{N} + q$ is a minimal left ideal if and only if the system $(\beta \mathbb{N} + q, \lambda_1)$ is minimal. (Indeed, the system $(\beta \mathbb{N} + q, \lambda_1)$ is minimal if and only if for all $p \in \beta \mathbb{N} + q$, the orbit closure $\beta \mathbb{N} + p$ -- a left ideal -- is equal to $\beta \mathbb{N} + q$.) In this case, the ultrafilter $q$ is called a \emph{minimal ultrafilter}.
nodes.section: 2.2.3 Dynamics on the space of ultrafilters

nodes.name: Action of ultrafilters on a system
nodes.statement: Concretely, for $p \in \beta \mathbb{N}$, the point $T^p x \in X$ is defined uniquely by the property that for all open $U \subseteq X$ containing $T^p x$, the set $R(x,U)$ is a member of $p$.
nodes.section: 2.2.3 Dynamics on the space of ultrafilters

nodes.name: Ultrafilter shift of a clopen return set
nodes.statement: The following fact will be useful for us later on: if $U \subseteq X$ is clopen and $p \in \beta \mathbb{N}$, then \begin{align} R(x,U) - p = R(T^p x, U). \end{align}
nodes.section: 2.2.3 Dynamics on the space of ultrafilters
conclusions: R(x,U) - p = R(T^p x, U).

nodes.name: R(x,U) - p = R(T^p x, U)
nodes.statement: R(x,U) - p = R(T^p x, U).
nodes.section: 2.2.3 Dynamics on the space of ultrafilters
nodes.label: eqn_ultrafilter_shift_of_return_set

nodes.name: Proof of the ultrafilter shift identity
nodes.statement: Indeed, for $n \in \mathbb{N}$, we see that $n \in R(x,U) - p$ if and only if $R(T^n x, U) = R(x,U) - n \in p$. If $R(T^n x, U) \in p$, then \[T^n T^p x = T^{n + p} x = T^{p + n} x = T^p T^n x \in \overline{U} = U,\] whereby $n \in R(T^p x, U)$. On the other hand, if $n \in R(T^p x, U)$, then $T^p T^n x = T^n T^p x \in U$, whereby $R(T^n x, U) \in p$.
nodes.section: 2.2.3 Dynamics on the space of ultrafilters
nodes.statement_short: Unwind the definitions: n lies in R(x,U) - p iff R(T^n x,U) belongs to p; use that U is clopen and T^p commutes with T^n.

nodes.name: Minimal left ideals are universal minimal systems
nodes.statement: Minimal left ideals of $\beta \mathbb{N}$ under addition by 1 are universal minimal dynamical systems.
nodes.section: 2.2.3 Dynamics on the space of ultrafilters

nodes.name: Proof of universality
nodes.statement: More precisely, let $L \subseteq \beta \mathbb{N}$ be a minimal left ideal, and let $(X,T)$ be a not-necessarily-metrizable, minimal dynamical system. Fix $x \in X$. The map $T^{\displaystyle \cdot} x: \beta \mathbb{N} \to X$ described in the previous paragraph is continuous and satisfies $T^{\lambda_1 p} x = T^{1 + p} x = T (T^p x)$ and hence is a factor map $(\beta \mathbb{N},\lambda_1) \to (X,T)$ of systems. Restricted to $L$, by the minimality of $(X,T)$, we see that $T^{\displaystyle \cdot} x: (L, \lambda_1) \to (X,T)$ is surjective and hence is a factor map of minimal systems.
nodes.section: 2.2.3 Dynamics on the space of ultrafilters
nodes.statement_short: The lifted orbit map p ↦ T^p x is a factor map from (βN, λ1); restricted to a minimal left ideal it is onto by minimality.

nodes.name: G sets and G families
nodes.statement: Let $\mathscr{G}$ be a family. A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is called a \emph{$\mathscr{G}$ set} if it is a member of $\mathscr{G}$, and a family $\mathscr{F}$ is called a \emph{$\mathscr{G}$ family} if all members of $\mathscr{F}$ are $\mathscr{G}$ sets, ie., $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{G}$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Families of sets from dynamics

nodes.name: Syndetic, thick and piecewise syndetic sets
nodes.statement: A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is \dots \begin{enumerate} \item \dots \emph{syndetic} if there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that \[ A \cup (A-1) \cup \cdots \cup (A-N) = \mathbb{N}; \] \item \dots \emph{thick} if for all finite $F \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, there exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $F + n \subseteq A$; \item \dots \emph{piecewise syndetic} if there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that the set \[A \cup (A-1) \cup \cdots \cup (A-N)\] is thick. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 2.3.1 Syndetic, thick, and piecewise syndetic sets

nodes.name: Families S, T, PS
nodes.statement: We denote by $\mathcal{S}$, $\mathcal{T}$, and $\mathcal{PS}$ the families of syndetic, thick, and piecewise syndetic subsets of $\mathbb{N}$, respectively.
nodes.section: 2.3.1 Syndetic, thick, and piecewise syndetic sets

nodes.name: Syndetic and thick sets are dual; PS = S ⊓ T
nodes.statement: It is well-known and not difficult to show that the families of syndetic and thick sets are dual and that \[\mathcal{PS} = \mathcal{S} \sqcap \mathcal{T}.\]
nodes.section: 2.3.1 Syndetic, thick, and piecewise syndetic sets

nodes.name: PS is partition regular and PS* is a filter
nodes.statement: By \cref{lemma_class_cap_is_pr}, the family $\mathcal{PS}$ is piecewise syndetic and its dual, $\mathcal{PS}^*$, is a filter.
nodes.section: 2.3.1 Syndetic, thick, and piecewise syndetic sets

nodes.name: Characterization of PS* sets
nodes.statement: It is not hard to show that a set $A$ belongs to $\mathcal{PS}^*$ if and only if for all finite $F \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, there exists a syndetic set $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that $F + S \subseteq A$.
nodes.section: 2.3.1 Syndetic, thick, and piecewise syndetic sets

nodes.name: Thickly syndetic set
nodes.statement: Thus, members of the filter $\mathcal{PS}^*$ are called \emph{thickly syndetic} sets.
nodes.section: 2.3.1 Syndetic, thick, and piecewise syndetic sets

nodes.name: Thick sets and translation-invariant filters
nodes.statement: \leavevmode \begin{enumerate} \item Every proper, translation-invariant filter is a thick, translation-invariant filter. \item A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is thick if and only if it is a member of a proper, translation-invariant filter. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 2.3.1 Syndetic, thick, and piecewise syndetic sets
conclusions: is a thick, translation-invariant filter
A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is thick if and only if it is a member of a proper, translation-invariant filter.
is a thick, translation-invariant filter

nodes.label: lemma_thick_set_filter_char

nodes.statement: \eqref{item_proper_filter_iff_thick} \ Let $\mathscr{F}$ be a proper, translation-invariant filter, and let $A \in \mathscr{F}$. For all $N \in \mathbb{N}$, the set $\bigcap_{n=0}^N (A-n) \in \mathscr{F}$, and hence is nonempty. It follows that $A$ contains an interval of length $N+1$, and hence that $A$ is thick. It follows that $\mathscr{F}$ is thick. \eqref{item_thick_iff_proper_filter} \ If $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is a member of a proper, translation-invariant filter, then it is thick, as shown in the proof of \eqref{item_proper_filter_iff_thick}. Conversely, if $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is thick, then the family \[\big\uparrow \left \{ \bigcap_{n=0}^N (A-n) \ \middle| \ N \in \mathbb{N} \right\}\] is quickly checked to be a thick (hence, proper), translation-invariant filter.
nodes.section: 2.3.1 Syndetic, thick, and piecewise syndetic sets
nodes.statement_short: Members of a proper translation-invariant filter contain long intervals; conversely, intersections of translates of a thick set generate such a filter.

nodes.name: (i) Finite intersections of translates are nonempty, giving long inter
nodes.statement: \eqref{item_proper_filter_iff_thick} \ Let $\mathscr{F}$ be a proper, translation-invariant filter, and let $A \in \mathscr{F}$. For all $N \in \mathbb{N}$, the set $\bigcap_{n=0}^N (A-n) \in \mathscr{F}$, and hence is nonempty. It follows that $A$ contains an interval of length $N+1$, and hence that $A$ is thick. It follows that $\mathscr{F}$ is thick.
nodes.statement_short: (i) Finite intersections of translates are nonempty, giving long intervals.
nodes.section: 2.3.1 Syndetic, thick, and piecewise syndetic sets

nodes.name: (ii) Converse via the filter generated by intersections of translates
nodes.statement: \eqref{item_thick_iff_proper_filter} \ If $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is a member of a proper, translation-invariant filter, then it is thick, as shown in the proof of \eqref{item_proper_filter_iff_thick}. Conversely, if $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is thick, then the family \[\big\uparrow \left \{ \bigcap_{n=0}^N (A-n) \ \middle| \ N \in \mathbb{N} \right\}\] is quickly checked to be a thick (hence, proper), translation-invariant filter.
nodes.statement_short: (ii) Converse via the filter generated by intersections of translates of A.
nodes.section: 2.3.1 Syndetic, thick, and piecewise syndetic sets

nodes.name: Thickly syndetic sets form the largest syndetic translation-invariant filter
nodes.statement: The family $\mathcal{PS}^*$ is a syndetic, translation-invariant filter. If $\mathscr{F}$ is a syndetic, translation-invariant filter, then $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathcal{PS}^*$.
nodes.section: 2.3.1 Syndetic, thick, and piecewise syndetic sets
conclusions: The family $\mathcal{PS}^*$ is a syndetic, translation-invariant filter.
$\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathcal{PS}^*$
nodes.label: lemma_condition_on_subfamily_of_ps_star

nodes.statement: That $\mathcal{PS}^*$ is a syndetic, translation-invariant filter was discussed above. Let $\mathscr{F}$ be a syndetic, translation-invariant filter, and let $A \in \mathscr{F}$. Since $\mathscr{F}$ is translation invariant, for all $N \in \mathbb{N}$, the sets $A-1$, \dots, $A-N$ all belong to $\mathscr{F}$. Since $\mathscr{F}$ is a syndetic filter, the set $(A - 1) \cap \cdots \cap (A - N)$ belongs to $\mathscr{F}$ and is syndetic. Since \[\{1, \ldots, N\} + \big( (A - 1) \cap \cdots \cap (A - N) \big) \subseteq A,\] we see that $A$ is thickly syndetic and hence is a member of $\mathcal{PS}^*$.
nodes.section: 2.3.1 Syndetic, thick, and piecewise syndetic sets
nodes.statement_short: Translation invariance puts A-1,...,A-N in F; their syndetic intersection shifted by {1..N} lies in A, so A is thickly syndetic.

nodes.statement: That $\mathcal{PS}^*$ is a syndetic, translation-invariant filter was discussed above.
nodes.statement_short: First claim was shown above.

Since $\mathscr{F}$ is translation invariant, for all $N \in \mathbb{N}$, the sets $A-1$, \dots, $A-N$ all belong to $\mathscr{F}$. Since $\mathscr{F}$ is a syndetic filter, the set $(A - 1) \cap \cdots \cap (A - N)$ belongs to $\mathscr{F}$ and is syndetic. Since \[\{1, \ldots, N\} + \big( (A - 1) \cap \cdots \cap (A - N) \big) \subseteq A,\] we see that $A$ is thickly syndetic and hence is a member of $\mathcal{PS}^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Intersect translates to exhibit A as thickly syndetic.

nodes.name: IP set
nodes.statement: A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is called an \emph{$\mathcal{IP}$ set} (also, an \emph{infinite, finite sums set}) if there exists a sequence $(x_i)_{i=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that \[\text{FS}(x_i)_{i=1}^\infty \vcentcolon= \left\{ \sum_{f \in F} x_f \ \middle | \ F \subseteq \mathbb{N} \text{ is finite and nonempty} \right\} \subseteq A.\]
nodes.section: 2.3.2 Finite sums sets and central sets

nodes.name: Hindman's theorem: IP is partition regular
nodes.statement: It is a consequence of Hindman's theorem \cite{hindman_1974} that the family $\mathcal{IP}$ is partition regular (see \cite[Lemma 2.1]{bergelson_hindman_1993}).
nodes.section: 2.3.2 Finite sums sets and central sets

nodes.name: IP sets are members of idempotent ultrafilters
nodes.statement: It is well known \cite[Thm. 5.12]{hindman_strauss_book_2012} that a set is an $\mathcal{IP}$ set if and only if it is member of an idempotent ultrafilter.
nodes.section: 2.3.2 Finite sums sets and central sets
conclusions: a set is an $\mathcal{IP}$ set if and only if it is member of an idempotent ultrafilter

it is member of an idempotent ultrafilter

nodes.name: IP sets are members of proper idempotent filters
nodes.statement: A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is an $\mathcal{IP}$ set if and only if it is a member of a proper, idempotent filter.

conclusions: A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is an $\mathcal{IP}$ set if and only if it is a member of a proper, idempotent filter.

it is a member of a proper, idempotent filter

nodes.statement: Suppose $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is an $\mathcal{IP}$ set. There exists $(x_i)_{i=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that $\text{FS}(x_i)_{i=1}^\infty \subseteq A$. We will check that the family \[\mathscr{F} \vcentcolon= \uparrow \big \{ \ \text{FS}(x_i)_{i=N}^\infty \ \big | \ N \in \mathbb{N} \big\}\] is a proper, idempotent filter containing $A$. It is easy to see from the definition that $\mathscr{F}$ is a proper filter. To see that $\mathscr{F}$ is idempotent, let $A \in \mathscr{F}$. We must show that $A - \mathscr{F} \in \mathscr{F}$. By definition, there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $\text{FS}(x_i)_{i=N}^\infty \subseteq A$. We claim that $\text{FS}(x_i)_{i=N}^\infty \subseteq A - \mathscr{F}$, from which it will follow that $A - \mathscr{F} \in \mathscr{F}$. Let $x \in \text{FS}(x_i)_{i=N}^\infty$. We must show that $A - x \in \mathscr{F}$. There exists $F \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ finite with $\min F \geqslant N$ such that $x = \sum_{f \in F} x_f$. We see that $A - x \supseteq \text{FS}(x_i)_{i=\max F + 1}^\infty$, which belongs to $\mathscr{F}$. Therefore, $A - x \in \mathscr{F}$, as desired. Conversely, suppose that $A$ is a member of a proper, idempotent filter $\mathscr{F}$. Since $A \in \mathscr{F}$ and $A - \mathscr{F} \in \mathscr{F}$, there exists $x_1 \in A \cap (A - \mathscr{F})$. Since $A \in \mathscr{F}$ and $A - x_1 \in \mathscr{F}$, we have that $A \cap (A-x_1) \in \mathscr{F}$, and hence that $\big(A \cap (A-x_1) \big) - \mathscr{F} \in \mathscr{F}$. There exists \[x_2 \in A \cap (A-x_1) \cap \big( \big(A \cap (A-x_1) \big) - \mathscr{F} \big).\] So far, we have found $x_1, x_2 \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $\{x_1, x_2, x_1 + x_2\} \subseteq A$. Iterating, we will take $x_3$ from the set \[A \cap (A-x_1) \cap \big( \big(A \cap (A-x_1) \big) - x_2 \big) \cap \bigg( \Big( A \cap (A-x_1) \cap \big( \big(A \cap (A-x_1) \big) - x_2 \big) \Big) - \mathscr{F} \bigg)\] so that all finite sums from the set $\{x_1, x_2, x_3\}$ belong to $A$. It is clear how to proceed to find $(x_i)_{i=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that $\text{FS}(x_i)_{i=1}^\infty \subseteq A$, as desired.
nodes.section: 2.3.2 Finite sums sets and central sets
nodes.statement_short: Tails of a finite-sums set generate a proper idempotent filter; conversely, iterate idempotency to build a finite-sums set inside A.

nodes.name: Define the filter generated by tails FS(x_i)_{i≥N}; it is a proper fil
nodes.statement: Suppose $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is an $\mathcal{IP}$ set. There exists $(x_i)_{i=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that $\text{FS}(x_i)_{i=1}^\infty \subseteq A$. We will check that the family \[\mathscr{F} \vcentcolon= \uparrow \big \{ \ \text{FS}(x_i)_{i=N}^\infty \ \big | \ N \in \mathbb{N} \big\}\] is a proper, idempotent filter containing $A$. It is easy to see from the definition that $\mathscr{F}$ is a proper filter.
nodes.statement_short: Define the filter generated by tails FS(x_i)_{i≥N}; it is a proper filter.

nodes.name: Idempotency: each finite sum x has A - x containing a later tail
nodes.statement: To see that $\mathscr{F}$ is idempotent, let $A \in \mathscr{F}$. We must show that $A - \mathscr{F} \in \mathscr{F}$. By definition, there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $\text{FS}(x_i)_{i=N}^\infty \subseteq A$. We claim that $\text{FS}(x_i)_{i=N}^\infty \subseteq A - \mathscr{F}$, from which it will follow that $A - \mathscr{F} \in \mathscr{F}$. Let $x \in \text{FS}(x_i)_{i=N}^\infty$. We must show that $A - x \in \mathscr{F}$. There exists $F \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ finite with $\min F \geqslant N$ such that $x = \sum_{f \in F} x_f$. We see that $A - x \supseteq \text{FS}(x_i)_{i=\max F + 1}^\infty$, which belongs to $\mathscr{F}$. Therefore, $A - x \in \mathscr{F}$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Idempotency: each finite sum x has A - x containing a later tail.

nodes.name: Converse: choose x_1, x_2, ... iteratively from A ∩ (A - F) to build F
nodes.statement: Conversely, suppose that $A$ is a member of a proper, idempotent filter $\mathscr{F}$. Since $A \in \mathscr{F}$ and $A - \mathscr{F} \in \mathscr{F}$, there exists $x_1 \in A \cap (A - \mathscr{F})$. Since $A \in \mathscr{F}$ and $A - x_1 \in \mathscr{F}$, we have that $A \cap (A-x_1) \in \mathscr{F}$, and hence that $\big(A \cap (A-x_1) \big) - \mathscr{F} \in \mathscr{F}$. There exists \[x_2 \in A \cap (A-x_1) \cap \big( \big(A \cap (A-x_1) \big) - \mathscr{F} \big).\] So far, we have found $x_1, x_2 \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $\{x_1, x_2, x_1 + x_2\} \subseteq A$. Iterating, we will take $x_3$ from the set \[A \cap (A-x_1) \cap \big( \big(A \cap (A-x_1) \big) - x_2 \big) \cap \bigg( \Big( A \cap (A-x_1) \cap \big( \big(A \cap (A-x_1) \big) - x_2 \big) \Big) - \mathscr{F} \bigg)\] so that all finite sums from the set $\{x_1, x_2, x_3\}$ belong to $A$. It is clear how to proceed to find $(x_i)_{i=1}^\infty \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that $\text{FS}(x_i)_{i=1}^\infty \subseteq A$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Converse: choose x_1, x_2, ... iteratively from A ∩ (A - F) to build FS(x_i) inside A.

nodes.name: Central set
nodes.statement: Furstenberg \cite[Def. 8.3]{furstenberg_book_1981} defined a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ to be \emph{central} if there exists a system $(X,T)$, a uniformly recurrent point $x \in X$, a point $y \in X$ proximal to $x$, and an open set $U \subseteq X$ containing $x$ such that $A = R(y,U)$.
nodes.section: 2.3.2 Finite sums sets and central sets

nodes.name: Family of central sets
nodes.statement: We denote the family of central sets by $\mathcal{C}$.
nodes.section: 2.3.2 Finite sums sets and central sets

nodes.name: Bergelson-Hindman-Weiss: central sets are members of minimal idempotent ultrafilters
nodes.statement: Bergelson, Hindman, and Weiss \cite{bergelson_hindman_1990} showed that a subset of $\mathbb{N}$ is central if and only if it is a member of a minimal idempotent ultrafilter on $\mathbb{N}$.
nodes.section: 2.3.2 Finite sums sets and central sets
also_stated_at: It is a result of Bergelson, Hindman, and Weiss \cite{bergelson_hindman_1990} that a subset of $\mathbb{N}$ is central if and only if it belongs to a minimal, idempotent ultrafilter on $\mathbb{N}$.

nodes.name: Central sets are partition regular
nodes.statement: It was stated by Furstenberg and follows immediately from the ultrafilter characterization of central sets that the family $\mathcal{C}$ is partition regular.
nodes.section: 2.3.2 Finite sums sets and central sets

nodes.name: Thick ⊆ central ⊆ PS ∩ IP
nodes.statement: It is well known that thick sets are central and that central sets are piecewise syndetic and $\mathcal{IP}$.
nodes.section: 2.3.2 Finite sums sets and central sets

nodes.name: IP and C are idempotent, not translation invariant
nodes.statement: The families $\mathcal{IP}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ are examples of idempotent families that are not translation invariant.

nodes.name: Proof that IP and C are idempotent
nodes.statement: Alternatively, one can note two things: first, by the characterizations given above, \[\mathcal{IP} = \bigcup_{\substack{p \in \beta \mathbb{N} \\ p \text{ idempotent}}} p \qquad \text{ and } \qquad \mathcal{C} = \bigcup_{\substack{p \in \beta \mathbb{N} \text{ minimal} \\ p \text{ idempotent}}} p,\] and second, a union of idempotent families is idempotent.
nodes.section: 2.3.2 Finite sums sets and central sets
nodes.statement_short: Write IP and C as unions of idempotent (minimal) ultrafilters; a union of idempotent families is idempotent.

nodes.name: Dynamically syndetic set
nodes.statement: A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is \emph{dynamically syndetic} if there exists a minimal topological dynamical system $(X,T)$, a point $x \in X$, and a nonempty, open set $U \subseteq X$ such that $R(x,U) \subseteq A$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Definitions and first characterizations
nodes.statement_short: A contains a return-time set R(x,U) of a point to a nonempty open set in a minimal system.
also_stated_at: A subset of the positive integers, $\mathbb{N}$, is called \emph{dynamically syndetic} if it contains a set of the form \[R_T(x,U) \vcentcolon= \big\{ n \in \mathbb{N} \ \big| \ T^n x \in U \big\}, \quad x \in X, \quad U \subseteq X \text{ nonempty, open},\] where $(X,d_X)$ is a compact metric space and the map $T: X \to X$ generates a minimal action of the semigroup $(\mathbb{N},+)$ on $X$ by continuous maps (see \cref{sec_top_dynamics}).

nodes.name: Dynamically central syndetic set
nodes.statement: If $x \in U$, the set $A$ is called \emph{dynamically central syndetic}.
nodes.section: 3.1 Definitions and first characterizations
also_stated_at: If $x \in U$, such a set is called \emph{dynamically central syndetic}.

nodes.name: Families dS and dcS
nodes.statement: The families of dynamically syndetic and dynamically central syndetic subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ are denoted $d\mathcal{S}$ and $dc\mathcal{S}$, respectively.
nodes.section: 3.1 Definitions and first characterizations

nodes.name: dcS ⊆ dS ⊆ S
nodes.statement: It is clear from the definitions and the facts in \cref{sec_top_dynamics} that \[dc\mathcal{S} \subseteq d\mathcal{S} \subseteq \mathcal{S}.\]
nodes.section: 3.1 Definitions and first characterizations

nodes.name: The inclusions dcS ⊆ dS ⊆ S are proper
nodes.statement: The set of odd, positive integers and the set in \eqref{eqn_intro_even_odd} from the introduction demonstrate that each of these inclusions is proper. (That $2\mathbb{N}-1 \not\in dc\mathcal{S}$ follows from, eg., \cref{lemma_dilates_of_dsyndetic_sets}.)
nodes.section: 3.1 Definitions and first characterizations

nodes.name: Examples of dynamically (central) syndetic sets
nodes.statement: Here is a short list of examples of dynamically (central) syndetic sets that may be helpful to have in mind. Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R} \backslash \mathbb{Q}$. \begin{enumerate} \item The irrational rotation $(\mathbb{R} / \mathbb{Z}, x \mapsto x + \alpha)$, where $\alpha$ is interpreted as an element of $\mathbb{R} / \mathbb{Z}$, is a minimal system. For all $x \in \mathbb{R} / \mathbb{Z}$ and all nonempty, open $U \subseteq \mathbb{R} / \mathbb{Z}$, the set \[R(x,U) = \big\{ n \in \mathbb{N} \ \big| \ x + n \alpha \in U \big\}\] is dynamically syndetic and, if $x \in U$, dynamically central syndetic. More generally, supersets of Bohr (Bohr$_0$) sets -- those arising in this way from compact group rotations -- are dynamically (central) syndetic. \item When $\alpha > 1$, the sequence $(\lfloor n \alpha \rfloor)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is called a \emph{Beatty sequence}. It is not hard to show that the image of this sequence is equal to the set \[\big\{ n \in \mathbb{N} \ \big| \ \big\{ n / \alpha \} \in \big( (\alpha-1) / \alpha, 1 \big) \big\},\] where $\{ \cdot \}: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R} / \mathbb{Z}$ is the quotient map. Thus, Beatty sequences yield Bohr, and hence dynamically syndetic, sets. What is not so clear is that, in fact, Beatty sequences yield dynamically central syndetic sets. We will see this as a consequence of \cref{thm:simple_equivalent_dcS}. \item Using the notation from \eqref{item:irrational_rotation_dcS_definition}, the set \[\big\{ n \in \mathbb{N} \ \big| \ n^2 \alpha \in U \big\}\] is a dynamically syndetic set. It is, in fact, an example of a nil-Bohr set, one that arises from a rotation on a compact homogeneous space of a nilpotent Lie group. Nil-Bohr (nil-Bohr$_0$) sets are dynamically (central) syndetic \cite{Host-Kra_nilbohr}. \item Denote by $\nu_2: \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}_0$ the 2-adic valuation. The set \[A \vcentcolon= \big\{ n \in \mathbb{N} \ \big | \ \nu_2(n) \text{ is even} \big \}\] is a dynamically syndetic set. To see this, one can show that the point $1_A$ is uniformly recurrent in the full shift $(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}_0},\sigma)$, whereby $A = R_\sigma(1_A,[1]_0)$ is dynamically syndetic. In fact, the point $1_{A \cup \{0\}} \in [1]_0$ is uniformly recurrent, and so $A$ is dynamically central syndetic. By \cref{lemma_dilates_of_dsyndetic_sets} and the fact that $\mathbb{N} \backslash A = A / 2$, the same can be said about the set of positive integers with odd 2-adic valuation. \item The \emph{Chacon word} $0010001010010 0010001010010 1 0010001010010\ldots$ is the unique, non-constant word in the symbols $0$ and $1$ that is fixed under the substitutions $0 \mapsto 0010$ and $1 \mapsto 1$. The set of locations of the 1's in the Chacon word is a dynamically syndetic set, for the same reason as in the previous point: the word, interpreted as a point in the full shift $(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}_0},\sigma)$, is known to be uniformly recurrent \cite[Sec. 5.6.6]{devries_2014}.\\ \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 3.1 Definitions and first characterizations
nodes.statement_short: Irrational-rotation return sets (Bohr sets), Beatty sequences, nil-Bohr sets, even 2-adic valuation, and the Chacon word give dynamically (central) syndetic sets.

nodes.name: Definitional robustness of dynamically syndetic sets
nodes.statement: Many of the results in this section demonstrate the robustness of the family of dynamically (central) syndetic sets under changes to the combinatorial, topological, or dynamical requirements in its definition. The family of dynamically (central) syndetic subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ remains unchanged if \dots \begin{enumerate} \item \dots \ the map $T$ is required to be a homeomorphism, that is, if the system $(X,T)$ is required to be invertible. This is shown in \cref{lemma_may_assume_invertible}. \item \dots \ the space $X$ is allowed to be non-metrizable. This is a consequence of \cref{lemma_metrizability_doesnt_matter}. \item \dots \ the space $X$ is required to be zero dimensional and the set $U$ is required to be clopen. This is a consequence of \cref{thm:simple_equivalent_dcS}. \item \dots \ (for dynamically central syndetic sets) the point $x$ is allowed to be in $\overline{U}$ instead of being required to be in $U$. Sets of this form are called \emph{very strongly central} in \cite[Def. 2.10]{bergelson_hindman_strauss_2012}, where a number of equivalent characterizations in terms of ultrafilters are given. That the families of very strongly central sets and dynamically central syndetic sets are the same is shown in \cref{thm:simple_equivalent_dcS}. \item \dots \ sets of return times $R(x,U)$ are considered up to equivalence on thickly syndetic sets ($\mathcal{PS}^*$ sets). This is a consequence of \cref{cor:largest_family_satisfies_cap}: a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is dynamically (central) syndetic if and only if for all thickly syndetic $B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, the set $A \cap B$ is dynamically (central) syndetic. We will have immediate need for a more basic version of this result for cofinite sets in \cref{lemma_ds_dcs_modifyable_on_a_finite_set}.\\ \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 3.1 Definitions and first characterizations
nodes.statement_short: dS and dcS are unchanged by requiring invertibility, allowing non-metrizable spaces, requiring zero-dimensional spaces and clopen sets, allowing x in the closure of U, or modifying on non-PS sets.

nodes.name: Limits of definitional robustness
nodes.statement: There are other directions, however, in which this definitional robustness does not extend. \begin{enumerate} \setcounter{enumi}{5} \item Minimality is a key feature of the definition. For all $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, there exists a system $(X,T)$, a point $x \in X$, and a nonempty, open set $U \subseteq X$ containing $x$ such that $A = R(x,U)$. Indeed, note that considering $A$ as a subset of $\mathbb{N}_0$, we have that $A = R(1_{A},[1]_0)$ in the full shift $(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}_0},\sigma)$. Thus, dropping the minimality assumption trivializes the definition of dynamical syndeticity. \item That we are considering actions of the semigroup $(\mathbb{N},+)$ instead of the group $(\mathbb{Z},+)$ matters. For example, if we define dynamically central syndetic subsets of $\mathbb{Z}$ analogously to those in $\mathbb{N}$, we see that all dynamically central syndetic subsets of $\mathbb{Z}$ contain 0. In this case, if $x \in \overline{U} \backslash U$, then the set $R(x,U) \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$ is, in contrast to \cref{thm:simple_equivalent_dcS}, not dynamically central syndetic because it does not contain 0. Other results from this paper for $(\mathbb{N},+)$-systems fail to generalize under this definition, too, most notably the fact that thickly syndetic ($\mathcal{PS}^*$) sets (which do not necessarily contain 0) are dynamically central syndetic. Along with other evidence, this suggests that allowing $x \in \overline{U}$ in the definition of the family of dynamically central syndetic sets (as in \cref{thm:simple_equivalent_dcS} \eqref{item:very_strongly_central}) may yield the ``right'' notion for more general (semi)group actions. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 3.1 Definitions and first characterizations
nodes.statement_short: Without minimality every set is a return-time set; and over Z the analogous dcS notion forces 0 in the set, so results do not transfer verbatim.

nodes.name: Dynamically syndetic sets via invertible systems

nodes.label: lemma_may_assume_invertible

nodes.statement: The ``if'' statement is immediate. To see the ``only if'' statement, suppose $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is dynamically syndetic. There exists a system $(X,T)$, a point $x \in X$, and a nonempty, open set $U \subseteq X$ such that $R(x,U) \subseteq A$. Let $\pi: (W,T) \to (X,T)$ be the natural extension (see \cite[Definition 6.8.10]{downarowiczbook}) of $(X,T)$, and let $w \in W$ be such that $\pi w = x$. Since $(X,T)$ is minimal, so is $(W,T)$ (see, for example, \cite[Lemma 2.9]{glasscock_koutsogiannis_richter_2019}). The system $(W,T)$ is invertible, and $R(w,\pi^{-1} U) = R(x,U)$. Thus, the set $A$ contains $R(w,\pi^{-1} U)$ from the invertible system $(W,T)$. Note that if $A$ is dynamically central syndetic and $x \in U$, then $w \in \pi^{-1} U$, whereby the set $R(x,U) = R(w,\pi^{-1} U)$ is dynamically central syndetic from the invertible system $(W,T)$.

nodes.statement: By the definition of dynamically (central) syndetic, it suffices to show that for all minimal systems $(X,T)$, all points $x \in X$, all nonempty, open sets $U \subseteq X$ (containing $x$), and all $N \in \mathbb{N}$, the set $R(x,U) \backslash \{1, \ldots, N\}$ is dynamically (central) syndetic. So, let $(X,T)$, $x \in X$, $U \subseteq X$ (contain $x$), and $N \in \mathbb{N}$ be as described. The set $V \vcentcolon= U \backslash \{Tx, T^2x, \ldots, T^N x\}$ is open and $R(x,U) \backslash \{1, \ldots, N\} \supseteq R(x, V)$. If $V$ is nonempty, then we see that the set $R(x,U) \backslash \{1, \ldots, N\}$ is dynamically syndetic, as desired. Note that if $x \in \{Tx, T^2x, \ldots, T^N x\}$, then the system is periodic, $X = \{Tx, T^2x, \ldots, T^N x\}$, and $V$ is empty. Therefore, if $V$ is nonempty and $x \in U$, then $x \in V$, and the set $R(x,U) \backslash \{1, \ldots, N\}$ is dynamically central syndetic, as desired. If, on the other hand, the set $V$ is empty, then $U \subseteq \{Tx, T^2x, \ldots, T^N x\}$. Since $U$ is open, we see that some $T^i x$ is an isolated point of $X$. By \cref{lemma_isolated_points_and_minimal_systems}, the system $(X,T)$ is finite and periodic. In this case, the set $R(x,U) \backslash \{1, \ldots, N\}$ contains an infinite arithmetic progression (of the form $k \mathbb{N}$), which is dynamically (central) syndetic, as desired.

nodes.statement: Let $x \in X$ and $U \subseteq X$ be nonempty and open. Fix $L \subseteq \beta \mathbb{N}$ a minimal left ideal. As described in \cref{sec_topology_and_ultrafilters}, the map $\pi: (L, \lambda_1) \to (X,T)$ given by $\pi(p) = T^p x$ is a factor map of minimal systems. By \cite[Thm. 19.23]{hindman_strauss_book_2012}, since $x$ is uniformly recurrent, there exists an idempotent $p \in L$ such that $\pi(p) = x$. It is quick to check that \[R_T(x, U) = R_{\lambda_1}(p, \pi^{-1} U).\] We will show that the set $R_{\lambda_1}(p, \pi^{-1} U)$ is dynamically syndetic. By the definition of the topology on $\beta \mathbb{N}$, since $\pi^{-1} U$ is nonempty and open, there exists $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that $\emptyset \neq \overline{A} \cap L \subseteq \pi^{-1} U$. In the notation defined in \cref{sec_family_algebra}, we see that \begin{align} R_{\lambda_1}(p, \pi^{-1} U) \supseteq R_{\lambda_1}(p, \overline{A}) = A - p. \end{align} Since $\overline{A} \cap L \neq \emptyset$ and $(L,\lambda_1)$ is minimal, we see that the set $A-p$ is nonempty (indeed, syndetic). Considering $1_A$ as an element of $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}_0}$, we see in the full shift $(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}_0}, \sigma)$ that $A = R_{\sigma}(1_A,[1]_0)$. It follows by \eqref{eqn_ultrafilter_shift_of_return_set} in \cref{sec_topology_and_ultrafilters} that \[A - p = R_{\sigma}(1_A,[1]_0) - p = R_{\sigma}(T^p 1_A, [1]_0).\] Since $p$ is a minimal idempotent ultrafilter, we have by \cite[Thm. 19.23]{hindman_strauss_book_2012} that the point $T^p 1_A$ is uniformly recurrent under the shift. Since $R_{\sigma}(T^p 1_A, [1]_0)$ is nonempty, we see that the set $R_{\sigma}(T^p 1_A, [1]_0)$, and hence the set $A - p = R_{\lambda_1}(p, \overline{A})$, is dynamically syndetic. Because these families are upward closed, by \eqref{eqn_requisite_containment_of_non_metrizable_returns}, the same can be said about the set $R_{\lambda_1}(p, \pi^{-1} U) = R_T(x, U)$, as was to be shown. In the case that $x \in U$, we wish to show that the set $R_T(x,U)$ is dynamically central syndetic. The argument given above can be followed with some additional information. First, since $x \in U$, the point $p \in \pi^{-1} U$. The set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ can then be assumed to be such that $p \in \overline{A} \cap L$. Considering $1_A$ as an element of $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}_0}$, we see \[R_\sigma(1_A,[1]_0) = A \in p,\] whereby $T^p 1_A \in [1]_0$. Thus, the set $A-p = R_{\sigma}(T^p 1_A, [1]_0)$ is dynamically central syndetic, as desired.

nodes.name: Translates of dynamically syndetic sets
nodes.statement: Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be dynamically syndetic. \begin{enumerate} \item For all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the set $A-n$ is dynamically syndetic. \item The set \begin{align} \big\{ n \in \mathbb{N} \ \big| \ A-n \text{ is dynamically central syndetic} \big\} \end{align} is dynamically syndetic. \item If $A$ is dynamically central syndetic, then the set in \eqref{eqn_translates_of_ds_set} is dynamically central syndetic. \end{enumerate} Moreover, \eqref{item_all_translates_are_ds}, \eqref{item_some_translates_are_dcs}, and \eqref{item_dcs_translates_of_dcs_are_dcs} hold with $A-n$ replaced by $A+n$. Finally, \begin{align} d\mathcal{S} = \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \big(dc\mathcal{S} - n \big) = \bigcup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \big(dc\mathcal{S} + n \big). \end{align}

nodes.statement: Since $A$ is dynamically syndetic, there exists a minimal system $(X,T)$, a point $x \in X$, and a nonempty, open set $U \subseteq X$ such that $R(x,U) \subseteq A$. According to \cref{lemma_may_assume_invertible}, we can assume the system $(X, T)$ is invertible. For $n \in \mathbb{N}$, we have that \begin{align} R(T^n x, U) = R(x,U) - n \subseteq A - n. \end{align} Thus, the set $A-n$ is dynamically syndetic, demonstrating \eqref{item_all_translates_are_ds}. It also follows from \eqref{eqn_translate_of_rxu_in_aminusn} that $R(x,U)$ is a subset of the set in \eqref{eqn_translates_of_ds_set}. Indeed, if $n \in R(x,U)$, then $T^n x \in U$, so the set $A-n$ is dynamically central syndetic. The set $R(x,U)$ is dynamically syndetic, whereby the set in \eqref{eqn_translates_of_ds_set} is dynamically syndetic, demonstrating \eqref{item_some_translates_are_dcs}. All of this holds in the case that $A$ is dynamically central syndetic, but we have additionally that $R(x,U)$ is dynamically central syndetic, demonstrating \eqref{item_dcs_translates_of_dcs_are_dcs}. Now we will show that \eqref{item_all_translates_are_ds}, \eqref{item_some_translates_are_dcs}, and \eqref{item_dcs_translates_of_dcs_are_dcs} hold with $A-n$ replaced by $A+n$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Recall that $T: X \to X$ is a homeomorphism. We claim that $R(x,U) + n = R(T^{-n}x, U) \cap \{n+1,n+2,\ldots\}$. Indeed, note that $m \in R(x,U) + n$ if and only if $m - n \in R(x,U)$ if and only if $T^{m-n} x \in U$ and $m \geqslant n+1$ if and only if $T^m T^{-n}x \in U$ and $m \geqslant n+1$ if and only if $m \in R(T^{-n}x,U) \cap \{n+1, n+2, \ldots\}$. By \cref{lemma_ds_dcs_modifyable_on_a_finite_set}, the set $R(T^{-n}x,U) \cap \{n+1,n+2,\ldots\}$ is dynamically syndetic. Therefore, the set $A + n$ is dynamically syndetic, demonstrating \eqref{item_all_translates_are_ds}. Since $(X,T)$ is minimal and invertible, the system $(X,T^{-1})$ is minimal (see, for example, \cite[Lemma 2.7]{glasscock_koutsogiannis_richter_2019}). We claim that the set $R_{T^{-1}}(x,U)$ is contained in the set in \eqref{eqn_translates_of_ds_set}. This will finish the proof of \eqref{item_some_translates_are_dcs} and \eqref{item_dcs_translates_of_dcs_are_dcs} since $R_{T^{-1}}(x,U)$ is dynamically syndetic and dynamically central syndetic when $x \in U$. Suppose $n \in R_{T^{-1}}(x,U)$ so that $T^{-n} x \in U$. From the previous paragraph, we see that $R(T^{-n}x, U) \cap \{n+1, n+2, \ldots\} = R(x,U) + n \subseteq A +n$. By \cref{lemma_ds_dcs_modifyable_on_a_finite_set}, we have that the set $A + n$ is dynamically central syndetic, whereby $n$ belongs to the set in \eqref{eqn_translates_of_ds_set}, as desired. Finally, that \eqref{eqn_relationship_between_ds_and_dcs_classes} holds follows immediately from \eqref{item_all_translates_are_ds} and \eqref{item_some_translates_are_dcs} for $A-n$ and $A+n$.

nodes.statement: It is interesting to formulate the conclusions of \cref{lemma_translates_of_dsyndetic_sets} in terms of the family algebra developed in \cref{sec_combinatorics}. Thus, \begin{enumerate} \item the family $d\mathcal{S}$ is translation invariant, that is, $d\mathcal{S} \subseteq \{\mathbb{N}\} + d\mathcal{S}$; \item $d\mathcal{S} \subseteq d\mathcal{S} + dc\mathcal{S}$; and \item the family $dc\mathcal{S}$ is idempotent, that is, $dc\mathcal{S} \subseteq dc\mathcal{S} + dc\mathcal{S}$.\\ \end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: The second equality is proven in \cite[Thm. 3.7]{Huang_Shao_Ye_2019}. We will derive the first from the second. Suppose $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is piecewise syndetic; it is not hard to see from the definition that there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $A \cup (A+1) \cup \cdots \cup (A+N)$ is thick. Since thick sets are central and the family of central sets is partition regular, some $A+i$ is central. By the second equality, there exists $B \in dc\mathcal{S}$ and $H \in \mathcal{T}$ such that $A+i \supseteq B \cap H$. Therefore, we have that $A \supseteq (B-i) \cap (H-i)$. By \cref{lemma_translates_of_dsyndetic_sets}, the set $B-i$ is dynamically syndetic and the set $H-i$ is thick, as was to be shown.

nodes.statement: Let $A \in dc\mathcal{S}$. Let $(X, T)$ be a minimal system, $x \in X$, and $U \subseteq X$ be an open neighborhood of $x$ such that $A \supseteq R(x, U)$. We will show that $k A \in dc\mathcal{S}$ by considering a suspension system with base $(X, T)$. More precisely, let $Y = X \times \{0, 1, \ldots, k - 1\}$, and define $S: Y \to Y$ by \[ S(x', \eta) = \begin{cases} (x', \eta + 1) \text{ if } \eta \leqslant k - 2, \\ (Tx', 0) \text{ if } \eta = k - 1. \end{cases} \] It is easy to see that the orbit of every point in $Y$ is dense, whereby $(Y, S)$ is minimal. Also, we see that $k R_T(x, U) = R_S ((x, 0), U \times \{0\}) \in dc\mathcal{S}$, as desired. To see that $A/k \in dc\mathcal{S}$, we appeal to a well-known fact (cf. \cite[Cor. 3.2]{Ye-D_function}): if a point in a system is uniformly recurrent under the transformation, then it is uniformly recurrent under every power of the transformation. Since $(X,T)$ is minimal, the point $x$ is uniformly recurrent under $T$, and hence uniformly recurrent under $T^k$. Therefore, the system $(\overline{T^{k \mathbb{N}_0} x}, T^k)$ is minimal, contains $x$, and $A/k \supseteq R_{T^k}(x, U \cap \overline{T^{k \mathbb{N}_0} x}) \in dc\mathcal{S}$, as desired. Suppose $A \in d\mathcal{S}$. By \cref{lemma_translates_of_dsyndetic_sets} \eqref{item_some_translates_are_dcs}, there exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $A - n \in dc\mathcal{S}$. By the first paragraph of this proof, we have $k(A - n) \in dc\mathcal{S}$. Therefore, by \cref{lemma_translates_of_dsyndetic_sets} \eqref{item_all_translates_are_ds}, we see $k A \supseteq k(A - n) + kn \in d\mathcal{S}$, whereby $kA \in d\mathcal{S}$, as desired.

nodes.name: Return set whose indicator is not uniformly recurrent
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha \in (0, 1)$ be irrational. Let $X \vcentcolon= \mathbb{R} / \mathbb{Z}$ and $T: X \to X$ be defined by $T(x) = x + \alpha$. Let $U \vcentcolon= X \backslash \{\alpha\}$ and $x \vcentcolon= 0$. We see that \[ 1_{R(0,U)} = (1_{U}(T^n x))_{n \in \mathbb{N}} = (1_U( \alpha), 1_U(2 \alpha), 1_U(3 \alpha), \ldots) = (0, 1, 1, \ldots). \] Since $\alpha$ is irrational, for all $n \geqslant 2$, $T^n \alpha \neq \alpha$. Therefore, the function $1_{R(0,U)}$ takes the value $0$ only at $1$. The point $1_{R(0,U)} \in [0]_1$ is not uniformly recurrent because it never returns to the neighborhood $[0]_1$.

nodes.name: Symbolic characterization of dynamically central syndetic sets
nodes.statement: Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. The following statements are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item The set $A$ is dynamically central syndetic. \item There exists a minimal system $(X,T)$, a nonempty, open set $U \subseteq X$, and a point $x \in \overline{U}$ such that $R(x,U) \subseteq A$. \item There exists a subset $B \subseteq A$ such that the point $1_{B \cup \{0\}}$ is uniformly recurrent in the full shift $(\{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}_0}, \sigma)$. In particular, the system $(X \vcentcolon= \overline{\sigma^{\mathbb{N}_0} 1_{B \cup \{0\}}}, \sigma)$ is minimal, the set $X \cap [1]_0$ is a clopen neighborhood of $1_{B \cup \{0\}}$, and $B = R(1_{B \cup \{0\}}, X \cap [1]_0) \subseteq A$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: (\ref{item:dcsyndetic}) $\Rightarrow$ (\ref{item:very_strongly_central}) \ This follows by definition. (\ref{item:very_strongly_central}) $\Rightarrow$ (\ref{item:1_A_0_uniformly_recurrent}) \ Assume that $A \supseteq R(x, U)$, where $(X, T)$ is a minimal system, $U \subseteq X$ is nonempty and open, and $x \in \overline{U}$. If $x$ is a periodic point of $(X, T)$, let $n_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ be least such that $T^{n_0} x = x$. Since $(X, T)$ is minimal, $X = \{x, Tx, \ldots, T^{n_0 - 1} x\}$. As $X$ is finite and $x \in \overline{U}$, it must be that $x \in U$. Letting $B = n_0 \mathbb{N}$ be the set of positive multiples of $n_0$, we have that $A \supseteq R(x, U) \supseteq B$ and that $1_{B \cup \{0\}}$ is a periodic, hence uniformly recurrent, point in $\{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}_0}$. Suppose that $x$ is not a periodic point of $(X,T)$. We claim that there exists a nonempty, open set $V \subseteq U$ such that $x \in \overline{V}$ and the boundary $\partial V$ is disjoint from $T^{\mathbb{N}} x \vcentcolon= \{T^n x \ | \ n \in \mathbb{N}\}$. If $x \in U$, choose $V = B_\delta(x)$ for some small $\delta > 0$. Note that the boundary of $B_\delta(x)$ is the set $\{z \in X \ | \ d_X(x, z) = \delta\}$, which may be empty. Since there are uncountably many choices for $\delta$, there exists a choice so that the boundary is disjoint from $T^{\mathbb{N}} x$. Suppose that $x \in \partial U = \overline{U} \backslash U$. There exists a sequence of pairwise distinct points $(x_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ in $U \backslash \{x\}$ such that $\lim_{k \to \infty }x_k = x$. Inductively, choose a sequence of disjoint balls $B_{\delta_k}(x_k) \subseteq U$ with $\lim_{k \to \infty} \delta_k = 0$ such that the boundary of each $B_{\delta_k}(x_k)$ has empty intersection with $T^{\mathbb{N}} x$. Let $V = \bigcup_{k = 1}^{\infty} B_{\delta_k}(x_k)$. It is clear that $V$ is an open subset of $U$. Since $\lim_{k \to \infty }x_k = x$, we have that $\partial V = \{x\} \cup \bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} \partial V_k$, and so the boundary of $V$ is disjoint from $T^{\mathbb{N}} x$. Our claim is proved. Let $B = R(x, V)$. Since $V$ is nonempty and $V \subseteq U$, we have that $B$ is nonempty and that $B \subseteq A$. It remains to show that $1_{B \cup \{0\}}$ is a uniformly recurrent point in $(\{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}_0}, \sigma)$. By the topology on the space $\{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}_0}$, we must show that for all $L \in \mathbb{N}$, there exists a syndetic set of positive integers $m$ such that \begin{align} \text{for all $i \in \{0, \ldots, L\}$}, \ 1_{B \cup \{0\}}(m+i) = 1_{B \cup \{0\}}(i). \end{align} Let $L \in \mathbb{N}$. As $\partial V \cap T^{\mathbb{N}} x = \emptyset$, for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the point $T^n x$ is either in $V$ or in $X \backslash \overline{V}$. For $n \in \{1, \ldots, L\}$, define \[ W_n = \begin{cases} V & \text{ if } T^n x \in V \\ X \backslash \overline{V} & \text{ if } T^n x \in X \backslash \overline{V}. \end{cases} \] It follows that $x \in \bigcap_{n = 1}^L T^{-n} W_n$. Since each $W_n$ is open, the set $\bigcap_{n = 1}^L T^{-n} W_n$ is an open neighborhood of $x$. Because $x \in \overline{V}$, the set $V \cap \bigcap_{n = 1}^L T^{-n} W_n$ is nonempty and open. Since $(X, T)$ is minimal, the set \[R \left( x, V \cap \bigcap_{n = 1}^L T^{-n} W_n \right)\] is syndetic, and all integers $m$ in this set satisfy the condition in \eqref{eq:syndetic_return_condition}. This demonstrates that $1_{B \cup \{0\}}$ is uniformly recurrent under the shift, as desired. (\ref{item:1_A_0_uniformly_recurrent}) $\Rightarrow$ (\ref{item:dcsyndetic}) \ Suppose $A$ contains a subset $B$ for which $1_{B \cup \{0\}}$ is uniformly recurrent in $(\{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}_0}, \sigma)$. The system $(X \vcentcolon= \overline{\sigma^{\mathbb{N}_0} 1_{B \cup \{0\}}}, \sigma)$ is minimal, and the cylinder set $X \cap [1]_0$ is open and contains $1_{B \cup \{0\}}$. Since $A \supseteq B = R(1_{B \cup \{0\}}, X \cap [1]_0)$, we have that $A$ is dynamically central syndetic, as desired.

The following statements are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item The set $A$ is dynamically syndetic. \item There exists a nonempty subset $B \subseteq A$ for which the point $1_B$ is uniformly recurrent in the full shift $(\{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}},\sigma)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 3.1.3 Symbolic characterizations of dynamically syndetic sets
conclusions: The following statements are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item The set $A$ is dynamically syndetic. \item There exists a nonempty subset $B \subseteq A$ for which the point $1_B$ is uniformly recurrent in the full shift $(\{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}},\sigma)$. \end{enumerate}
equivalent_conditions: The set $A$ is dynamically syndetic.
There exists a nonempty subset $B \subseteq A$ for which the point $1_B$ is uniformly recurrent in the full shift $(\{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}},\sigma)$.
nodes.label: thm:simple_equivalent_dS

nodes.statement: (\ref{item:dsyndetic_one}) $\Rightarrow$ (\ref{item:1_A_uniform_recurrent_one}) \ Suppose $A$ is dynamically syndetic. By \cref{lemma_translates_of_dsyndetic_sets}, there exists $k \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $A + k$ is dynamically central syndetic. By \cref{thm:simple_equivalent_dcS}, there exists a set $B \subseteq A + k$ such that $1_{B \cup \{0\}}$ is uniformly recurrent in $(\{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}_0},\sigma)$. Note that $B - k \subseteq A$. Since $1_{B \cup \{0\}}$ is uniformly recurrent in $(\{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}_0},\sigma)$, we have that $1_{B}$ is a uniformly recurrent point in $(\{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}},\sigma)$. Applying $\sigma^k$, we have that $\sigma^k 1_B = 1_{B-k}$ is uniformly recurrent, as was claimed. (\ref{item:1_A_uniform_recurrent_one}) $\Rightarrow$ (\ref{item:dsyndetic_one}) \ Suppose $A$ contains a nonempty subset $B$ for which $1_{B}$ is uniformly recurrent in $(\{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}},\sigma)$. Let $k = \min B$. Since $1_{B}$ is uniformly recurrent, so is $\sigma^k 1_B = 1_{B-k}$. Since $k \in B$, we have that $1_{(B-k) \cup \{0\}}$ is uniformly recurrent in $\{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}_0}$. By \cref{thm:simple_equivalent_dcS}, the set $B - k \in dc\mathcal{S}$. Since $A - k \supseteq B - k$, the set $A - k$ is dynamically central syndetic. By \cref{lemma_translates_of_dsyndetic_sets}, the set $A \supseteq (A-k) + k$ is dynamically syndetic, as desired.

nodes.name: N partitions into infinitely many dcS sets
nodes.statement: This theorem is best contextualized as a strengthening of \cite[Thm. 2.13]{bergelson_hindman_strauss_2012}, which (when combined with \cref{thm:simple_equivalent_dcS}) says that $\mathbb{N}$ can be partitioned into infinitely many disjoint $dc\mathcal{S}$ sets.
nodes.section: 3.1.4 Partitioning dynamically central syndetic sets: a proof of E

nodes.statement: Let $A \in dc\mathcal{S}$. We will prove that $A$ can be partitioned into two disjoint $dc\mathcal{S}$ sets. Then, by repeatedly partitioning the second set into disjoint $dc\mathcal{S}$ sets, \[A = A_0 \cup A_1 = A_{0} \cup A_{10} \cup A_{11} = A_{0} \cup A_{10} \cup A_{110} \cup A_{111} = \cdots,\] we see that $A$ can be partitioned into infinitely many disjoint $dc\mathcal{S}$ sets. Let $(X, T)$ be a minimal system and $U \subseteq X$ be an open neighborhood of $x$ such that $A \supseteq R(x, U)$. We consider two cases. Case 1: the point $x$ is an isolated point of $X$. By \cref{lemma_isolated_points_and_minimal_systems}, the system $(X,T)$ is finite and periodic. Let $(\mathbb{T} \vcentcolon= \mathbb{R} / \mathbb{Z}, S)$ be the rotation on the one-dimensional torus by an irrational $\alpha$. Let $V_1 = (0, 1/2), V_2 = (1/2, 1)$, which are two disjoint, open subsets of $\mathbb{T}$ whose closures contain $0$. Then $\{x\} \times V_1$ and $\{x\} \times V_2$ are two disjoint, open subsets of $X \times \mathbb{T}$ whose closures contain $(x, 0)$. Note that the system $(X \times \mathbb{T}, T \times S)$ is minimal, and so by \cref{thm:simple_equivalent_dcS}, the sets $R((x, 0), \{x\} \times V_1)$ and $R((x, 0), \{x\} \times V_2)$ are $dc\mathcal{S}$. Moreover, \[ A \supseteq R(x, U) \supseteq R(x, \{x\}) \supseteq R((x, 0), \{x\} \times V_1) \cup R((x, 0), \{x\} \times V_2). \] Case 2: the point $x$ is a limit point of $U$. Arguing as in the proof of \cref{thm:simple_equivalent_dcS}, there exists a sequence of disjoint open balls $B_{\delta_k}(x_k)$ in $U$ such that $x_k \to x$ and $\delta_k \to 0$. Take \[ V_0 = \bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} B_{\delta_{2k}}(x_{2k}) \text{ and } V_1 = \bigcup_{k=1}^{\infty} B_{\delta_{2k - 1}}(x_{2k - 1}). \] Then $V_0, V_1$ are disjoint open subsets of $U$ satisfying $x \in \overline{V_0} \cap \overline{V_1}$. By \cref{thm:simple_equivalent_dcS}, the sets $R(x, V_0)$ and $R(x, V_1)$ are $dc\mathcal{S}$ sets and, by construction, they are disjoint subsets of $A$. Put $A_0 \vcentcolon= R(x,V_0)$ and $A_1 \vcentcolon= A \backslash R(x,V_0)$ to see that $A = A_0 \cup A_1$ is a disjoint partition of $A$ into $dc\mathcal{S}$ sets, as desired.
nodes.section: 3.1.4 Partitioning dynamically central syndetic sets: a proof of E
nodes.statement_short: Split A into two dcS sets and iterate; for isolated x use a product with an irrational rotation, otherwise two disjoint unions of balls accumulating at x (Theorem 3.8).

nodes.name: Central syndetic set
nodes.statement: A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is a \emph{central syndetic} if it is a member of a syndetic, idempotent filter on $\mathbb{N}$.

nodes.name: Closure of a family in βN
nodes.statement: In what follows, for a family $\mathscr{F}$ on $\mathbb{N}$, we denote by $\overline{\mathscr{F}}$ the set $\bigcap_{A \in \mathscr{F}} \overline{A}$ in $\beta \mathbb{N}$.

nodes.name: Syndetic filters meet every minimal left ideal
nodes.statement: For all syndetic filters $\mathscr{F}$ on $\mathbb{N}$ and all minimal left ideals $L \subseteq \beta \mathbb{N}$, we have $L \cap \overline{\mathscr{F}} \neq \emptyset$.

conclusions: $L \cap \overline{\mathscr{F}} \neq \emptyset$

nodes.statement: We will use the following well-known fact (\cite[Thm. 4.48]{hindman_strauss_book_2012}): for all syndetic sets $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and all minimal left ideals $L \subseteq \beta \mathbb{N}$, we have $\overline{A} \cap L \neq \emptyset$. Let $\mathscr{F}$ be a syndetic filter on $\mathbb{N}$, and let $L \subseteq \beta \mathbb{N}$ be a minimal left ideal. Consider the set $\{\overline{A} \cap L \ | \ A \in \mathscr{F}\}$. By the fact from the previous paragraph, the set consists of closed, nonempty subsets of $L$. Since $\mathscr{F}$ is a filter, the set has the finite intersection property. Since $L$ is compact, we have that $\overline{\mathscr{F}} \cap L$ is nonempty, as desired.

nodes.name: Syndetic idempotent filters lie in minimal idempotent ultrafilters
nodes.statement: For all syndetic, idempotent filters $\mathscr{F}$ on $\mathbb{N}$ and all minimal left ideals $L \subseteq \beta \mathbb{N}$, there exists an idempotent ultrafilter in $L$ containing $\mathscr{F}$.
nodes.section: 3.2.1 Central syndetic sets are central
conclusions: there exists an idempotent ultrafilter in $L$ containing $\mathscr{F}$
nodes.label: thm_sifs_are_contained_in_idempotents

nodes.statement: Let $\mathscr{F}$ be a syndetic, idempotent filter on $\mathbb{N}$. By \cref{lemma_syndetic_contained_in_minimal}, there exists a minimal ultrafilter $p \in \beta \mathbb{N}$ such that $\mathscr{F} \subseteq p$. Define $L = \beta \mathbb{N} + p$. Since $p$ is minimal, the set $L$ is a minimal left ideal, and hence subsemigroup, of $(\beta \mathbb{N}, +)$. By \cite[Thm. 2.6]{hindman_strauss_book_2012}, the set $L$ is compact. Therefore, the set $L$ is a compact subsemigroup of $(\beta \mathbb{N}, +)$ containing $p$. It follows from the proof of \cref{thm_equiv_forms_of_max_idempot_filter} that the set $\overline{\mathscr{F}}$ is a compact subsemigroup of $(\beta \mathbb{N}, +)$. It clearly contains $p$. Define $X = L \cap \overline{\mathscr{F}}$. Since both $L$ and $\overline{\mathscr{F}}$ are compact subsemigroups of $(\beta \mathbb{N}, +)$ containing $p$, so is $X$. By \cite[Thm. 2.5]{hindman_strauss_book_2012}, there exists an idempotent ultrafilter $q \in X$. Since $X \subseteq L$, we see that $q$ is minimal. Since $X \subseteq \overline{\mathscr{F}}$, we see that $\mathscr{F} \subseteq q$. Thus, we have shown that $\mathscr{F}$ is contained in a minimal, idempotent ultrafilter in $L$, as desired.

nodes.statement: Since $A$ is central syndetic, there exists a syndetic, idempotent filter $\mathscr{F}$ containing $A$. Let $L \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a minimal left ideal. By \cref{thm_sifs_are_contained_in_idempotents}, there exists an idempotent $p \in L$ such that $\mathscr{F} \subseteq p$. In particular, we have that $A \in p$. If $H \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is thick, by \cite[Thm. 4.48]{hindman_strauss_book_2012}, there exists a minimal left ideal $L \subseteq \overline{H}$. By the reasoning in the previous paragraph, there exists an idempotent $p \in L$ containing $A$. Therefore, $A \cap H \in p$, whereby the set $A \cap H$ is central.

nodes.name: Strongly central sets
nodes.statement: In \cite{bergelson_hindman_strauss_2012}, a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is called \emph{strongly central} if it has the property that for all minimal left ideals $L \subseteq \beta \mathbb{N}$, there exists an idempotent $p \in L$ containing $A$. Thus, \cref{cor_central_syndetic_is_strongly_central} shows that central syndetic sets are strongly central. It will follow, however, from our main result in this section, \cref{thm_dcs_iff_cs}, that strongly central sets need not be central syndetic. Indeed, a corollary of \cref{thm:simple_equivalent_dcS,thm_dcs_iff_cs} is that the family of central syndetic sets is the same as the family of \emph{very strongly central sets}, in the terminology of \cite{bergelson_hindman_strauss_2012}. An example of a strongly central, but not very strongly central, set is given in \cite[Thm. 2.17]{bergelson_hindman_strauss_2012}.

nodes.name: Combinatorial characterization of central syndetic sets
nodes.statement: Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. \begin{enumerate} \item If $A$ is central syndetic and $\mathscr{F}$ is a syndetic, idempotent filter to which $A$ belongs, then the set $A \cap (A-\mathscr{F})$ satisfies the condition in \eqref{eqn_def_of_cssd}. \item If $A$ satisfies the condition in \eqref{eqn_def_of_cssd}, then the family \[\mathscr{F} \vcentcolon= \big\uparrow \bigg\{ A \cap \bigcap_{f \in F} (A - f) \ \bigg | \ F \subseteq A \text{ is finite} \bigg\}\] is a syndetic, idempotent filter that contains $A$, whereby $A$ is central syndetic. \end{enumerate} In particular, the set $A$ is central syndetic if and only if some subset of it satisfies the condition in \eqref{eqn_def_of_cssd}.
nodes.section: 3.2.2 A combinatorial characterization of central syndetic sets

nodes.statement: \eqref{item_central_syndetic_implies_comb_condition} \ Suppose $A$ belongs to a syndetic, idempotent filter $\mathscr{F}$. Define $A_1 \vcentcolon= A \cap (A-\mathscr{F})$. We claim that this set satisfies the condition in \eqref{eqn_def_of_cssd}. First we will show that $A_1 \in \mathscr{F}$ and $A_1 \subseteq A_1 - \mathscr{F}$. That $A_1 \in \mathscr{F}$ follows because $A \in \mathscr{F}$ and $A-\mathscr{F} \in \mathscr{F}$ (since $\mathscr{F}$ is idempotent). Because $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$, using the algebra in \cref{lemma_filter_algebra}, we see \begin{align*} A_1 = A \cap (A-\mathscr{F}) \subseteq A - \mathscr{F} &\subseteq (A - \mathscr{F}) \cap \big(A - (\mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}) \big) \\ &= (A - \mathscr{F}) \cap \big((A - \mathscr{F}) - \mathscr{F} \big) \\ &= \big( A \cap (A - \mathscr{F}) \big) - \mathscr{F} \\ &= A_1 - \mathscr{F}. \end{align*} To see that the condition in \eqref{eqn_def_of_cssd} is satisfied, let $F \subseteq A_1$ be finite. Since $F \subseteq A_1 - \mathscr{F}$, the set $\bigcap_{f \in F} (A_1 - f) \in \mathscr{F}$. Since $A_1 \in \mathscr{F}$, we have that $A_1 \cap \bigcap_{f \in F} (A_1 - f) \in \mathscr{F}$, whereby it is syndetic, as desired. \eqref{item_comb_condition_implies_central_syndetic} \ That $\mathscr{F}$ is a filter is immediate from its definition. That $A \in \mathscr{F}$ follows immediately from the fact that $\mathscr{F}$ is upward closed. To see that $\mathscr{F}$ is syndetic, it suffices to show that for all $F \subseteq A$ finite, the set $B \vcentcolon= A \cap \bigcap_{f \in F} (A - f)$ is syndetic. But this is immediate from \eqref{eqn_def_of_cssd}. To see that $\mathscr{F}$ is idempotent, we must show that $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$. Since $\mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$ is a filter, it suffices to show that for all $a \in A \cup\{0\}$, the set $A - a \in \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$. Let $a \in A \cup\{0\}$. We will show that $(A - a) - \mathscr{F} \in \mathscr{F}$. Since $A - a \in \mathscr{F}$, it suffices to show that $A - a \subseteq (A - a) - \mathscr{F}$. This holds since for any $n \in A - a$, we have that $(A - a) - n = A - (n + a)$, which is a member of $\mathscr{F}$ by the definition of $\mathscr{F}$ since $n+a \in A$.

nodes.name: (i): A_1 = A ∩ (A - F) satisfies (3.6)
nodes.statement: \eqref{item_central_syndetic_implies_comb_condition} \ Suppose $A$ belongs to a syndetic, idempotent filter $\mathscr{F}$. Define $A_1 \vcentcolon= A \cap (A-\mathscr{F})$. We claim that this set satisfies the condition in \eqref{eqn_def_of_cssd}. First we will show that $A_1 \in \mathscr{F}$ and $A_1 \subseteq A_1 - \mathscr{F}$. That $A_1 \in \mathscr{F}$ follows because $A \in \mathscr{F}$ and $A-\mathscr{F} \in \mathscr{F}$ (since $\mathscr{F}$ is idempotent). Because $\mathscr{F} \subseteq \mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}$, using the algebra in \cref{lemma_filter_algebra}, we see \begin{align*} A_1 = A \cap (A-\mathscr{F}) \subseteq A - \mathscr{F} &\subseteq (A - \mathscr{F}) \cap \big(A - (\mathscr{F} + \mathscr{F}) \big) \\ &= (A - \mathscr{F}) \cap \big((A - \mathscr{F}) - \mathscr{F} \big) \\ &= \big( A \cap (A - \mathscr{F}) \big) - \mathscr{F} \\ &= A_1 - \mathscr{F}. \end{align*} To see that the condition in \eqref{eqn_def_of_cssd} is satisfied, let $F \subseteq A_1$ be finite. Since $F \subseteq A_1 - \mathscr{F}$, the set $\bigcap_{f \in F} (A_1 - f) \in \mathscr{F}$. Since $A_1 \in \mathscr{F}$, we have that $A_1 \cap \bigcap_{f \in F} (A_1 - f) \in \mathscr{F}$, whereby it is syndetic, as desired.

nodes.statement: If $A$ satisfies the condition in \eqref{eqn_stronger_than_cssd}, then it clearly satisfies the one in \eqref{eqn_def_of_cssd}. Conversely, suppose that $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ satisfies the condition in \eqref{eqn_def_of_cssd}. To see that it satisfies \eqref{eqn_stronger_than_cssd}, let $F \subseteq A$ be finite and $m \in \mathbb{N}$. To see that the set $A \cap \bigcap_{f \in F} (A-f) \cap m\mathbb{N}$ is syndetic, we will show that it has nonempty intersection with all thick sets. Let $H \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be thick. By \cref{thm_conditions_for_central_syndetic}, we see that the set $A \cap \bigcap_{f \in F} (A-f)$ belongs to a syndetic, idempotent filter, and hence is central syndetic. It follows from \cref{cor_central_syndetic_is_strongly_central} that the set $A \cap \bigcap_{f \in F} (A-f) \cap H$ is central. The set $m \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathcal{IP}^*$, hence $\mathcal{C}^*$, and so the set $A \cap \bigcap_{f \in F} (A-f) \cap m \mathbb{N} \cap H$ is nonempty, as was to be shown.

nodes.statement_short: Show the set meets every thick set: it is central syndetic, so its intersection with H is central, and mN is IP*, hence C*.

nodes.statement: By assumption, there exists a minimal system $(X,T)$, a point $x \in X$, and an open set $U \subseteq X$ containing $x$ such that $R(x,U) \subseteq A$. Define \[ \mathscr{F} \vcentcolon= \uparrow \big\{ R(x,V) \ \big| \ V \subseteq X \text{ is an open set containing $x$} \big\}. \] We claim that $\mathscr{F}$ is a syndetic, idempotent filter containing $A$. That $\mathscr{F}$ is a filter, that $A \in \mathscr{F}$, and that $\mathscr{F}$ is syndetic are all immediate. To see that $\mathscr{F}$ is idempotent, it suffices by \cref{rmk_showing_idempotency} to show that for all open $V \subseteq X$ with $x \in V$, we have that $R(x,V) \subseteq R(x,V) - \mathscr{F}$. Since $R(x,V) \in \mathscr{F}$, this shows that $R(x,V) - \mathscr{F} \in \mathscr{F}$, as desired. Let $V \subseteq X$ be open and contain $x$. To see that $R(x,V) \subseteq R(x,V) - \mathscr{F}$, let $n \in R(x,V)$. Thus, $x \in T^{-n} V$. Since $T^{-n} V$ is an open neighborhood of $x$, we have that $R(x,V) - n = R(x,T^{-n} V) \in \mathscr{F}$, as desired.

nodes.name: Main idea of the proof that central syndetic sets are dcS
nodes.statement: Here is the main idea behind the proof of the ``if'' statement in \cref{thm_dcs_iff_cs}. By \cref{thm_conditions_for_central_syndetic}, we may assume that the set $A$ satisfies the condition in \eqref{eqn_def_of_cssd}. Our aim is to show that the set $A$ contains a set of the form $R(x,U)$, where the point $x$ belongs to the open set $U$ in a minimal system. In view of \cref{thm:simple_equivalent_dcS}, it suffices to find a subset $B \subseteq A$ for which $1_{B \cup \{0\}} \in \{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}_0}$ is uniformly recurrent under the shift map $\sigma$. Note that the condition in \eqref{eqn_def_of_cssd} is not sufficient for $1_{A \cup \{0\}}$ to be uniformly recurrent under $\sigma$. (Indeed, the set $\mathbb{N}_0 \backslash \{n^2 \ | \ n \in \mathbb{N}\}$ satisfies the condition in \eqref{eqn_def_of_cssd} but has an indicator function that is not uniformly recurrent under $\sigma$.) To find the set $B$, the idea is to modify the shift map $\sigma$ into a ``shift-punch'' map $\kappa$ under which the point $1_A$ becomes uniformly recurrent. We append the integer $0$ to $A$ and consider it as a subset of $\mathbb{N}_0$. The ``punch map'' $\pi: \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}_0} \to \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}_0}$, which depends on the set $A$, is described roughly as follows. At $1_C \in \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}_0}$, we find the maximal $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $A \cap [N] \subseteq C$. Then, $\pi(1_C) = 1_D$, where $D \cap [N] = A \cap [N]$ and $D \cap (\mathbb{N}_0 \backslash [N]) = C \cap (\mathbb{N}_0 \backslash [N])$. Roughly, the map $\pi$ ``punches out'' or ``deletes'' the elements of $C$ on the interval $[N]$ that are not in $A \cap [N]$. The map $\pi$ continuously moves points of $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}_0}$ closer to $1_A$. The shift-punch map $\kappa$ is defined to be $\pi \circ \sigma$. The dynamics of the shift-punch system $(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}_0}, \kappa)$ is thus a shift followed by a punch. The idea is to show that in this system, the point $1_A$ is uniformly recurrent. This happens because the set $A$ satisfies the condition in \eqref{eqn_def_of_cssd} and thus syndetically often contains an initial interval of itself. Keeping track of which elements of $A$ are deleted as the shift-punch map is repeatedly applied to $1_A$, we end up with a subset $B \subseteq A$. We will show that the point $1_B \in \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}_0}$ is uniformly recurrent under the usual shift map, as desired. The outline just given is difficult to control in practice because the punches can seemingly overlap in complicated ways. To overcome this, we find it useful to have more control over the length of intervals on which the punches occurs. Thus, the actual shift-punch system is defined as a skew product over a 2-adic odometer. The odometer functions only to control the length of the punch intervals, which are restricted to occur only on dyadic intervals. Dyadic intervals are convenient because a nonempty intersection implies containment. This control on the punch intervals allows us to realize the outline above.

nodes.statement_short: Proof sketch: modify the shift by a 'punch' map pulling points toward 1_A, controlled by a 2-adic odometer, so that 1_A becomes uniformly recurrent and the punched subset B has 1_B uniformly recurrent.

nodes.section: 3.3.2 Notation and spaces

nodes.name: Two-adic valuation
nodes.statement: Denote by $\nu_2: \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{N}_{0,\infty}$ the two-adic valuation on $\mathbb{Z}$, defined by $\nu_2(n) \vcentcolon= \sup \{k \in \mathbb{N}_0 \ | \ 2^k \text{ divides } n \}$.
nodes.section: 3.3.3 Dyadic valuation and intervals

nodes.name: Dyadic interval
nodes.statement: A finite interval $\{a, a+1, \ldots, a+\ell - 1\}$ in $\mathbb{N}_0$ is a \emph{dyadic interval} if $\ell = 2^k$ for some $k \in \mathbb{N}_0$ and $\ell \mid a$.
nodes.section: 3.3.3 Dyadic valuation and intervals

nodes.name: Dyadic intervals of given size
nodes.statement: Denote by $\mathcal{Q}_{2^n}$ the set of dyadic intervals of cardinality $2^n$.
nodes.section: 3.3.3 Dyadic valuation and intervals

nodes.name: Basic facts on dyadic intervals
nodes.section: 3.3.3 Dyadic valuation and intervals
assumptions: Let $Q$ and $P$ be finite dyadic intervals in $\mathbb{N}_0$.
conclusions: $Q \cap 2^{\nu_2(\min Q)}\mathbb{N} = \{\min Q\}$.
For all $\ell \in \mathbb{N}_0$, if $\big(Q \backslash \{\min Q\} \big) \cap 2^{\ell} \mathbb{N} \neq \emptyset$, then $|Q| \geqslant 2^{\ell + 1}$.
If $P \cap Q \neq \emptyset$, then either $P \subseteq Q$ or $Q \subseteq P$.
nodes.label: lemma_basic_dyadic_cubes_facts

nodes.section: 3.3.3 Dyadic valuation and intervals
nodes.statement_short: Write Q = n + [2^k] with k ≤ ν2(n) and compare 2-adic valuations; nesting by contradiction using (ii).

nodes.name: (i) from Q = n + [2^k] with k ≤ ν2(n)
nodes.statement_short: (i) from Q = n + [2^k] with k ≤ ν2(n).
nodes.section: 3.3.3 Dyadic valuation and intervals

nodes.name: (ii) compare valuations of elements of Q
nodes.statement: \eqref{item_dyadic_prop_three} \ Write $Q = n + [2^k]$ as in \eqref{item_dyadic_prop_two}. Let $\ell \in \mathbb{N}_0$, and suppose that $\big(Q \backslash \{n\} \big) \cap 2^{\ell} \mathbb{N}$ is nonempty. It follows from the previous paragraph that $\ell < \nu_2(n)$. Let $a \in \big(Q \backslash \{n\} \big) \cap 2^{\ell} \mathbb{N}$. Since $|Q| = 2^k > a-n$ and $\nu_2(a-n) \geqslant \ell$, we see that $k \geqslant \ell + 1$. Therefore, $|Q| \geqslant 2^{\ell + 1}$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: (ii) compare valuations of elements of Q.
nodes.section: 3.3.3 Dyadic valuation and intervals

nodes.name: (iii) reduce to: min P in Q minus min Q implies P ⊆ Q
nodes.statement: \eqref{item_dyadic_prop_one} \ Let $P$ and $Q$ be dyadic intervals. Note that if $\min P = \min Q$, then $P \subseteq Q$ or $Q \subseteq P$, and we are done. Otherwise, we will show that if $\min P \in Q \backslash \{\min Q\}$, then $P \subseteq Q$. It will follow that either $P$ and $Q$ are disjoint or that one is contained in the other.
nodes.statement_short: (iii) reduce to: min P in Q minus min Q implies P ⊆ Q.
nodes.section: 3.3.3 Dyadic valuation and intervals

nodes.name: Contradiction via (ii) applied in both directions
nodes.statement: Suppose for a contradiction that $\min P \in Q \backslash \{\min Q\}$ and $P \not\subseteq Q$. Then $\max Q + 1 = \min Q + |Q| \in P$ and is divisible by $|Q|$. It follows from \eqref{item_dyadic_prop_three} that $|P| \geqslant 2 |Q|$. But since $P \not\subseteq Q$ and $|P|$ divides $\min P$, we see by \eqref{item_dyadic_prop_three} that $|Q| \geqslant 2 |P|$, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction via (ii) applied in both directions.
nodes.section: 3.3.3 Dyadic valuation and intervals

nodes.name: Dual of dyadic intervals
nodes.statement: We denote by $\mathcal{Q}_{2^n}^*$ the collection of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ that have nonempty intersection with all members of $\mathcal{Q}_{2^n}$.
nodes.section: 3.3.3 Dyadic valuation and intervals

nodes.name: Syndeticity via dyadic intervals
nodes.statement: A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}_0$ is syndetic if and only if there exists $k \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $A \in \mathcal{Q}_{2^k}^*$.
nodes.section: 3.3.3 Dyadic valuation and intervals
conclusions: A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}_0$ is syndetic if and only if there exists $k \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $A \in \mathcal{Q}_{2^k}^*$.
equivalent_conditions: A set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}_0$ is syndetic
there exists $k \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $A \in \mathcal{Q}_{2^k}^*$
nodes.label: lemma_syndetic_characterization
