nodes.name: 2-adic odometer
nodes.statement: We denote by $(Z,\rho)$ the 2-adic odometer, the inverse limit of the family of rotations $(\mathbb{Z} / 2^k \mathbb{Z}, \allowbreak +1)$, $k \in \mathbb{N}_0$, as topological dynamical systems.
nodes.section: 3.3.4 The 2-adic odometer

nodes.name: Embedding of the integers in the odometer
nodes.statement: For $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, we denote by $n$ the element of $Z$ that projects, for all $k \in \mathbb{N}_0$, to $n \in \mathbb{Z} / 2^k \mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.section: 3.3.4 The 2-adic odometer

nodes.name: 2-adic valuation is uniformly continuous on Z
nodes.statement: The two-adic valuation $\nu_2: \mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{N}_{0,\infty}$ is uniformly continuous in the subspace topology that $\mathbb{Z}$ inherits from the space $Z$.
nodes.section: 3.3.4 The 2-adic odometer

nodes.name: Proof of continuity of the 2-adic valuation
nodes.statement:
Indeed, if the images of integers $n$ and $m$ are the same in $\mathbb{Z} / 2^k \mathbb{Z}$ for a large value of $k$, then $2^k$ divides $n-m$, so $
u_2(n)$ is large if and only if $
u_2(m)$ is large. Therefore, the map $
u_2: \mathbb{Z} 	o \mathbb{N}_{0,\infty}$ extends uniquely to a continuous map $
u_2: Z 	o \mathbb{N}_{0,\infty}$.
nodes.section: 3.3.4 The 2-adic odometer
nodes.statement_short: Integers close in Z differ by a high power of 2, so their valuations are both large or equal; extend by uniform continuity.

nodes.name: Valuation ν_A relative to A
nodes.section: 3.3.5 The punch maps

nodes.name: Definition of ν_A
nodes.statement: \nu_A(\omega) \vcentcolon= \sup \big\{n \in \mathbb{N}_0 \ \big| \ A \cap [2^{n}] \subseteq {\normalfont\text{supp}}\,(\omega) \big\},
nodes.section: 3.3.5 The punch maps
nodes.label: eqn_def_of_M_set

nodes.name: Punch interval
nodes.statement: For $n \in \mathbb{N}_{0,\infty}$ and $\omega \in X$, we define the \emph{punch interval} \[I_n(\omega) \vcentcolon= \big[2^{\min(\nu_A(\omega),n)} \big],\] where $[2^{-\infty}]$ and $[2^{\infty}]$ are interpreted to be the empty set and $\mathbb{N}_0$, respectively.
nodes.section: 3.3.5 The punch maps

nodes.name: Punch map
nodes.statement: Then, we define the \emph{punch map} $\pi_n: X \to X$ by \[\big(\pi_n (\omega) \big)(i) = \begin{cases} 1_A(i) & \text{ if $i \in I_n(\omega)$} \\ \omega(i) & \text{ if $i \in \mathbb{N}_0 \backslash I_n(\omega)$} \end{cases}.\]
nodes.section: 3.3.5 The punch maps
nodes.statement_short: π_n(ω) agrees with 1_A on the punch interval and with ω elsewhere.

nodes.name: Continuity of the punch maps
nodes.statement: Each of the maps $\pi_n: X \to X$, $n \in \mathbb{N}_{0,\infty}$, is continuous, and the map $\mathbb{N}_{0,\infty} \to C(X,X)$ given by $n \mapsto \pi_n$ is continuous, where $C(X,X)$ has the supremum topology.
nodes.section: 3.3.5 The punch maps
conclusions: Each of the maps $\pi_n: X \to X$, $n \in \mathbb{N}_{0,\infty}$, is continuous
the map $\mathbb{N}_{0,\infty} \to C(X,X)$ given by $n \mapsto \pi_n$ is continuous
nodes.label: lemma_continuity_of_family_of_punches

nodes.statement:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}_{0,\infty}$. To see that $\pi_n: X 	o X$ is continuous, let $\omega \in X$ and $N \in \mathbb{N}$. If $
u_A(\omega) \in \mathbb{N}_{0,-\infty}$, then for all $\omega' \in X$ sufficiently close to $\omega$, the points $\omega'$ and $\omega$ agree on $[N]$ and $
u_A(\omega') = 
u_A(\omega)$. If, on the other hand, $
u_A(\omega) = \infty$, then for all $\omega' \in X$ sufficiently close to $\omega$, the points $\omega'$ and $\omega$ agree on $[N]$ and $
u_A(\omega') \geqslant N$. In both cases, we see that $\pi_n(\omega')$ and $\pi_n(\omega)$ agree on $[N]$. By the topology of the space $X$, this shows that $\pi_n$ is continuous. To show that the map $\mathbb{N}_{0,\infty} 	o C(X,X)$ given by $n \mapsto \pi_n$ is continuous, it suffices by the topology on $\mathbb{N}_{0,\infty}$ to show that $\lim_{n 	o \infty} \pi_n = \pi_\infty$, that is, for all $\varepsilon > 0$ and all sufficiently large $n \in \mathbb{N}$, \[\sup_{\omega \in X} d_X ig(\pi_n(\omega), \pi_\infty(\omega)  ig) < \varepsilon.\] Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\omega \in X$. If $
u_A(\omega) = -\infty$, then for all $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$, $\pi_\infty(\omega) = \pi_n(\omega)$. If $
u_A(\omega) \in \mathbb{N}_0$, then for all $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$ with $n \geqslant 
u_A(\omega)$, $\pi_\infty(\omega) = \pi_n(\omega)$. If $
u_A(\omega) = \infty$, then $\pi_n(\omega)$ and $\pi_\infty(\omega)$ match on $[2^n]$, because they both match $1_A$ on $[2^n]$. Thus, in all cases, for $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$ sufficiently large, $d_X(\pi_n(\omega), \pi_\infty(\omega)) < \varepsilon$, as was to be shown.
nodes.section: 3.3.5 The punch maps
nodes.statement_short: Points close to ω share its ν_A value (or have large ν_A), so punches agree on long initial segments; π_n → π_∞ uniformly.

nodes.name: Continuity of each π_n by cases on ν_A(ω)
nodes.statement:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}_{0,\infty}$. To see that $\pi_n: X 	o X$ is continuous, let $\omega \in X$ and $N \in \mathbb{N}$. If $
u_A(\omega) \in \mathbb{N}_{0,-\infty}$, then for all $\omega' \in X$ sufficiently close to $\omega$, the points $\omega'$ and $\omega$ agree on $[N]$ and $
u_A(\omega') =

u_A(\omega') \geqslant N$. In both cases, we see that $\pi_n(\omega')$ and $\pi_n(\omega)$ agree on $[N]$. By the topology of the space $X$, this shows that $\pi_n$ is continuous.

nodes.name: π_n converges uniformly to π_∞ by cases on ν_A(ω)
nodes.statement:
To show that the map $\mathbb{N}_{0,\infty} 	o C(X,X)$ given by $n \mapsto \pi_n$ is continuous, it suffices by the topology on $\mathbb{N}_{0,\infty}$ to show that $\lim_{n 	o \infty} \pi_n = \pi_\infty$, that is, for all $\varepsilon > 0$ and all sufficiently large $n \in \mathbb{N}$, \[\sup_{\omega \in X} d_X ig(\pi_n(\omega), \pi_\infty(\omega)  ig) < \varepsilon.\] Let $\varepsilon > 0$ and $\omega \in X$. If $
u_A(\omega) = -\infty$, then for all $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$, $\pi_\infty(\omega) = \pi_n(\omega)$. If $
u_A(\omega) \in \mathbb{N}_0$, then for all $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$ with $n \geqslant 
u_A(\omega)$, $\pi_\infty(\omega) = \pi_n(\omega)$. If $
u_A(\omega) = \infty$, then $\pi_n(\omega)$ and $\pi_\infty(\omega)$ match on $[2^n]$, because they both match $1_A$ on $[2^n]$. Thus, in all cases, for $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$ sufficiently large, $d_X(\pi_n(\omega), \pi_\infty(\omega)) < \varepsilon$, as was to be shown.
nodes.statement_short: π_n converges uniformly to π_∞ by cases on ν_A(ω).

nodes.name: Punch maps agree on agreeing points
nodes.statement: Let $n, \ell \in \mathbb{N}_0$ with $\ell \geqslant 2^n$. If $\omega, \xi \in X$ agree on $[\ell]$, then $I_n(\omega) = I_n(\xi)$, and $\pi_n(\omega)$ and $\pi_n(\xi)$ agree on $[\ell]$.
nodes.section: 3.3.5 The punch maps
conclusions: $I_n(\omega) = I_n(\xi)$
$\pi_n(\omega)$ and $\pi_n(\xi)$ agree on $[\ell]$
nodes.label: lemma_continuity_of_pins

nodes.section: 3.3.5 The punch maps
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on the values of ν_A(ω) and ν_A(ξ) relative to n.

nodes.name: Set up the case analysis
nodes.statement: Suppose that $\omega, \xi \in X$ agree on $[\ell]$. We consider the following cases.
nodes.statement_short: Set up the case analysis.
nodes.section: 3.3.5 The punch maps

nodes.name: Case ν_A = -∞: nothing is punched
nodes.statement:
Case 1: $
u_A(\omega) = -\infty$ or $
u_A(\xi) = -\infty$. In this case, since $\omega$ and $\xi$ agree on $[\ell]$, we have that $
u_A(\omega) = 
u_A(\xi) = -\infty$ and $I_n(\omega) = I_n(\xi) = \emptyset$. Since $\omega$ and $\xi$ are unchanged by $\pi_{n}$, we have that $\pi_{n} (\omega)$ and $\pi_{n} (\xi)$ agree on $[\ell]$.
nodes.statement_short: Case ν_A = -∞: nothing is punched.
nodes.section: 3.3.5 The punch maps

nodes.name: Case 0 ≤ ν_A(ω) < n: valuations agree, same punch interval
nodes.statement_short: Case 0 ≤ ν_A(ω) < n: valuations agree, same punch interval.
nodes.section: 3.3.5 The punch maps

nodes.name: Symmetric case
nodes.statement: Case 3: $0 \leqslant \nu_A(\xi) < n$. We argue just as in Case 2 to arrive at the same conclusion.
nodes.statement_short: Symmetric case.
nodes.section: 3.3.5 The punch maps

nodes.name: Case both ≥ n: punch interval [2^n] ⊆ [ℓ]
nodes.statement: Case 4: $\nu_A(\omega) \geqslant n$ and $\nu_A(\xi) \geqslant n$. In this case, we see that $I_n(\omega) = I_n(\xi) = [2^{n}]$. Since $2^{n} \leqslant \ell$ and $\omega$ matches $\xi$ on $[\ell]$, we see that $\pi_{n} (\omega)$ and $\pi_{n} (\xi)$ agree on $[\ell]$, as desired. \end{enumerate} This concludes the casework and the proof of the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Case both ≥ n: punch interval [2^n] ⊆ [ℓ].

nodes.name: Shift-punch system
nodes.statement: The \emph{shift-punch system} $(Z \times X, \kappa)$ is the topological skew product system defined by the \emph{shift-punch map} $\kappa: Z \times X \to Z \times X$, \[\kappa(z,\omega) \vcentcolon= \big(\rho z, \pi_{\nu_2( \rho z)}(\sigma \omega) \big).\]
nodes.section: 3.3.6 The shift-punch system
nodes.statement_short: Skew product over the 2-adic odometer: shift ω, then punch it on a dyadic interval of length governed by ν2(ρz).

nodes.name: The shift-punch system is a topological dynamical system
nodes.statement: The shift-punch system $(Z \times X, \kappa)$ is a topological dynamical system.
nodes.section: 3.3.6 The shift-punch system
3.3.6 The shift-punch system
nodes.statement_short: κ is a skew product whose fibre maps depend continuously on z, as a composition of continuous maps.

nodes.name: Pre- and post-punch coordinates α^(n), β^(n)
nodes.statement: Define $\beta^{(0)} = 1_{\mathbb{N}_0}$ and $\alpha^{(0)} = 1_A$, and for $n \in \mathbb{N}$, define $\beta^{(n)}, \alpha^{(n)} \in X$ to be such that \begin{align*} (\rho \times \sigma) \kappa^{n-1}(0,1_A) &= \big(n, \beta^{(n)}\big),\\ \kappa^n (0,1_A) &= \big(n, \alpha^{(n)} \big). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 3.3.6 The shift-punch system

nodes.name: Punch window
nodes.statement: The \emph{punch window} at $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$ is defined to be \[W(n) \vcentcolon= n + I_{\nu_2(n)}\big( \beta^{(n)} \big),\] where $W(n)$ is understood to be the empty set if $I_{\nu_2(n)}\big( \beta^{(n)} \big)$ is the empty set.
nodes.section: 3.3.6 The shift-punch system

nodes.name: Explicit description of the shift-punch orbit
nodes.statement: For all $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$, \begin{enumerate} \item \begin{align} {\normalfont\text{supp}}\,(\beta^{(n)}) = \bigcap_{m=0}^{n-1} \Big( \big( A - (n-m) \big) \cup \big( \mathbb{N}_0 \backslash \big( W(m)-n \big) \big) \Big), \end{align} where the empty intersection is interpreted as $\mathbb{N}_0$; \item \begin{align} {\normalfont\text{supp}}\,(\alpha^{(n)}) = \bigcap_{m=0}^{n} \Big( \big( A - (n-m) \big) \cup \big( \mathbb{N}_0 \backslash \big( W(m)-n \big) \big) \Big). \end{align} \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 3.3.6 The shift-punch system
conclusions: \begin{align} {\normalfont\text{supp}}\,(\beta^{(n)}) = \bigcap_{m=0}^{n-1} \Big( \big( A - (n-m) \big) \cup \big( \mathbb{N}_0 \backslash \big( W(m)-n \big) \big) \Big), \end{align} where the empty intersection is interpreted as $\mathbb{N}_0$;
\begin{align} {\normalfont\text{supp}}\,(\alpha^{(n)}) = \bigcap_{m=0}^{n} \Big( \big( A - (n-m) \big) \cup \big( \mathbb{N}_0 \backslash \big( W(m)-n \big) \big) \Big). \end{align}

nodes.statement: {\normalfont\text{supp}}\,(\beta^{(n)}) = \bigcap_{m=0}^{n-1} \Big( \big( A - (n-m) \big) \cup \big( \mathbb{N}_0 \backslash \big( W(m)-n \big) \big) \Big),

nodes.statement: {\normalfont\text{supp}}\,(\alpha^{(n)}) = \bigcap_{m=0}^{n} \Big( \big( A - (n-m) \big) \cup \big( \mathbb{N}_0 \backslash \big( W(m)-n \big) \big) \Big).

nodes.section: 3.3.6 The shift-punch system
nodes.statement_short: Simultaneous induction on n, tracking which coordinates each punch changes.

nodes.name: Base case n = 0 by set algebra
nodes.statement: We will prove both \eqref{item_explicit_description_of_omega_and_kappa_one} and \eqref{item_explicit_description_of_omega_and_kappa_two} simultaneously by induction on $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$. The base case $n=0$ follows by set algebra, recalling that, by definition, $\beta^{(0)} = 1_{\mathbb{N}_0}$ and $\alpha^{(0)} = 1_A$.
nodes.statement_short: Base case n = 0 by set algebra.
nodes.section: 3.3.6 The shift-punch system

nodes.name: Inductive step for (i): shift the description of α^(n)
nodes.statement: Suppose both \eqref{item_explicit_description_of_omega_and_kappa_one} and \eqref{item_explicit_description_of_omega_and_kappa_two} hold for some $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$. Let $i \in \mathbb{N}_0$. Since $\beta^{(n+1)} = \sigma \alpha^{(n)}$, we see that $\big(\beta^{(n+1)} \big)(i) = 1$ if and only if $\big(\alpha^{(n)} \big)(i+1) = 1$. By the inductive hypothesis, we have that $\big(\alpha^{(n)} \big)(i+1) = 1$ if and only if \[i+1 \in \bigcap_{m=0}^{n} \Big( \big( A - (n-m) \big) \cup \big( \mathbb{N}_0 \backslash \big( W(m)-n \big) \big) \Big).\] The previous line rearranges to \begin{align} i \in \bigcap_{m=0}^{n} \Big( \big( A - (n+1-m) \big) \cup \big( \mathbb{N}_0 \backslash \big( W(m)-(n+1) \big) \big) \Big), \end{align} which shows \eqref{item_explicit_description_of_omega_and_kappa_one} for $n+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step for (i): shift the description of α^(n).

nodes.name: Inductive-step description
nodes.statement: i \in \bigcap_{m=0}^{n} \Big( \big( A - (n+1-m) \big) \cup \big( \mathbb{N}_0 \backslash \big( W(m)-(n+1) \big) \big) \Big),

Note that by the definition of the map $\pi_{\nu_2(n+1)}$, $\big(\alpha^{(n+1)} \big)(i) = \big(\pi_{\nu_2(n+1)} \beta^{(n+1)} \big)(i) = 1$ if and only if $\big(\beta^{(n+1)}\big)(i) = 1$ and either

nodes.name: Combine with (i) to get the description for n+1
nodes.statement: By the previous paragraph, we have that $\big(\beta^{(n+1)}\big)(i) = 1$ if and only if \eqref{eqn_big_set_description_for_inductive_step} holds, and so we see by the previous sentence that $\big(\alpha^{(n+1)} \big)(i) = 1$ if and only if $i$ belongs to the set \[\bigcap_{m=0}^{n} \Big( \big( A - (n+1-m) \big) \cup \big( \mathbb{N}_0 \backslash \big( W(m)-(n+1) \big) \big) \Big) \cap \big(A \cup \big(\mathbb{N}_0 \backslash (W(n+1)-(n+1))\big) \big).\] The set on the previous line simplifies to the one in \eqref{eqn_set_indicated_by_kappa_n} for $n+1$, demonstrating \eqref{item_explicit_description_of_omega_and_kappa_two} for $n+1$, as desired.

nodes.name: Self-similarity of the shift-punch orbit
nodes.statement: Let $m \in \mathbb{N}_0$. For all $i \in W(m) - m$, the points $\alpha^{(i)}$ and $\alpha^{(m+i)}$ agree on the interval $W(m) - m - i$.

nodes.statement: The conclusion is trivial for $m = 0$, so suppose $m \in \mathbb{N}$. Let $\ell = |W(m)|$. We must show that for all $i \in [\ell]$, the points $\alpha^{(i)}$ and and $\alpha^{(m+i)}$ agree on $W(m) - m - i = [\ell - i]$. We will prove this by induction on $i$. The base case $i = 0$ follows from the definition of $W(m)$: the points $\alpha^{(0)} = 1_A$ and $\alpha^{(m)}$ agree on $W(m) - m = [\ell]$.

nodes.statement: Let $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$. It follows by \cref{lemma_explicit_description_of_omega_and_kappa} that $\big(\alpha^{(n)}\big)(0) = 1$ if and only if \[0 \in \bigcap_{m=0}^{n} \Big( \big( A - (n-m) \big) \cup \big( \mathbb{N}_0 \backslash \big( W(m)-n \big) \big) \Big).\] By set algebra, the previous line holds if and only if \[n \in \bigcap_{m=0}^{n} \Big( \big( A +m \big) \cup \big( \mathbb{N}_0 \backslash W(m) \big) \Big).\] Since for all $m \in \mathbb{N}_0$ greater than $n$, $W(m) \subseteq \{n+1, n+2, \ldots \}$, we see that the previous line holds if and only if \[n \in \bigcap_{m=0}^{\infty} \Big( \big( A +m \big) \cup \big( \mathbb{N}_0 \backslash W(m) \big) \Big) = B,\] as was to be shown.

nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Choose $\ell \in \mathbb{N}_0$ so that if two points in $X$ agree on $[2^\ell]$, then they are at a distance of no more than $\varepsilon$. Let $n \in L(\ell)$. By \cref{lemma_second_coords_agree}, for all $i \in [2^\ell] \subseteq W(n) - n$, the points $\alpha^{(i)}$ and $\alpha^{(n+i)}$ agree on $W(n) - n - i$. In particular, they agree at 0. It follows from \cref{lemma_dynamical_description_of_B} that for all $i \in [2^\ell]$, $1_B(i) = 1_B(i+n) = 1_{B-n}(i) = (\sigma^{n} 1_B)(i)$. Since $1_B$ and $\sigma^{n} 1_B$ agree on $[2^\ell]$, we see that $n \in R_\sigma(1_B,B_\varepsilon(1_B))$, as was to be shown.

nodes.name: If 0 is not in A then B is empty
nodes.statement:
If $0 
ot\in A$, then $B = \emptyset$. Indeed, since $0 
ot\in A$, for all $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$, the map $\pi_{
u_2(n)}$ will punch $ eta^{(n)}$ at least at the zero coordinate (that is, $n \in W(n)$), changing that coordinate to 0 if it is 1. Thus, $\alpha^{(n)}(0) = 0$, and according to \cref{lemma_dynamical_description_of_B}, the set $B$ is empty. In this case, we see that $R_\sigma ig(1_B, B_\varepsilon ig(1_B  ig)  ig) = \mathbb{N}$. This shows that a result analogous to \cref{lemma_punch_windows_and_return_times} for the point $1_B$ under the shift $\sigma$ does not necessarily hold: it may be that there exists $\ell \in \mathbb{N}_0$ such that for all $\varepsilon > 0$, the set $R_\sigma ig(1_B, B_\varepsilon(1_B )  ig)$ is not contained in $L(\ell)$.

nodes.name: Proof of the 'if' statement of Theorem 3.18 (setup)
nodes.statement: To finish the proof of \cref{thm_dcs_iff_cs}, we must show that central syndetic sets are dynamically central syndetic. It suffices by \cref{thm_conditions_for_central_syndetic} and \cref{lemma_upgraded_cssd_property} to show: if $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ satisfies the condition in \eqref{eqn_stronger_than_cssd}, then $A$ is dynamically central syndetic. We carry forward all of the notation from the previous sections. Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ satisfy the condition in \eqref{eqn_stronger_than_cssd}. We append $0$ to $A$ and, by a slight abuse of notation, consider $A$ as a subset of $\mathbb{N}_0$. The key step is to show that the condition in \eqref{eqn_stronger_than_cssd} implies that the sets $L(\ell)$ defined in the previous section are syndetic.

nodes.statement_short: Show L(ℓ) meets every dyadic interval of length 2^{k+1} by induction on its position, using new positions (Lemma 3.27) and the fractal window structure (Lemma 3.26).

nodes.name: L(ℓ) is nonempty via Lemma 3.27 or dyadic facts
nodes.statement: Let $\ell \in \mathbb{N}_0$. We will show first that the set $L(\ell)$ is nonempty. It follows from \eqref{eqn_stronger_than_cssd} that there exists $n \in 2^\ell \mathbb{N}$ such that $n + \big(A \cap [2^\ell]\big) \subseteq A$. Let $m \in [n]$ be the greatest integer such that $n \in W(m)$. If $m=0$, then by \cref{lemma_punches_at_new_elements}, we have that $|W(n)| \geqslant 2^\ell$, whereby $n \in L(\ell)$. Otherwise, we have that $1 \leqslant m < n$ and $n \in W(m)$, whereby $\big( W(m) \backslash \{m\} \big) \cap 2^\ell \mathbb{N} \neq \emptyset$. It follows from \cref{lemma_basic_dyadic_cubes_facts} that $|W(m)| \geqslant 2^{\ell + 1}$, so $m \in L(\ell)$.
nodes.statement_short: L(ℓ) is nonempty via Lemma 3.27 or dyadic facts.
nodes.section: 3.3.7 Central syndetic sets are dynamically central syndetic

nodes.name: Fix k so that (3.13) holds; reduce to L(ℓ) ∈ Q*_{2^{k+1}}
nodes.statement: By \eqref{eqn_stronger_than_cssd}, \cref{lemma_syndetic_characterization}, and the previous paragraph, there exists $k \in \mathbb{N}$ so that \begin{align} 2^\ell \mathbb{N}_0 \cap \bigcap_{a \in A \cap [2^{\ell}]} (A-a) \in \mathcal{Q}_{2^{k}}^* \end{align} and so that $L(\ell) \cap [2^k] \neq \emptyset$. We will show that $L(\ell)$ is syndetic by showing that $L(\ell) \in \mathcal{Q}_{2^{k+1}}^*$ and appealing again to \cref{lemma_syndetic_characterization}.
nodes.statement_short: Fix k so that (3.13) holds; reduce to L(ℓ) ∈ Q*_{2^{k+1}}.

nodes.name: Dyadic syndeticity from condition (3.7)
nodes.statement: 2^\ell \mathbb{N}_0 \cap \bigcap_{a \in A \cap [2^{\ell}]} (A-a) \in \mathcal{Q}_{2^{k}}^*
nodes.section: 3.3.7 Central syndetic sets are dynamically central syndetic
nodes.label: eqn_cube_syndeticity_from_upgraded_membership_property

nodes.name: Induction on the dyadic block start a; base case done
nodes.statement: To show that $L(\ell) \in \mathcal{Q}_{2^{k+1}}^*$, we will show that for all $a \in 2^{k+1}\mathbb{N}_0$, the set $L(\ell) \cap \big(a + ([2^{k+1}]\backslash \{0\})\big)$ is nonempty. We proceed by induction on $a$. We have already shown the base case $a=0$. (Recall that, by definition, $L(\ell) \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, so that $L(\ell) \cap [2^k] \neq \emptyset$ implies $L(\ell) \cap ([2^k] \backslash \{0\}) \neq \emptyset$.)
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the dyadic block start a; base case done.
nodes.section: 3.3.7 Central syndetic sets are dynamically central syndetic

nodes.name: Pick n in the block; if n is a new position, done
nodes.statement: Let $a \in 2^{k+1}\mathbb{N}$, and define $Q = a + [2^{k+1}]$. From \eqref{eqn_cube_syndeticity_from_upgraded_membership_property}, there exists \[n \in \big( Q \backslash \{a\} \big) \cap 2^\ell \mathbb{N}_0 \cap \bigcap_{a \in A \cap [2^{\ell}]} (A-a).\] Let $m \in [n]$ be the greatest integer such that $n \in W(m)$. If $m=0$, then by \cref{lemma_punches_at_new_elements}, we have that $|W(n)| \geqslant 2^\ell$, whereby $n \in L(\ell) \cap \big( Q \backslash \{a\} \big)$, as desired. Otherwise, we have that $1 \leqslant m < n$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick n in the block; if n is a new position, done.
nodes.section: 3.3.7 Central syndetic sets are dynamically central syndetic

nodes.name: If m > a, then m itself is a long punch time
nodes.statement: If $m > a$, then $m \in Q \backslash \{a\}$. Since $m < n$ and $n \in W(m)$, we have that $\big( W(m) \backslash \{m\} \big) \cap 2^\ell \mathbb{N} \neq \emptyset$. It follows from \cref{lemma_basic_dyadic_cubes_facts} that $|W(m)| \geqslant 2^{\ell + 1}$, so $m \in L(\ell) \cap \big( Q \backslash \{a\} \big)$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: If m > a, then m itself is a long punch time.
nodes.section: 3.3.7 Central syndetic sets are dynamically central syndetic

nodes.name: If m ≤ a, use the induction hypothesis and Lemma 3.26
nodes.statement: If, on the other hand, $m \leqslant a$, then the fact that $W(m)$ and $Q$ are intersecting dyadic intervals (both contain $n$) implies that $m \in 2^{k+1} \mathbb{N}$, that $Q \subseteq W(m)$, and that $Q - m \in \mathcal{Q}_{2^{k+1}}$. It follows by the induction hypothesis that there exists $q \in Q \backslash \{a\}$ such that $q-m \in L(\ell) \cap (Q-m)$. Thus, $|W(q-m)| \geqslant 2^\ell$. Since $q \in W(m)$ and $m \leqslant a < q$, it follows from \cref{lemma_fractal_windows} that $W(q-m) = W(q) - m$. Therefore, $|W(q)| \geqslant 2^\ell$, whereby $q \in L(\ell) \cap (Q \backslash \{a\})$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: If m ≤ a, use the induction hypothesis and Lemma 3.26.
nodes.section: 3.3.7 Central syndetic sets are dynamically central syndetic

nodes.name: Proof of the 'if' statement of Theorem 3.18 (conclusion)
nodes.statement: Let $B \subseteq A$ be the subset of $A$ defined in \eqref{eqn_result_of_set_after_punches} in the previous section. Since $0 \in A$, we see that $0 \in B$. It follows by combining \cref{lemma_punch_returns_vs_shift_returns} and \cref{prop_long_punch_times_are_syndetic} that the point $1_B$ is uniformly recurrent in the shift $(X,\sigma)$. Since $0 \in B$, it follows from \cref{thm:simple_equivalent_dcS} that the set $B \backslash \{0\} \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is dynamically central syndetic. Therefore, we have that the set $A \backslash \{0\}$ is dynamically central syndetic, concluding the proof of \cref{thm_dcs_iff_cs}.
nodes.section: 3.3.7 Central syndetic sets are dynamically central syndetic

nodes.statement: \eqref{item_intro_ds_def_condition} $\iff$ \eqref{item_intro_translate_belongs_to_sif} \ If follows by \cref{lemma_translates_of_dsyndetic_sets} that $A$ is dynamically syndetic if and only if there exists $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$ such that $A-n$ is dynamically central syndetic. By \cref{intro_mainthm_full_chars_of_dcsyndetic}, a set is dynamically central syndetic if and only if it belongs to a syndetic, idempotent filter. The desired equivalence is shown by combining these two results. \eqref{item_intro_translate_belongs_to_sif} $\implies$ \eqref{item_intro_ds_combo_condition} \ Suppose that there exists $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$ such that $A' \vcentcolon= A - n$ belongs to a syndetic, idempotent filter. We have by \cref{intro_mainthm_full_chars_of_dcsyndetic} that there exists $B' \subseteq A'$ such that for all finite $F' \subseteq B'$, the set $B' \cap \bigcap_{f' \in F'} (B' - f')$ is syndetic. Put $B = B' + n$, and note that $B$ is a nonempty subset of $A$. Let $F \subseteq B$ be finite, and note that $\min F \geqslant n+1$. We have that $F-n \subseteq B'$ is finite, and hence that the set \[\bigcap_{f' \in F-n} (B' - f')\] is syndetic. But this set is contained in $\bigcap_{f \in F} (B - f)$, demonstrating syndeticity, as desired. \eqref{item_intro_ds_combo_condition} $\implies$ \eqref{item_intro_translate_belongs_to_sif} \ Let $b \in B$. We will show that the set $B - b \subseteq A-b$ satisfies: for all finite $F \subseteq B-b$, the set \[(B-b) \cap \bigcap_{f \in F} (B - b - f)\] is syndetic. It will follow by \cref{thm_conditions_for_central_syndetic} that the set $A-b$ is contained in a syndetic, idempotent filter. Let $F \subseteq B-b$ be finite. By assumption, since $\{b\} \cup (F + b) \subseteq B$ is finite, we have that the set \[\bigcap_{f \in \{b\} \cup (F + b)} (B - f) = (B-b) \cap \bigcap_{f \in F} (B - b - f)\] is syndetic, as was to be shown.

nodes.name: Examples of dynamically (central) thick sets
nodes.statement:
Here is a short list of examples of dynamically (central) thick sets that may be helpful to have in mind; more elaborate examples are given in \cref{sec_dy_thick_examples}.  egin{enumerate} \item For $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the set of positive multiples of $k$, $k\mathbb{N}$, is a set of pointwise recurrence. In fact, for all thick sets $H \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, the set $k \mathbb{N} \cap H$ is a set of pointwise recurrence. Indeed, this follows from \cref{lemma_dilates_of_dsyndetic_sets} and the fact that $H / k$ is thick: if $A \in dc\mathcal{S}$, then $A / k \in dc\mathcal{S}$, whereby $A / k \cap H / k 
eq \emptyset$, whereby $A \cap k\mathbb{N} \cap H 
eq \emptyset$. \item If $A$ is not dynamically (central) syndetic, then its complement, $\mathbb{N}  ackslash A$, is dynamically (central) thick. This follows immediately from \cref{lemma_dt_and_ds_duals}. The set in \eqref{eqn_intro_even_odd} from the introduction is not dynamically syndetic, hence its complement, a set of the same form, is dynamically thick. A more general class of dynamically thick sets is described in \cref{ex:type2-special}. \item If $x \in X \vcentcolon= \{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ has a dense orbit in the full shift $(X,\sigma)$, then for all nonempty, open $U \subseteq X$, the set $R_\sigma(x,U)$ is dynamically thick. This is a consequence of a theorem of Furstenberg \cite[Thm. II.2]{Furstenberg-disjointness}: the full shift is \emph{disjoint} (cf. \cite[Def. II.1]{Furstenberg-disjointness}) from every minimal system. (This result is generalized in \cite[Thm. 6.2]{glasner_tsankov_weiss_zucker_2021} to arbitrary countable, infinite group actions.) Indeed, we will argue that for all minimal systems $(Y,S)$, all $y \in Y$, and all nonempty, open $V \subseteq Y$, the set  egin{align} R_{\sigma 	imes S} ((x,y), U 	imes V) = R_\sigma(x,U) \cap R_S(y,V) 
eq \emptyset. \end{align} By an equivalent definition of the disjointness of $(X,\sigma)$ and $(Y,S)$ (cf. \cite[Lemma II.1]{Furstenberg-disjointness}), the system $(X 	imes Y, \sigma 	imes S)$ is the only subsystem of the product system that projects to $X$ in the first coordinate and $Y$ in the second. Because $x$ and $y$ have dense orbits in $X$ and $Y$, respectively, the subsystem $(\overline{(\sigma 	imes S)^{\mathbb{N}}(x,y)}, \sigma 	imes S)$ projects to $X$ and $Y$ in the first and second coordinates, respectively, and hence is the product system. Since the point $(x,y)$ has a dense orbit in the product system, we see that \eqref{eqn_disjointness_leads_to_non_empty_set_returns_in_prod} holds. We offer an alternative explanation of this example in \cref{rem:combinatorial_primes} and \cref{rmk_why_transitive_works} below. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Definitional robustness of dynamically thick sets
nodes.statement: The robustness of the families of dynamically (central) syndetic sets was discussed in \cref{sec_dy_synd_def_and_char}. Because of the duality shown in \cref{lemma_dt_and_ds_duals}, the families of dynamically (central) thick sets exhibit a similar robustness under changes to the combinatorial, topological, or dynamical requirements in their definitions. Thus, the families of dynamically (central) thick subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ remain unchanged if \dots \begin{enumerate} \item \dots \ ``for all minimal systems'' is changed to ``for all invertible minimal systems,'' ``for all zero dimensional minimal systems ,'' or ``for all (not-necessarily-metrizable) minimal systems.'' By \cref{lemma_dt_and_ds_duals}, these follow immediately from \cref{lemma_may_assume_invertible} and \cref{thm:simple_equivalent_dcS,lemma_metrizability_doesnt_matter}, respectively. \item \dots \ (for sets of pointwise recurrence) ``all open $U \subseteq X$ with $x \in U$'' is changed to ``all open $U \subseteq X$ with $x \in \overline{U}$.'' This is a consequence of \cref{lemma_dt_and_ds_duals} and \cref{thm:simple_equivalent_dcS}. \item \dots \ sets are considered up to equivalence on thickly syndetic ($\mathcal{PS}^*$) sets. This is a consequence of \cref{cor:largest_family_satisfies_cap}: a set $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is dynamically (central) thick if and only if for all thickly syndetic $B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, the set $A \cap B$ is dynamically (central) thick. \end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: \eqref{item_all_translates_are_dt} \ Suppose $A \in d\mathcal{T}$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$. To see that $A - n \in d\mathcal{T}$, by \cref{lemma_dt_and_ds_duals}, it suffices to show that $A-n \in d\mathcal{S}^*$. Let $B \in d\mathcal{S}$. By \cref{lemma_translates_of_dsyndetic_sets}, the set $B + n \in d\mathcal{S}$. By \cref{lemma_intersection_of_ds_and_dt_is_infinite}, the set $A \cap (B+n)$ is infinite, so $(A-n) \cap B \supseteq (A-n) \cap (B+n - n) \neq \emptyset$, as desired. \eqref{item_some_translates_are_dct} \ In the language of the family algebra developed in \cref{sec_combinatorics}, this statement is equivalent to $d\mathcal{T} + dc\mathcal{T} \subseteq d\mathcal{T}$. Recall from \cref{lemma_translates_of_dsyndetic_sets} that $d\mathcal{S} \subseteq d\mathcal{S} + dc\mathcal{S}$. Taking the dual and simplifying using the algebra in \cref{lemma_fam_dual_sums}, we see that $d\mathcal{T} + dc\mathcal{T} \subseteq d\mathcal{T}$. \eqref{item_dcs_translates_of_dct_are_dct} \ This statement is equivalent to $dc\mathcal{T} + dc\mathcal{T} \subseteq dc\mathcal{T}$. Taking the dual of $dc\mathcal{S} \subseteq dc\mathcal{S} + dc\mathcal{S}$ from \cref{lemma_translates_of_dsyndetic_sets}, we see that $dc\mathcal{T} + dc\mathcal{T} \subseteq dc\mathcal{T}$. That \eqref{item_all_translates_are_dt} holds with $A-n$ replaced with $A+n$ follows the same argument used in \eqref{item_all_translates_are_dt}. That \eqref{item_some_translates_are_dct} and \eqref{item_dcs_translates_of_dct_are_dct} hold with $A-n$ replaced by $A+n$ requires different reasoning, since the set algebra explanation only treats negative translates. Suppose that $A$ is such that the set in \eqref{eqn_translates_of_dt_set} (with $A+n$ instead of $A-n$) is dynamically thick. We wish to show that $A$ is dynamically thick. It suffices by \cref{lemma_dt_and_ds_duals,lemma_may_assume_invertible} to show: for all minimal, invertible $(X,T)$, all $x \in X$, and all nonempty, open $U \subseteq X$, there exists $a \in A$ such that $T^a x \in U$. Thus, let $(X,T)$ be a minimal, invertible system, $x \in X$, and $U \subseteq X$ open and nonempty. Since the system $(X,T^{-1})$ is minimal (see, for example, \cite[Lemma 2.7]{glasscock_koutsogiannis_richter_2019}) and the set in \eqref{eqn_translates_of_dt_set} is dynamically thick, there exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $T^{-n} x \in U$ and $A + n \in dc\mathcal{T}$. By the definition of set of pointwise recurrence, there exists $m \in A+n$ (so $m > n$) such that $T^m T^{-n} x \in U$. We see that $m - n \in A$ and $T^{m-n} x \in U$, as desired. The argument that \eqref{item_dcs_translates_of_dct_are_dct} holds with $A-n$ replaced by $A+n$ is very similar and is left to the interested reader. Finally, that \eqref{eqn_relationship_between_dt_and_dct_classes} holds follows immediately from \eqref{item_all_translates_are_dt} and \eqref{item_some_translates_are_dct} for $A-n$ and $A+n$.

nodes.statement_short: Dualize Lemma 3.4 via family algebra for negative translates; for positive translates use the inverse map of an invertible minimal system.

nodes.name: (i): A - n meets every dS set B via B + n and Lemma 4.4
nodes.statement: \eqref{item_all_translates_are_dt} \ Suppose $A \in d\mathcal{T}$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$. To see that $A - n \in d\mathcal{T}$, by \cref{lemma_dt_and_ds_duals}, it suffices to show that $A-n \in d\mathcal{S}^*$. Let $B \in d\mathcal{S}$. By \cref{lemma_translates_of_dsyndetic_sets}, the set $B + n \in d\mathcal{S}$. By \cref{lemma_intersection_of_ds_and_dt_is_infinite}, the set $A \cap (B+n)$ is infinite, so $(A-n) \cap B \supseteq (A-n) \cap (B+n - n) \neq \emptyset$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: (i): A - n meets every dS set B via B + n and Lemma 4.4.
nodes.section: 4.1.2 Translates and dilates of dynamically thick sets

nodes.name: (ii): dualize dS ⊆ dS + dcS
nodes.statement: \eqref{item_some_translates_are_dct} \ In the language of the family algebra developed in \cref{sec_combinatorics}, this statement is equivalent to $d\mathcal{T} + dc\mathcal{T} \subseteq d\mathcal{T}$. Recall from \cref{lemma_translates_of_dsyndetic_sets} that $d\mathcal{S} \subseteq d\mathcal{S} + dc\mathcal{S}$. Taking the dual and simplifying using the algebra in \cref{lemma_fam_dual_sums}, we see that $d\mathcal{T} + dc\mathcal{T} \subseteq d\mathcal{T}$.
nodes.statement_short: (ii): dualize dS ⊆ dS + dcS.
nodes.section: 4.1.2 Translates and dilates of dynamically thick sets

nodes.name: (iii): dualize dcS ⊆ dcS + dcS
nodes.statement: \eqref{item_dcs_translates_of_dct_are_dct} \ This statement is equivalent to $dc\mathcal{T} + dc\mathcal{T} \subseteq dc\mathcal{T}$. Taking the dual of $dc\mathcal{S} \subseteq dc\mathcal{S} + dc\mathcal{S}$ from \cref{lemma_translates_of_dsyndetic_sets}, we see that $dc\mathcal{T} + dc\mathcal{T} \subseteq dc\mathcal{T}$.
nodes.statement_short: (iii): dualize dcS ⊆ dcS + dcS.
nodes.section: 4.1.2 Translates and dilates of dynamically thick sets

nodes.name: Positive translates need a different argument
nodes.statement: That \eqref{item_all_translates_are_dt} holds with $A-n$ replaced with $A+n$ follows the same argument used in \eqref{item_all_translates_are_dt}. That \eqref{item_some_translates_are_dct} and \eqref{item_dcs_translates_of_dct_are_dct} hold with $A-n$ replaced by $A+n$ requires different reasoning, since the set algebra explanation only treats negative translates.
nodes.statement_short: Positive translates need a different argument.
nodes.section: 4.1.2 Translates and dilates of dynamically thick sets

nodes.name: Positive translates via the inverse of an invertible minimal system
nodes.statement: Suppose that $A$ is such that the set in \eqref{eqn_translates_of_dt_set} (with $A+n$ instead of $A-n$) is dynamically thick. We wish to show that $A$ is dynamically thick. It suffices by \cref{lemma_dt_and_ds_duals,lemma_may_assume_invertible} to show: for all minimal, invertible $(X,T)$, all $x \in X$, and all nonempty, open $U \subseteq X$, there exists $a \in A$ such that $T^a x \in U$. Thus, let $(X,T)$ be a minimal, invertible system, $x \in X$, and $U \subseteq X$ open and nonempty. Since the system $(X,T^{-1})$ is minimal (see, for example, \cite[Lemma 2.7]{glasscock_koutsogiannis_richter_2019}) and the set in \eqref{eqn_translates_of_dt_set} is dynamically thick, there exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $T^{-n} x \in U$ and $A + n \in dc\mathcal{T}$. By the definition of set of pointwise recurrence, there exists $m \in A+n$ (so $m > n$) such that $T^m T^{-n} x \in U$. We see that $m - n \in A$ and $T^{m-n} x \in U$, as desired. The argument that \eqref{item_dcs_translates_of_dct_are_dct} holds with $A-n$ replaced by $A+n$ is very similar and is left to the interested reader.
nodes.statement_short: Positive translates via the inverse of an invertible minimal system.
nodes.section: 4.1.2 Translates and dilates of dynamically thick sets

nodes.name: The family identity follows
nodes.statement: Finally, that \eqref{eqn_relationship_between_dt_and_dct_classes} holds follows immediately from \eqref{item_all_translates_are_dt} and \eqref{item_some_translates_are_dct} for $A-n$ and $A+n$.
nodes.statement_short: The family identity follows.

nodes.name: Family-algebra form of the dynamically thick translate lemma
nodes.statement: As demonstrated in the proof of \cref{lemma_translates_of_dthick_sets}, it is interesting and useful to formulate the lemma's conclusions in terms of the family algebra developed in \cref{sec_combinatorics}. Thus, \begin{enumerate} \item the family $d\mathcal{T}$ is translation invariant, that is, $d\mathcal{T} \subseteq \{\mathbb{N}\} + d\mathcal{T}$; \item $d\mathcal{T} + dc\mathcal{T} \subseteq d\mathcal{T}$; \item $dc\mathcal{T} + dc\mathcal{T} \subseteq dc\mathcal{T}$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Combinatorial characterizations of dynamically thick sets
nodes.statement: Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. The following are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item The set $A$ is dynamically thick. \item For all $\mathbb{N} \supsetneq B \supseteq A$, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq \mathbb{N} \backslash B$ such that the set $B-F$ is thick. \item For all syndetic $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq A$ such that for all syndetic $S' \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, the set $F \cap (S - S')$ is nonempty. \item For all piecewise syndetic $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq A$ such that the set $S-F$ is thick. \item For all piecewise syndetic $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and all minimal left ideals $L \subseteq \beta \mathbb{N}$ with $\overline{S} \cap L \neq \emptyset$, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq A$ such that $L \subseteq \overline{S-F}$. \end{enumerate}

\eqref{item_dthick_def} $\iff$ \eqref{item:dyn_thick_idempotent} Because $d\mathcal{S}$ and $d\mathcal{T}$ are dual, the set $A$ is dynamically thick if and only if the set $A' \vcentcolon= \mathbb{N}  ackslash A$ is not dynamically syndetic. By \cref{mainthm_ds_equivalents}, the set $A'$ is not dynamically syndetic if and only if for all nonempty subsets $B' \subseteq A'$, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq B'$ such that the set $ igcap_{f \in F} (B' - f)$ is not syndetic. Taking the complement of this set in $\mathbb{N}$, we see that this happens if and only if the set \[  igcup_{f \in F}  ig( (\mathbb{N}  ackslash B') - f  ig) =  ig( \mathbb{N}  ackslash B'  ig) - F\] is thick. Set $B \vcentcolon= \mathbb{N}  ackslash B'$. Note that $B' \subseteq A'$ if and only if $A \subseteq B$ and that $B' 
eq \emptyset$ if and only if $B 
eq \mathbb{N}$. Summarizing the previous paragraph, we have shown that the set $A$ is dynamically thick if and only if for all $A \subseteq B \subsetneq \mathbb{N}$, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq \mathbb{N}  ackslash B$ such that the set $B - F$ is thick, as was to be shown. \eqref{item_dthick_def} $\implies$ \eqref{item:complement_psstar_dt_characterization_star_fixed} \ Suppose that $A \in d\mathcal{T}$. Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be piecewise syndetic and $L \subseteq  eta \mathbb{N}$ be a minimal left ideal such that $\overline{S} \cap L 
eq \emptyset$. Note that $\overline{S} \cap L$ is nonempty and open in $L$. By the definitional robustness of $d\mathcal{T}$ sets regarding non-metrizable systems (see \cref{sec_dy_thick_def_and_char}), for all $p \in L$, there exists $a \in A$ such that $a + p \in \overline{S}$. Therefore, \[L \subseteq  igcup_{a \in A} \overline{S - a}.\] Because $L$ is compact, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq A$ such that \[L \subseteq  igcup_{f \in F} \overline{S - f} \subseteq \overline{S-F},\] as was to be shown. \eqref{item:complement_psstar_dt_characterization_star_fixed} $\implies$ \eqref{item:complement_thick_dt_characterization_v2} \ Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a piecewise syndetic set. It follows by \cite[Thm. 4.40]{hindman_strauss_book_2012} that there exists a minimal left ideal $L \subseteq  eta \mathbb{N}$ such that $\overline{S} \cap L 
eq \emptyset$. Let $F \subseteq A$ be the finite set guaranteed by \eqref{item:complement_psstar_dt_characterization_star_fixed}. Since $\overline{S-F}$ contains a minimal left ideal, by \cite[Thm. 4.48]{hindman_strauss_book_2012}, the set $S-F$ is thick, as desired. \eqref{item:complement_thick_dt_characterization_v2} $\implies$ \eqref{item_condition_one} \ Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be syndetic. Let $F \subseteq A$ be the finite set guaranteed by \eqref{item:complement_thick_dt_characterization_v2}. Since $S-F$ is thick, for all $S' \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ syndetic, the set $S' \cap (S-F)$ is nonempty, whereby $F \cap (S-S') 
eq \emptyset$, as desired. \eqref{item_condition_one} $\implies$ \eqref{item_dthick_def} \ We will prove the contrapositive: if $A$ is not dynamically thick, then there exists a syndetic set $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that for all finite $F \subseteq A$, the set $S - F$ is not thick. Taking complements and considering $B$ as $\mathbb{N}  ackslash A$ and $C$ as $\mathbb{N}  ackslash S$, we must show: if a set $B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is dynamically syndetic, then there exists a set $C \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ that is not thick such that for all finite $F \subseteq \mathbb{N}  ackslash B$, the set $ igcap_{f \in F} (C - f)$ is syndetic. Suppose $B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is dynamically syndetic. If $B = \mathbb{N}$, put $C = \emptyset$ and note that the conclusion holds since the empty intersection is $\mathbb{N}$. Suppose $B 
eq \mathbb{N}$. By \cref{thm:simple_equivalent_dcS}, there exists a minimal system $(X,T)$, a point $x \in X$, and a nonempty, clopen set $U \subseteq X$ such that $R(x,U) \subseteq B$. Define $V \vcentcolon= X  ackslash U$ and $C \vcentcolon= \mathbb{N}  ackslash R(x,U) = R(x, V)$. Since $U 
eq X$ and the set $R(x,U)$ is syndetic, the set $C$ is nonempty but not thick. Let $F \subseteq \mathbb{N}  ackslash B$ be finite. Since $F \subseteq C$, we have that for all $f \in F$, the set $T^{-f}V$ is an open neighborhood of $x$. We see that \[ igcap_{f \in F} (C - f) = R igg( x,  igcap_{f \in F}T^{-f}V  igg),\] which is syndetic since the set $ igcap_{f \in F}T^{-f}V$ is an open neighborhood of $x$, as desired.

nodes.name: (i)⇔(ii): complement and apply Theorem A
nodes.statement: \eqref{item_dthick_def} $\iff$ \eqref{item:dyn_thick_idempotent} Because $d\mathcal{S}$ and $d\mathcal{T}$ are dual, the set $A$ is dynamically thick if and only if the set $A' \vcentcolon= \mathbb{N} \backslash A$ is not dynamically syndetic. By \cref{mainthm_ds_equivalents}, the set $A'$ is not dynamically syndetic if and only if for all nonempty subsets $B' \subseteq A'$, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq B'$ such that the set $\bigcap_{f \in F} (B' - f)$ is not syndetic. Taking the complement of this set in $\mathbb{N}$, we see that this happens if and only if the set \[ \bigcup_{f \in F} \big( (\mathbb{N} \backslash B') - f \big) = \big( \mathbb{N} \backslash B' \big) - F\] is thick. Set $B \vcentcolon= \mathbb{N} \backslash B'$. Note that $B' \subseteq A'$ if and only if $A \subseteq B$ and that $B' \neq \emptyset$ if and only if $B \neq \mathbb{N}$. Summarizing the previous paragraph, we have shown that the set $A$ is dynamically thick if and only if for all $A \subseteq B \subsetneq \mathbb{N}$, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq \mathbb{N} \backslash B$ such that the set $B - F$ is thick, as was to be shown.

nodes.statement: \eqref{item_dthick_def} $\implies$ \eqref{item:complement_psstar_dt_characterization_star_fixed} \ Suppose that $A \in d\mathcal{T}$. Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be piecewise syndetic and $L \subseteq \beta \mathbb{N}$ be a minimal left ideal such that $\overline{S} \cap L \neq \emptyset$. Note that $\overline{S} \cap L$ is nonempty and open in $L$. Therefore, \[L \subseteq \bigcup_{a \in A} \overline{S - a}.\] Because $L$ is compact, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq A$ such that \[L \subseteq \bigcup_{f \in F} \overline{S - f} \subseteq \overline{S-F},\] as was to be shown.

nodes.name: (iii)⇒(i) by contrapositive via a clopen return set
nodes.statement: \eqref{item_condition_one} $\implies$ \eqref{item_dthick_def} \ We will prove the contrapositive: if $A$ is not dynamically thick, then there exists a syndetic set $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that for all finite $F \subseteq A$, the set $S - F$ is not thick. Taking complements and considering $B$ as $\mathbb{N} \backslash A$ and $C$ as $\mathbb{N} \backslash S$, we must show: if a set $B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is dynamically syndetic, then there exists a set $C \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ that is not thick such that for all finite $F \subseteq \mathbb{N} \backslash B$, the set $\bigcap_{f \in F} (C - f)$ is syndetic. Suppose $B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is dynamically syndetic. If $B = \mathbb{N}$, put $C = \emptyset$ and note that the conclusion holds since the empty intersection is $\mathbb{N}$. Suppose $B \neq \mathbb{N}$. By \cref{thm:simple_equivalent_dcS}, there exists a minimal system $(X,T)$, a point $x \in X$, and a nonempty, clopen set $U \subseteq X$ such that $R(x,U) \subseteq B$. Define $V \vcentcolon= X \backslash U$ and $C \vcentcolon= \mathbb{N} \backslash R(x,U) = R(x, V)$. Since $U \neq X$ and the set $R(x,U)$ is syndetic, the set $C$ is nonempty but not thick. Let $F \subseteq \mathbb{N} \backslash B$ be finite. Since $F \subseteq C$, we have that for all $f \in F$, the set $T^{-f}V$ is an open neighborhood of $x$. We see that \[\bigcap_{f \in F} (C - f) = R\bigg( x, \bigcap_{f \in F}T^{-f}V \bigg),\] which is syndetic since the set $\bigcap_{f \in F}T^{-f}V$ is an open neighborhood of $x$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: (iii)⇒(i) by contrapositive via a clopen return set.

nodes.name: Combinatorial characterizations of sets of pointwise recurrence
nodes.statement: Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. The following are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item The set $A$ is a set of pointwise recurrence. \item For all $B \supseteq A$, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq \mathbb{N} \backslash B$ such that the set $B \cup \big( B-F \big)$ is thick. \item For all syndetic $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq A$ such that for all syndetic $S' \subseteq S$, the set $F \cap (S - S')$ is nonempty. \item For all syndetic $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and all thick $H \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, the piecewise syndetic set $P \vcentcolon= S \cap H$ satisfies the following. There exists a finite set $F \subseteq A$ such that for all syndetic $S' \subseteq S$, the piecewise syndetic set $P' \vcentcolon= S' \cap H$ is such that the set $P' \cap (P - F)$ is nonempty. \item For all piecewise syndetic $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and all minimal left ideals $L \subseteq \beta \mathbb{N}$ with $\overline{S} \cap L \neq \emptyset$, there exists a finite set $F \subseteq A$ such that $\overline{S} \cap L \subseteq \overline{S-F}$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: (iii)⇒(i) by contrapositive via a clopen return set
nodes.statement: \eqref{item_condition_one_dct} $\implies$ \eqref{item_dct_def_char} \ We will prove the contrapositive: if $A$ is not a set of pointwise recurrence, then there exists a syndetic set $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that for all finite $F \subseteq A$, there exists a syndetic set $S' \subseteq S$ such that $F \cap (S - S') = \emptyset$. Since $F \cap (S - S') = \emptyset$ if and only if $S' \cap (S - F) = \emptyset$, it is equivalent to show: there exists a syndetic set $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that for all finite $F \subseteq A$, the set $S \cap (\mathbb{N} \backslash (S-F))$ is syndetic. Taking complements and considering $B$ as $\mathbb{N} \backslash A$ and $C$ as $\mathbb{N} \backslash S$, we must show: if a set $B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is dynamically central syndetic, then there exists a set $C \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ that is not thick such that for all finite $F \subseteq \mathbb{N} \backslash B$, the set $(\mathbb{N} \backslash C) \cap \bigcap_{f \in F} (C - f)$ is syndetic. Suppose $B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is dynamically central syndetic. If $B = \mathbb{N}$, put $C = \emptyset$ and note that the conclusion holds since the empty intersection is $\mathbb{N}$. Suppose $B \neq \mathbb{N}$. By \cref{thm:simple_equivalent_dcS}, there exists a minimal system $(X,T)$, a point $x \in X$, and a clopen set $U \subseteq X$ with $x \in U$ such that $R(x,U) \subseteq B$. Define $V \vcentcolon= X \backslash U$ and $C \vcentcolon= \mathbb{N} \backslash R(x,U) = R(x, V)$. Since $U \neq X$ and the set $R(x,U)$ is syndetic, the set $C$ is nonempty but not thick. Let $F \subseteq \mathbb{N} \backslash B$ be finite. Since $F \subseteq C$, we have that for all $f \in F$, the set $T^{-f}V$ is an open neighborhood of $x$. We see that \[\big(\mathbb{N} \backslash C\big) \cap \bigcap_{f \in F} (C - f) = R\bigg( x, U \cap \bigcap_{f \in F}T^{-f}V \bigg),\] which is syndetic since the set $U \cap \bigcap_{f \in F}T^{-f}V$ is an open neighborhood of $x$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: (iii)⇒(i) by contrapositive via a clopen return set.

nodes.name: Dynamically thick sets from primes and thick sets
nodes.statement: Let $(p_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}} \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a sequence of distinct primes, $(c_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}} \subseteq \mathbb{Z}$, and $(H_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of thick sets. The set \[ A \vcentcolon= \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty \big ((p_i \mathbb{N} + c_i) \cap H_i \big) \] is dynamically thick. Moreover, if for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, we have that $c_n \not\equiv 0 \bmod {p_n}$ and, for all but finitely many distinct pairs $i, j$ of positive integers, the set $H_i \cap (H_j - n)$ is empty, then the set $A$ is not an $\mathcal{IP}$ set.

nodes.statement: We will apply \cref{lemma_our_fav_dy_thick} \eqref{item:dyn_thick_idempotent}. Let $\mathbb{N} \supsetneq B \supseteq A$. We want to show there exists a finite set $F \subseteq \mathbb{N} \backslash B$ such that $B - F$ is thick. Consider two cases. Case 1: There exists $i \in \mathbb{N}$ for which the set $\mathbb{N} \backslash B$ contains a complete residue system modulo $p_i$. Let $F = \{f_0, \ldots, f_{p_i - 1}\} \subseteq \mathbb{N} \backslash B$ be a complete system of modulo $p_i$ residues. We see that \[B - F \supseteq A - F \supseteq \big((p_i \mathbb{N} + c_i) \cap H_i \big) - F \supseteq \bigcap_{\ell = 0}^{p_i - 1} (H_i - f_{\ell}),\] which is thick, as desired. Case 2: For all $i \in \mathbb{N}$, the set $\mathbb{N} \backslash B$ avoids some modulo $p_i$ congruence class. In this case, for all $i \in \mathbb{N}$, there exists $a_i \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $B \supseteq p_i \mathbb{N} + a_i$. We will show that $B$ is thick. Indeed, let $k \in \mathbb{N}$. It suffices to show there exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $n + i \in p_i \mathbb{N} + a_i$ for all $1 \leqslant i \leqslant k$. This is equivalent to showing that there exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $n \equiv a_i - i \bmod p_i$ for $1 \leqslant i \leqslant k$. This is an immediate consequence of the Chinese Remainder Theorem since the $p_i$'s are distinct primes. To see that the set $A$ is not an $\mathcal{IP}$ set under the stipulated conditions, note that for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the set $A \cap (A-n)$ is contained in a finite union of sets of the form $(p \mathbb{N} + c ) \cap H$, where $c \not \equiv 0 \bmod p$ and $H$ is thick. If $A$ was an $\mathcal{IP}$ set, there would exist $n \in \mathbb{N}$ for which $A \cap (A-n)$ is an $\mathcal{IP}$ set. Since the family $\mathcal{IP}$ is partition regular, it would follow that a set of the form $(p \mathbb{N} + c ) \cap H$ is an $\mathcal{IP}$ set, which is clearly false.

nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem 4.7(ii): either the complement of B contains a full residue system mod some p_i, or B contains a progression mod every p_i and is thick by the Chinese Remainder Theorem.

nodes.name: Reduce to Theorem 4.7(ii) for supersets B
nodes.statement: We will apply \cref{lemma_our_fav_dy_thick} \eqref{item:dyn_thick_idempotent}. Let $\mathbb{N} \supsetneq B \supseteq A$. We want to show there exists a finite set $F \subseteq \mathbb{N} \backslash B$ such that $B - F$ is thick. Consider two cases.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to Theorem 4.7(ii) for supersets B.

nodes.name: Complement contains a complete residue system mod p_i
nodes.statement: Case 1: There exists $i \in \mathbb{N}$ for which the set $\mathbb{N} \backslash B$ contains a complete residue system modulo $p_i$. Let $F = \{f_0, \ldots, f_{p_i - 1}\} \subseteq \mathbb{N} \backslash B$ be a complete system of modulo $p_i$ residues. We see that \[B - F \supseteq A - F \supseteq \big((p_i \mathbb{N} + c_i) \cap H_i \big) - F \supseteq \bigcap_{\ell = 0}^{p_i - 1} (H_i - f_{\ell}),\] which is thick, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Complement contains a complete residue system mod p_i.

nodes.name: Otherwise B is thick by the Chinese Remainder Theorem
nodes.statement: Case 2: For all $i \in \mathbb{N}$, the set $\mathbb{N} \backslash B$ avoids some modulo $p_i$ congruence class. In this case, for all $i \in \mathbb{N}$, there exists $a_i \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $B \supseteq p_i \mathbb{N} + a_i$. We will show that $B$ is thick. Indeed, let $k \in \mathbb{N}$. This is an immediate consequence of the Chinese Remainder Theorem since the $p_i$'s are distinct primes.

nodes.name: KLMPR: a non-IP set of pointwise recurrence for distal systems
nodes.statement: Recently, the second author with Koutsogiannis, Moreira, Pavlov, and Richter \cite{Koutsogiannis_Le_Moreira_Pavlov_Richter_interpolation_sets} gave an example of a set of pointwise recurrence for distal systems which is not an $\mathcal{IP}$ set, answering a question of Host, Kra and Maass \cite[Question 3.11]{HostKraMaass2016}.

nodes.name: A dynamically thick set that is not IP
nodes.statement: Choosing the thick sets $H_i$ appropriately, the set $A \vcentcolon= \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty \big((p_i \mathbb{N} + 1) \cap H_i \big)$ is, according to \cref{rem:combinatorial_primes}, dynamically thick but not an $\mathcal{IP}$ set.

nodes.name: Why visit times of transitive points are dynamically thick
nodes.statement: \cref{rem:combinatorial_primes} can be used to explain why the set described in \eqref{ex_transitive_point_visit_times} at the beginning of \cref{sec_dy_thick_def_and_char} is dynamically thick. Indeed, let $x$ be a point with a dense orbit in the full shift $(\{0, 1\}^{\mathbb{N}},\sigma)$, and suppose $U \subseteq X$ contains the cylinder set of all of those words in $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$ beginning with some word $w$ of length $\ell$. We see that \[R(x,U) \supseteq \{n \in \mathbb{N} \ | \ w \text{ appears at the $n^{\text{th}}$ position in } x\}.\] Let $p > \ell$ be prime, and let $w_1$ be any word of length $p$ starting with $w$. Let $k \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $w_2 = w_1 w_1 \cdots w_1$ be the word consisting of $k$ copies of $w_1$. Since $x$ is transitive, the word $w_2$ must appear in $x$: there exists $N_k \in \mathbb{N}$ and $c_k \in \{0, \ldots, p-1\}$ such that $p \{N_k, N_k+1, \ldots, N_k+k - 1\} + c_k \subseteq R(x,U)$. Let $c \in \{0, \ldots, p-1\}$ be such that for infinitely many $k \in \mathbb{N}$, $c_k = c$. We see that there exists a thick set $H \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that $(p \mathbb{N} + c) \cap H \subseteq R(x,U)$. Since $p$ was an arbitrary prime greater than $\ell$, we see that the set $R(x,U)$ contains a set of the form in \cref{rem:combinatorial_primes} and hence is dynamically thick, as desired.

nodes.statement_short: Visit times of a transitive point of the full shift to a cylinder contain sets of the form in Lemma 4.9, hence are dynamically thick.
nodes.label: rmk_transitive_point_visit_times

nodes.name: Dynamically thick sets from residue classes and thick sets
nodes.statement: Let $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and $(H_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of thick subsets of $\mathbb{N}$. The set \[A \vcentcolon= \bigcup_{i=0}^{k-1} \big ((k \mathbb{N} + i) \cap H_i \big)\] is dynamically thick.
nodes.section: 4.2.1 Examples of dynamically thick sets via the combinatorial characterizations
assumptions: Let $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and $(H_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ be a sequence of thick subsets of $\mathbb{N}$.
conclusions: is dynamically thick.
nodes.label: ex:type2-special

nodes.statement: We will apply \cref{lemma_our_fav_dy_thick} \eqref{item:complement_thick_dt_characterization_v2}. Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be piecewise syndetic. Since piecewise syndeticity is partition regular and $S = \bigcup_{i=0}^{k-1} \big(S \cap (k\mathbb{N} - i)\big)$, there exists $i \in \{0, \ldots, k-1\}$ such that $S \cap (k \mathbb{N} - i)$ is piecewise syndetic. Since demonstrating \eqref{item:complement_thick_dt_characterization_v2} for a subset of $S+i$ suffices to demonstrate it for $S$, by replacing $S$ with $(S+i) \cap k\mathbb{N}$, we can proceed under the assumption that $S \subseteq k \mathbb{N}$. Write $S = B \cap C$ where $B$ is syndetic with gap lengths less than $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$ and $C$ is thick. For $i \in \{0, \ldots, k-1\}$, choose an interval $I_i$ of $H_i$ such that $|I_i| > \ell$ and $\max I_i < \min I_{i+1}$. The set \[ F \vcentcolon= \bigcup_{i=0}^{k-1} \big( (k\mathbb{N} + i) \cap I_i \big) \] is a finite subset of $A$. We will show that for all $M \in \mathbb{N}$, there is a finite subset $S' \subseteq S$ for which the set $S' - F$ contains an interval of length greater than $M$. It will follow that the set $S - F$ is thick. Let $M \in \mathbb{N}$. Choose $S' \subseteq S$ to be the set $S$ intersected with a long interval (whose length will be specified later) on which the distance between consecutive elements of $S$ is less than $\ell$. Since $\ell < |I_i|$ and $S' \subseteq k\mathbb{N}$, the set $S' - \big((k\mathbb{N} + i) \cap I_i \big)$ contains the set $(k \mathbb{N} - i) \cap J_i$, where \[ J_i \vcentcolon= \big\{\min S' - \max I_i, \ \ldots, \max S' - \min I_i \big\}. \] It follows that \[ S' - F \supseteq \bigcup_{i=0}^{k-1} \big((k \mathbb{N} - i) \cap J_i\big) \supseteq \bigcap_{i=0}^{k-1} J_i = \big\{\min S' - \max I_0, \ \ldots, \max S' - \min I_{k-1} \big\}, \] provided $\min S' - \max I_0 \leqslant \max S' - \min I_{k-1}$. This interval has length $\max S' - \min S' - (\min I_{k-1} - \max I_0)$ which is greater than $M$ if $\max S' - \min S' > M + \min I_{k-1} - \max I_0$.

nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem 4.7(iv): reduce to S ⊆ kN, pick long intervals in each H_i, and show S' - F contains arbitrarily long intervals.

nodes.name: Disjoint collection of minimal systems
nodes.statement: We call a collection of minimal systems $(X_i, T_i)$, $i \in I$, \emph{disjoint} if the product system $(\Pi_i X_i, \Pi_i T_i)$ is minimal.
nodes.section: 4.3.1 Dynamically thick sets from disjointness

nodes.name: Joining (as a subsystem)
nodes.statement: For our purposes below, a \emph{joining} of the systems $(X,T)$ and $(Y,S)$ is a subsystem $(Z \subseteq X \times Y, T \times S)$ of the product system for which $\pi_X Z = X$ and $\pi_Y Z = Y$.
nodes.section: 4.3.1 Dynamically thick sets from disjointness

nodes.name: Subsystems of products of minimal systems are joinings
nodes.statement: It is easy to see that if $(X,T)$ and $(Y,S)$ are both minimal, then every subsystem of $(X \times Y, T \times S)$ is a joining.
nodes.section: 4.3.1 Dynamically thick sets from disjointness

nodes.name: Bessel-type inequality for disjoint systems
nodes.statement: Let $(Z_i,R_i)$, $i \in \mathbb{N}$, be a disjoint collection of minimal systems. For all minimal $(X,T)$, all $\varepsilon > 0$, and all sufficiently large $i$ (depending on the $(Z_i,R_i)$'s, $(X,T)$, and $\varepsilon$), all joinings $(J,T \times R_i)$ of $(X,T)$ and $(Z_i,R_i)$ satisfy: for all $z \in Z_i$, the set $\pi_1(J \cap (X \times \{z\}))$ is $\varepsilon$-dense in $X$.
nodes.section: 4.3.1 Dynamically thick sets from disjointness
nodes.statement_short: A minimal system is nearly disjoint from all but finitely many members of a disjoint collection: fibres of joinings are ε-dense.
assumptions: Let $(Z_i,R_i)$, $i \in \mathbb{N}$, be a disjoint collection of minimal systems.
conclusions: all joinings $(J,T \times R_i)$ of $(X,T)$ and $(Z_i,R_i)$ satisfy: for all $z \in Z_i$, the set $\pi_1(J \cap (X \times \{z\}))$ is $\varepsilon$-dense in $X$.
nodes.label: thm_bessel

nodes.statement: Let $(X,T)$ be minimal and $\varepsilon > 0$. Suppose for a contradiction that there are infinitely many $i$'s for which there exists a joining $(J_i, T \times R_i)$ of $(X,T)$ and $(Z_i,R_i)$ and a point $y_i \in Z_i$ for which $\pi_1(J_i \cap (X \times \{y_i\}))$ is not $\varepsilon$ dense in $X$. To save on notation, by relabeling, we will ignore those $(Z_i,R_i)$'s which do not fall into this infinite set. By passing to minimal subsystems, we may assume without loss of generality that the joinings $(J_i, T \times R_i)$ are minimal. Since $J_i$ is closed, there exists an $\varepsilon$-ball $U_i \subseteq X$ and an open set $V_i \subseteq Z_i$ containing $y_i$ such that $J_i \cap (U_i \times V_i) = \emptyset$. Fix $x_0 \in X$. Since $(J_i,T \times R_i)$ is a joining of $(X,T)$ and $(Z_i,R_i)$ and is minimal, there exists $z_i \in Z_i$ such that $J_i = \overline{(T \times R_i)^{\mathbb{N}}(x_0,z_i)}$. Since $J_i \cap (U_i \times V_i) = \emptyset$, we have that \begin{align} R_{R_i}(z_i,V_i) \subseteq R_T(x_0, X \backslash U_i). \end{align} Let $c_1, c_2, \ldots, c_m \in X$ be an $\varepsilon/2$ dense subset of $X$. For $\ell \in \{1, \ldots, m\}$, define \[ E_\ell = \{i \in \mathbb{N} \ \big| \ B_{\varepsilon/2}(c_\ell) \subseteq U_i \}. \] Note that $\mathbb{N} = \bigcup_{\ell=1}^m E_\ell$. There exists $\ell \in \{1, \ldots, m\}$ for which $E_\ell$ is infinite. Put $U = B_{\varepsilon/2}(c_\ell)$. It follows now from \eqref{eqn_main_return-time_set_containment} that \begin{align} H \coloneqq \bigcup_{i \in E_\ell} R_{R_i}(z_i,V_i) \subseteq \bigcup_{i \in E_\ell} R_T(x_0, X \backslash U_i) \subseteq R_T(x_0, X \backslash U). \end{align} We will show that the set $H$ is thickly syndetic and, hence, thick. This will yield a contradiction since, by the minimality of $(X,T)$, the set $R_T(x_0, X \backslash U)$ cannot be thick. Let $k \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $e_1, \ldots, e_k \in E_\ell$. We see that \[\bigcap_{i=1}^k (H-i) \supseteq \bigcap_{i=1}^k R_{R_{e_i}}(R_{e_i}^{i}z_{e_i},V_{e_i}) = R_{R_{e_1} \times \cdots \times R_{e_k}}\big((R_{e_1}^1z_{e_1}, \ldots, R_{e_k}^{k}z_{e_k}),V_{e_1} \times \cdots \times V_{e_k}\big),\] which is syndetic by the minimality of the product system $(Z_{e_1} \times \cdots \times Z_{e_k},R_{e_1} \times \cdots \times R_{e_k})$. Therefore, intervals of length $k$ appear in $H$ syndetically. Since $k \in \mathbb{N}$ was arbitrary, this shows that the set $H$ is thickly syndetic, as desired.
nodes.section: 4.3.1 Dynamically thick sets from disjointness
nodes.statement_short: By contradiction: infinitely many bad joinings give return-time sets avoiding a fixed ball; their union is thickly syndetic by minimality of finite products, contradicting minimality of X.

nodes.name: Assume infinitely many bad minimal joinings with avoided product boxes
nodes.statement: Let $(X,T)$ be minimal and $\varepsilon > 0$. Suppose for a contradiction that there are infinitely many $i$'s for which there exists a joining $(J_i, T \times R_i)$ of $(X,T)$ and $(Z_i,R_i)$ and a point $y_i \in Z_i$ for which $\pi_1(J_i \cap (X \times \{y_i\}))$ is not $\varepsilon$ dense in $X$. nodes.name: Return times of z_i to V_i avoid U_i along the orbit of x_0

nodes.name: Uniform syndeticity of returns for disjoint collections
nodes.statement: Let $(X_i,T_i)$, $i \in \mathbb{N}$, be a disjoint collection of minimal systems. For all minimal systems $(Y,S)$ and all nonempty, open $V \subseteq Y$, there exists $i \in \mathbb{N}$ such that the following holds. For all nonempty, open $U \subseteq X_i$, there exists $s \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $(x,y) \in X_i \times Y$, the set $R_{T_i \times S}((x,y), U \times V) = R_{T_i}(x,U) \cap R_S(y,V)$ is syndetic with gap size bounded by $s$.

assumptions: Let $(X_i,T_i)$, $i \in \mathbb{N}$, be a disjoint collection of minimal systems.
conclusions: the set $R_{T_i \times S}((x,y), U \times V) = R_{T_i}(x,U) \cap R_S(y,V)$ is syndetic with gap size bounded by $s$.
nodes.label: thm_quantitative_strengthening_of_type_1_example

nodes.statement: Let $(Y,S)$ be minimal and $V \subseteq Y$ be nonempty and open. Let $\varepsilon > 0$ be such that $V$ contains an $\varepsilon$-ball. According to \cref{thm_bessel}, there exists $i \in \mathbb{N}$ such that all joinings $(J,T_i \times S)$ of $(X_i,T_i)$ and $(Y,S)$ satisfy: for all $x \in X_i$, the set $\pi_2(J \cap (\{x\} \times Y))$ is $\varepsilon$-dense in $Y$. Let $U \subseteq X$ be nonempty and open. We claim that for all $(x,y) \in X_i \times Y$, there exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $(T_i \times S)^n (x,y) \in U \times V$. Indeed, let $(x,y) \in X_i \times Y$. By a theorem of Auslander \cite{auslander_1960} and Ellis \cite{ellis_1957}, the point $(x,y)$ is proximal to a point $(x_0,y_0) \in X_i \times Y$ that is uniformly recurrent under $T_i \times S$. Since $J \vcentcolon= \overline{(T_i \times S)^{\mathbb{N}_0}(x_0,y_0)}$ is a (minimal) joining of $(X_i,T_i)$ and $(Y,S)$, it is $\varepsilon$-dense in every fiber over $X_i$. Since $V$ contains an $\varepsilon$-ball, we see that $J \cap (U \times V) \neq \emptyset$. Because $(x,y)$ is proximal to $(x_0,y_0)$ and $R_{T_i \times S}((x_0,y_0), U \times V)$ is syndetic, we see that $R_{T_i \times S}((x,y),U \times V)$ is piecewise syndetic, hence nonempty. We have shown that for all $(x,y) \in X_i \times Y$, there exists $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $(T_i \times S)^n (x,y) \in U \times V$. It follows that $\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty (T_i \times S)^{-n} (U \times V) = X_i \times Y$. By compactness, there exists $s \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $\bigcup_{n=1}^s (T_i \times S)^{-n} (U \times V) = X_i \times Y$. It follows that for all $(x,y) \in X_i \times Y$, there exists $n \in \{1, \ldots, s\}$ such that $(T_i \times S)^n(x,y) \in U \times V$, whereby for all $(x,y) \in X_i \times Y$, the set $R_{T_i \times S}((x,y), U\times V)$ is syndetic with gap size bounded by $s$, as was to be shown.

nodes.statement: To see that $A \in d\mathcal{T}$, we must show that for all minimal $(Y,S)$, all nonempty, open $V \subseteq Y$, and all $y \in Y$, the set $A \cap R_S(y,V)$ is nonempty. This follows immediately from \cref{thm_quantitative_strengthening_of_type_1_example}.

nodes.name: Orbits along piecewise syndetic sets are somewhere dense
nodes.statement: Let $(X,T)$ be a minimal system and $x \in X$. For all piecewise syndetic sets $P \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, the set $T^P x$ is somewhere dense, ie., $(\overline{T^P x})^\circ \neq \emptyset$.

assumptions: Let $(X,T)$ be a minimal system and $x \in X$.
conclusions: the set $T^P x$ is somewhere dense, ie., $(\overline{T^P x})^\circ \neq \emptyset$.

nodes.statement: Since the set $P$ is piecewise syndetic, there exists $k \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $H \vcentcolon= \bigcup_{i=1}^k (P-i)$ is thick. Since $(X,T)$ is minimal, the set $T^H x$ is dense. We see that \[X = \overline{\bigcup_{i=1}^k T^{-i} T^{P}x} = \bigcup_{i=1}^k T^{-i} \overline{T^{P}x}.\] By the Baire Category Theorem, there exits $i \in \{1, \ldots, k\}$ such that the set $T^{-i} \overline{T^{P}x}$ has nonempty interior. By semiopenness of minimal maps \cite[Thm 2.4]{kolyada_snoha_trofimchuk_2001}, applying $i$ many times the map $T$, the set $\overline{T^{P}x}$ has nonempty interior, as desired.

nodes.statement_short: Finitely many translates of P form a thick set, so finitely many preimages of the closure of T^P x cover X; apply Baire category and semiopenness.

nodes.name: Finitely many preimages of the orbit closure along P cover X
nodes.statement: Since the set $P$ is piecewise syndetic, there exists $k \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $H \vcentcolon= \bigcup_{i=1}^k (P-i)$ is thick. nodes.name: Dynamically thick sets from distal points
nodes.statement: Let $(X, T)$ be a minimal system and $U_1, U_2, \ldots$ be nonempty, open subsets of $X$. Let $x \in X$ be a distal point and $H_1, H_2, \ldots \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be thick sets. The set \[ A \vcentcolon= \bigcup_i \big(R(x,U_i) \cap H_i \big) \] is dynamically thick if and only if the set $\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty U_i$ is dense in $X$.
nodes.section: 4.3.2 Dynamically thick sets from distal points
assumptions: Let $(X, T)$ be a minimal system and $U_1, U_2, \ldots$ be nonempty, open subsets of $X$.
Let $x \in X$ be a distal point and $H_1, H_2, \ldots \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be thick sets.
conclusions: is dynamically thick if and only if the set $\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty U_i$ is dense in $X$.

the set $\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty U_i$ is dense in $X$

nodes.statement: If the set $\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty U_i$ is not dense in $X$, then it is disjoint from a nonempty, open set $V \subseteq X$. The set $A$ is clearly disjoint from the set $R(x,V)$, whereby $A$ is not dynamically thick. Suppose that $\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty U_i$ is dense. Let $(Y,S)$ be a minimal system, $y \in Y$, and $V \subseteq Y$ be nonempty and open. Since the set $R_S(y,V)$ is syndetic, by \cref{lemma_orbit_along_ps_is_somewhere_dense}, the set $T^{R_S(y,V)} x$ is somewhere dense. Therefore, there exists $i \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $T^{R_S(y,V)} x \cap U_i \neq \emptyset$. It follows that the set $R_{T \times S} ((x,y), U_i \times V)$ is nonempty. Since $x$ is a distal point, by \cite[Thm. 9.11]{furstenberg_book_1981}, the point $(x,y)$ is uniformly recurrent under $T \times S$. Since $U_i \times V$ is open, we have that $R_{T \times S} ((x,y), U_i \times V)$ is (dynamically) syndetic. Therefore, the set $R_{T \times S} ((x,y), U_i \times V) \cap H_i$ is nonempty, which implies that $A \cap R_S(y,V)$ is nonempty, as desired.
nodes.section: 4.3.2 Dynamically thick sets from distal points
nodes.statement_short: Non-density gives a disjoint return set; density plus Lemma 4.15 and Furstenberg's distal-point theorem give syndetic product returns meeting each H_i.

nodes.name: Robustly syndetic collection
nodes.statement: A collection $\mathscr{C}$ of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ is \emph{robustly syndetic} if for all dynamically syndetic sets $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, there exists $B \in \mathscr{C}$ such that $A \cap B$ is syndetic.
nodes.section: 4.3.3 A general form for dynamically thick sets: a proof of F
also_stated_at: A collection $\mathscr{C}$ of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$ is \emph{robustly syndetic} if for all dynamically syndetic sets $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, there exists $B \in \mathscr{C}$ such that the set $A \cap B$ is syndetic.
nodes.label: def_robust_syndetic

nodes.statement: Suppose that $\mathscr{C}$ is robustly syndetic and that, for each $B \in \mathscr{C}$, the set $H_B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ is thick such that \eqref{eqn_A_contains_family_cap_thick} holds. To see that $A \in d\mathcal{T}$, let $C \in d\mathcal{S}$. There exists $B \in \mathscr{C}$ such that $B \cap C$ is syndetic. Thus, the set $B \cap C \cap H_B$ is nonempty, whereby $A \cap C \neq \emptyset$, as desired. Conversely, suppose that $A$ is dynamically thick. For all $S \in d\mathcal{S}$, we will define a thick set $G_S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ and a set $B_S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ in such a way that the collection $\mathscr{C} \vcentcolon= \{ B_S \ | \ S \in d\mathcal{S}\}$ is robustly syndetic and \[A \supseteq \bigcup_{S \in d\mathcal{S}} \big( B_S \cap G_S \big).\] This suffices to reach the conclusion: the collection $\mathscr{C} \cup \{A\}$ is robustly syndetic, and setting $H_A \vcentcolon= \mathbb{N}$ and, for $B = B_S \in \mathscr{C}$, setting $H_B \vcentcolon= G_{S}$, we see that equality in \eqref{eqn_A_contains_family_cap_thick} holds. Let $S \in d\mathcal{S}$. The set $A \cap S$ is an intersection of a dynamically thick set and a dynamically syndetic set and, hence, by \cref{thm_dcps_and_dps_are_ps}, is piecewise syndetic. There exist $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$ and finite, disjoint intervals $I_1$, $I_2$, \dots of consecutive positive integers satisfying: a) $\lim_{i \to \infty} |I_i| \to \infty$ and, for all $i \in \mathbb{N}$, b) $\max I_i + i< \min I_{i+1}$; and c) the set $A \cap S$ has nonempty intersection with all subintervals of $I_i$ of length at least $\ell$. Define $G_S \vcentcolon= \bigcup_{i=1}^\infty I_i$, and note that it is thick. Define \begin{align} B_S \vcentcolon= (A \cap G_S) \cup (\mathbb{N} \backslash G_S). \end{align} Since the set $\mathbb{N} \backslash G_S$ is a disjoint union of finite intervals whose lengths tend to infinity, the set \begin{align} B_S \cap S = (A \cap G_S \cap S) \cup \big((\mathbb{N} \backslash G_S) \cap S \big) \text{ is syndetic.} \end{align} Indeed, the set $S$ has nonempty intersection with any interval of length $\ell' \in \mathbb{N}$. Therefore, on $G_S$, the set $B_S \cap S$ has nonempty intersection with any interval of length at least $\ell$, while on $\mathbb{N} \backslash G_S$, the set $B_S \cap S$ has nonempty intersection with any interval of length $\ell'$. Now \eqref{eq:B_ScapS} shows that the collection $\mathscr{C} \vcentcolon= \{B_S \ | \ S \in d\mathcal{S}\}$ is robustly syndetic, and \eqref{eq:B_S} shows that $A \supseteq \bigcup_{S \in d\mathcal{S}} (B_S \cap G_S)$, as desired.

nodes.name: Interleaving partition technique
nodes.statement: Let $\mathscr{F}$ be a family of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$, and suppose we wish to show that for all $A \in \mathscr{F}$, there exists a disjoint union $A = A_1 \cup A_2$ such that $A_1, A_2 \in \mathscr{F}$. Let $N_1 < N_2 < \cdots$ be a rapidly increasing sequence of positive integers. Assign the set $A \cap [N_1]$ to $A_1$, the set $A \cap ([N_2] \backslash [N_1])$ to $A_2$, the set $A \cap ([N_3] \backslash [N_2])$ to $A_1$, and so forth. If the family $\mathscr{F}$ is ``suitable'' and the $N_i$'s are chosen appropriately, the sets $A_1$ and $A_2$ will both belong to $\mathscr{F}$.

nodes.name: Syndetic sets form a σ-compact family
nodes.statement: For $N \in \mathbb{N}$, denote by $\mathcal{S}_N$ the family of sets that have nonempty intersection with every interval in $\mathbb{N}$ of length $N$. The family $\mathcal{S}_N$ is compact. Indeed, given $B \in \mathcal{S}_N^*$, the set $B$ is thick. If $M \in \mathbb{N}$ is large so that $B \cap [M]$ contains an interval of length at least $N$, then $B \cap [M] \in \mathcal{S}_N^*$. We see that the family of syndetic sets, $\mathcal{S}$, is equal to $\bigcup_{N=1}^\infty \mathcal{S}_N$, whereby it is $\sigma$-compact.

nodes.name: IP_N families and IP_0
nodes.statement: Let $N \in \mathbb{N}$. Denote by $\mathcal{IP}_N$ the upward closure of the collection of sets of the form \[\text{FS}(x_i)_{i=1}^N \vcentcolon= \left\{ \sum_{f \in F} x_f \ \middle | \ \emptyset \neq F \subseteq \{1, \ldots, N\} \right\}, \quad x_1, \ldots, x_N \in \mathbb{N}.\] As in the previous example, the family $\mathcal{IP}_N^*$ is easily seen from the definition to be compact. The dual of the family $\mathcal{IP}_0 \vcentcolon= \bigcap_{N = 1}^\infty \mathcal{IP}_N$ is $\sigma$-compact, since $\mathcal{IP}_0^* = \bigcup_{N=1}^\infty \mathcal{IP}_N^*$. The family $\mathcal{IP}_0^*$ is important in quantitative strengthenings of recurrence theorems and appears again in this paper in \cref{sec_open_quests_dps_sets}.

nodes.name: Return times of minimal systems form a σ-compact family
nodes.statement: The family of sets of return times in minimal systems is $\sigma$-compact. More precisely, let $\mathscr{F}$ be the upward closure of collection of sets of the form \begin{equation} \big\{n \in \mathbb{N} \ \big| \ U \cap T^{-n} U \neq \emptyset \big\}, \end{equation} where $(X, T)$ is a minimal system and $U \subseteq X$ is a nonempty, open set. The family $\mathscr{F}$ is $\sigma$-compact, as shown in \cite[Prop. 5.8]{boshernitzan_glasner_2009}. The argument is short, so we give it here. It is a fact \cite[Thm. 2.4]{bergelson_mccutcheon_1998} that $A \in \mathscr{F}$ if and only if there exists a syndetic set $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ such that $A \supseteq S-S$. Thus, using the notation from \eqref{ex_syndetic_is_sigma_compact}, if for $N \in \mathbb{N}$ we define \[\mathscr{F}_N \vcentcolon= \uparrow \big\{ S - S \ \big| \ S \in \mathcal{S}_N \big\},\] we have that $\mathscr{F} = \bigcup_{N=1}^{\infty} \mathscr{F}_N$. We have only to show that for all $N \in \mathbb{N}$, the family $\mathscr{F}_N$ is compact. Let $N \in \mathbb{N}$ and $B \in \mathscr{F}_N^*$. We must show that there exists $M \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for all $A \in \mathscr{F}_N$, the set $A \cap B \cap [M]$ is nonempty. Assume for the sake of a contradiction that no such $M$ exists. Thus, for all $M \in \mathbb{N}$, there exists $S_M \in \mathcal{S}_N$ such that \begin{align} (S_M - S_M) \cap B \cap [M] = \emptyset. \end{align} Since $\mathcal{S}_N$ is compact, passing to a subsequence of $(S_M)_{M \in \mathbb{N}}$, there exists $S \in \mathcal{S}_N$ such that $\lim_{M \to \infty} 1_{S_M} = 1_S$. Since $S \in \mathcal{S}_N$, the set $S-S$ is a member of $\mathscr{F}_N$. It follows from \eqref{eqn_sm_limit} that $(S-S) \cap B = \emptyset$, contradicting the fact that $B \in \mathscr{F}_N^*$.

nodes.name: Measurable return times form a σ-compact family
nodes.statement: In analogy to \cref{example:set-topological-partition}, the family of sets of return times in measure preserving systems is $\sigma$-compact. More precisely, the upward closure $\mathscr{F}$ of the collection of sets of the form \begin{equation} R(E,E) \vcentcolon= \big\{n \in \mathbb{N} \ \big| \ \mu(E \cap T^{-n} E) > 0 \big\}, \end{equation} where $(X, \mu, T)$ is a measure preserving system (see \cref{sec_dcps_and_set_recurrence}) and $E \subseteq X$ is a set of positive measure, is $\sigma$-compact. This is most readily seen as a consequence of a result of Forrest \cite{Forrest_recurrence-in-dynamical-systems}: for all sets $B \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ of single measurable recurrence (i.e. for all $B \in \mathscr{F}^*$) and all $\delta > 0$, there exists $M \in \mathbb{N}$ such that for all sets $E$ with measure at least $\delta$, the set $B \cap R(E,E) \cap [M]$ is nonempty. For $N \in \mathbb{N}$, defining \[ \mathscr{F}_N \vcentcolon= \uparrow \big\{R(E,E) \subseteq \mathbb{N} \ \big| \ \text{$(X,\mu,T)$ is a measure preserving system, $E \subseteq X$, $\mu(E) > 1/N$} \big\}, \] we see that $\mathscr{F}_N$ is compact and $\mathscr{F} = \bigcup_{N =1}^\infty \mathscr{F}_N$ is $\sigma$-compact.
